.
.
Continuum
.

Figure 1:
Spectrum for a single, massive scalar
field. The two particle states form a continuum
above and including
-(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=4m^{2}
hyperboloid.

Note:
If there are “internal symmetries” (i.e.
non-space-time symmetries), then it is conceivable that the
zero eigenvalue of
P^{\mu}
is degenerate, and carries some
representation of the internal symmetry group (usually compact).
Every one of these states must still be singlets of the Poincare
group. But now, these vacua themselves carry some quantum
numbers and quantum fields acting on these will create single
particle states labeled by tensor product of representations of
the internal symmetry group. This is not done and one stipulates
the vacuum to be a singlet under
all symmetries
.

Note:
We have taken the stable particles to have a
non-zero mass. This is a statement about the spectrum of
P^{2}

in the full, exact interacting quantum field theory and not at
some approximation of it. This would seem to exclude the
massless representations of the Poincare group for interacting
quantum fields. In practice i.e. in perturbation theory we will
use massless photons and see the accompanying infrared problems.

3.

•

An interacting field operator, denoted schematically by

\Phi(x)
satisfies an operator equation of the form,

(\Box-m_{0}^{2})\Phi(x)=J(x)
where
J(x)
is an
operator built out of
\Phi
and possibly other field
operators. We re-write the field equation as
(\Box-m^{2})\Phi(x)=J(x)-(m^{2}-m_{0}^{2})\Phi(x)=:\tilde{J}(x)

•

The field obeys the equal time (anti-)commutation
relations:

\left[\Phi(t,\vec{x}),\Phi(t,\vec{y})\right]=0=\left[\Pi(t,\vec{x}),\Pi(t,\vec{y})\right]~,~\left[\Phi(t,\vec{x}),\Pi(t,\vec{y})\right]=i\delta^{3}(\vec{x}-\vec{y})\ .

If
J(x)
has no derivatives of fields, the momentum
field is
\Pi(t,\vec{x})=\dot{\Phi}(t,\vec{x})
. This
stipulates the quantized nature of the field while the
equation of motion stipulates the nature of interaction.

•

\exists
another set of fields, quantized
\Phi_{in}(x),\Phi_{out}(x)
, build out of the interacting field

\Phi(x)
, and satisfying the same set of equal time
(anti-)commutation relations but obeying free field
equations:
(\Box-m^{2})\Phi_{in/out}=0
where
m
is
the “physical” mass.

The in and out fields thus have the same mode
decomposition introducing the creation/annihilation
operators which create/destroy stable particles with
physical mass
m
. These fields also transform the same
way as the field
\Phi(x)
under the symmetries, in
particular,
\Phi_{in}(x+a)=e^{ia\cdot P}\Phi_{in}(x)e^{-ia\cdot P}
.

4.

Asymptotic conditions:
The exact interacting quantum
field
\Phi(x)
is linked to the in and out fields by the
asymptotic conditions,

\boxed{\left.\Phi(x)\right|_{t\to-\infty}~\longrightarrow\sqrt{Z}\Phi_{in}(x)~~,~~\left.\Phi(x)\right|_{t\to\infty}~\longrightarrow\sqrt{Z}\Phi_{out}(x)}

Here
Z
is a possible normalization constant which we will show
to be necessarily different from 1.

Note:
The asymptotic conditions are
not
operator
equations but are
weak
equations i.e. hold for arbitrary matrix
elements in the basis of normalized states.

Below we elaborate the conditions and note a number of properties.

Asymptotic conditions are consistent with Poincare covariance:
A
formal solution of the equation satisfied by
\Phi(x)
is given by,

\Phi(x)~=~\int d^{4}y\ G_{ret}(x-y,m)\tilde{J}(y)+\sqrt{Z}\Phi_{in}(x).

(10.6)

As
t\to-\infty
, the first term vanishes (property of retarded Green
function) recovering the asymptotic condition. This is a heuristic
argument since
J(y)
it built out of
\Phi(x)
and some iterative
procedure is implicit. The consistency with covariance is seen as,

\displaystyle\sqrt{Z}\Phi_{in}(x-a)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Phi(x-a)-\int d^{4}y\ G_{ret}(x-a-y,m)\tilde{J}(y)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{-ia\cdot P}\Phi(x)e^{ia\cdot P}-\int d^{4}y\ G_{ret}(x-y,m)\tilde{J}(y-a)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{-ia\cdot P}\left[\Phi(x)-\int d^{4}y\ G_{ret}(x-y,m)\tilde{J}(y)\right]e^{ia\cdot P}~=~\sqrt{Z}e^{-ia\cdot P}\Phi_{in}(x)e^{ia\cdot P}\ .

Note:
Only the
G_{ret}
is used in the formal solution and
not
G_{Feynman}
.

\Phi_{in}(x)
creates states with physical mass
m
:
The
infinitesimal form of the transformation law for
\Phi_{in}(x)
implies,

[P^{\mu},\Phi_{in}(x)]=-i\partial^{\mu}\Phi_{in}(x)
and we also
have the equation of motion
(\Box-m^{2})\Phi_{in}=0
.

For any physical state
|k,\alpha\rangle,P^{\mu}|k,\alpha\rangle=k^{\mu}|k,\alpha\rangle
. Therefore,

\displaystyle-i\partial^{\mu}\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle k,\alpha|[P^{\mu},\Phi_{in}(x)]|k,\alpha\rangle=k^{\mu}\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle

\displaystyle\therefore-\Box\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle k^{2}\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle

\displaystyle\therefore(-\Box+m^{2})\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=0=

\displaystyle(k^{2}+m^{2})\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle~\Rightarrow~k^{2}=-m^{2}\ .

Thus,
\Phi_{in}(x)
behaves exactly like a free field producing
physical states from the vacuum and we can be taken to have the usual
mode decomposition,

\displaystyle\Phi_{in}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\left[a_{in}(\vec{k})e^{ik\cdot x}+a_{in}^{\dagger}(\vec{k})e^{-ik\cdot x}\right]

\displaystyle\partial_{0}\Phi_{in}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\left[-i\omega_{\vec{k}}a_{in}(\vec{k})e^{ik\cdot x}+i\omega_{\vec{k}}a_{in}^{\dagger}e^{-ik\cdot x}\right]~~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle a_{in}^{\dagger}(\vec{k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{-i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}x\ e^{ik\cdot x}\ \overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\ \Phi_{in}(x)~~,~~f\overleftrightarrow{\partial}g:=f\partial g-\partial(f)g\ .

(10.7)

\displaystyle\mbox{And,~}a_{in}(\vec{k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}x\ e^{-ik\cdot x}\ \overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\ \Phi_{in}(x)

Note:
In writing the inversion formula, we have done the
spatial integration over a
t=
constant hypersurface
\Sigma_{t}
. The
choice of this hypersurface does not matter (
a_{in}^{\dagger}(\vec{k})

is independent of
t
).
This is kept implicit in all the inversion
formulae below.

It follows immediately,
\langle 0|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle=0
and,

\displaystyle\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle k,\alpha|e^{-ix\cdot P}\Phi_{in}(0)e^{ix\cdot P}|0\rangle~=~e^{-ik\cdot x}\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(0)|0\rangle

\displaystyle\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(0)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{2}}}~\Rightarrow~\boxed{\langle k,\alpha|\Phi_{in}(x)|0\rangle=\frac{e^{-ik\cdot x}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}.}

Suffice it to say that corresponding expressions exist for
\phi_{out}
.
In particular the heuristic expression take the form,

\Phi(x)=\sqrt{Z}\Phi_{out}(x)+\int d^{4}y\ G_{adv}(x-y,m^{2})\tilde{J}(y).

How far can we get with Lorentz covariance and the assumptions on
the spectrum?

10.3
Kallen-Lehmann Representation

Consider the vacuum expectation values of the commutator of interacting
field,
i\Delta^{\prime}(x,x^{\prime}):=\langle 0|[\Phi(x),\Phi(x^{\prime})]0\rangle
. We had
evaluated this for the free fields while considering the
spin-statistics,
\sim\Delta_{+}(x-x^{\prime})
. We evaluate it as,

\displaystyle i\Delta(x,x^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{n}\langle 0|\Phi(x)|n\rangle\langle n|\Phi(x^{\prime})|0\rangle-(x\leftrightarrow x^{\prime}),

(10.8)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{n}\langle 0|\Phi(0)e^{ix\cdot P}|n\rangle\langle n|e^{-ix^{\prime}\cdot P}\Phi(0)|0\rangle-(x\leftrightarrow x^{\prime}),

(10.9)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{n}|\langle 0|\Phi(0)|n\rangle|^{2}\left(e^{i(x-x^{\prime})\cdot k_{n}}-e^{-i(x-x^{\prime})\cdot k_{n}}\right)~~~\mbox{a function of
$(x-x^{\prime})$.}~~~~

(10.10)

The states
|n\rangle
contain the vacuum, the single particle states on
the isolated hyperboloid
k_{n}^{2}=-m^{2}
as well as the multi-particles
continuum. To collect terms with the same total
k^{\mu}_{n}
, insert
1=\int d^{4}q\delta^{4}(q-k_{n})
and write,

\displaystyle\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{i}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}q\left[(2\pi)^{3}\sum_{n}\delta^{4}(q-k_{n})|\langle 0|\Phi(0)|n\rangle|^{2}\left(e^{i(x-x^{\prime})\cdot k_{n}}-e^{-i(x-x^{\prime})\cdot k_{n}}\right)\right]

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle-\frac{i}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}q\left(e^{i(x-x^{\prime})\cdot q}-e^{-i(x-x^{\prime})\cdot q}\right)\rho(q)~~~~\mbox{where, }

\displaystyle\rho(q)

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\left[(2\pi)^{3}\sum_{n}\delta^{4}(q-k_{n})|\langle 0|\Phi(0)|n\rangle|^{2}\right]~~~\mbox{(the spectral density).}

Claim:
The spectral density is a scalar function of
q^{2}
.

Proof:
Under a Lorentz transformation,
U(\Lambda)
, we have

U(\Lambda)|0\rangle=|0\rangle
and
U(\Lambda)\Phi(0)U^{-1}(\Lambda)=\Phi(\Lambda 0)=\Phi(0)
. Hence,

\rho(q)=(2\pi)^{3}\sum_{n}\delta^{4}(q-k_{n})|\langle 0|\Phi(0)U(\Lambda)|n\rangle|^{2}\ .

Next,

\displaystyle\delta^{4}(k)

\displaystyle\sim

\displaystyle\int d^{4}xe^{ik\cdot x}=\int d^{4}(\Lambda x)e^{ik\cdot(\Lambda x)}=\int d^{4}xe^{i(\Lambda^{-1}k)\cdot x}\sim\delta^{4}(\Lambda^{-1}k)\ .

\displaystyle\therefore\rho(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(2\pi)^{3}\sum_{n}\delta^{4}(\Lambda^{-1}(q-k_{n}))|\langle 0|\Phi(0)U^{-1}(\Lambda)|n\rangle|^{2}\ .

Let
U(\Lambda)|n\rangle=|m\rangle
. Then
U^{-1}(\Lambda)P^{\mu}U(\Lambda)=\Lambda^{\mu}_{~\nu}P^{\nu}
. Acting on
|n\rangle

implies,
P^{\mu}|m\rangle=k^{\mu}_{m}|m\rangle
and we already had

P^{\mu}|n\rangle=k^{\mu}_{n}|n\rangle
. This in turn implies,

k^{\mu}_{m}U^{-1}(\Lambda)|m\rangle=\Lambda^{\mu}_{~\nu}k^{\nu}_{n}|n\rangle
or,
k^{\mu}_{m}=\Lambda^{\mu}_{~\nu}k^{\nu}_{n}
. Lowering
the Lorentz index gives,
(k_{m})_{\mu}=(k_{n})_{\nu}(\Lambda^{-1})^{\nu}_{~\mu}
. Replacing the sum over
n
by that over

m
gives,

\rho(q)=(2\pi)^{3}\sum_{m}\delta^{4}(k_{m}-\Lambda^{-1}q)|\langle 0|\Phi(0)|m\rangle|^{2}=\rho(\Lambda^{-1}q)\ .

Thus,
\rho(q)
can only depend on
q
through
q^{2}
.

Since the physical spectrum has
q^{2}<0
with
q^{0}>0
, we write

\rho(q):=\theta(q^{0})\rho(q^{2}),\ \rho(q^{2})=0~\mathrm{for}~q^{2}>0
. Substituting in
\Delta^{\prime}
gives,

\displaystyle\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{-i}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}q\rho(q^{2})\theta(q^{0})\left(e^{iq\cdot(x-x^{\prime})}-e^{-iq\cdot(x-x^{\prime})}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\rho(\sigma^{2})\left[\frac{-i}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}q\delta(q^{2}-\sigma^{2})\epsilon(q^{0})e^{iq\cdot(x-x^{\prime})}\right]\ .

\displaystyle\therefore\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\ \rho(\sigma^{2})\Delta(x-x^{\prime},\sigma^{2})\ .

(10.11)

Here we have introduced the function
\epsilon(x)=\theta(x)-\theta(-x)
to combine the two exponentials and also recognized that the
the square bracket is just
-i[\Phi_{in}(x),\Phi_{in}(x^{\prime})]
for
m^{2}=\sigma^{2}
. The last equation is known as the
Kallen-Lehmann
representation
or the
spectral representation
for the commutator
function
\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime})
of the exact interacting quantum fields. This
has followed from Poincare covariance (separation of the

x-
dependence), the assumptions regarding the spectrum of the
interacting system (
\rho(q^{2}>0)=0
)
and
normalizations used for

\Phi_{in}
in identifying the
\Delta(x-x^{\prime},\sigma^{2})
.

We can separate the contribution of the 1-particle states at
\sigma^{2}=m^{2}
. We obtain the
\langle 0|\Phi(x)|k\rangle
using the asymptotic
condition,

\displaystyle\langle 0|\Phi(x)|k\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{Z}\langle 0|\Phi_{in}(x)|k\rangle+\int d^{4}y\ G_{ret}(x-y,m)\langle 0|\tilde{J}(y)|k\rangle~,~\mbox{but}

\displaystyle\langle 0|\tilde{J}(y)|k\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|(\Box-m^{2})\Phi(x)|k\rangle=(\Box-m^{2})\left(\langle 0|\Phi(0)|k\rangle e^{ik\cdot x}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-k^{2}-m^{2})\left(\langle 0|\Phi(0)|k\rangle e^{ik\cdot x}\right)~=~0.~~\mbox{The first term then gives,}

\displaystyle\langle 0|\Phi(x)|k\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{Z}\langle 0|\Phi_{in}(x)|k\rangle=\sqrt{Z}\frac{e^{ik\cdot x}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\Rightarrow|\langle 0|\Phi(x)|k\rangle|^{2}=\frac{Z}{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}\ .

\displaystyle\therefore\rho(q^{2})|_{1-particle}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(2\pi)^{3}\int d^{3}k\delta^{4}(k-q)\frac{Z}{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}=Z\delta(q^{2}-m^{2})\theta(q^{0})

(10.12)

\displaystyle\therefore

\displaystyle\boxed{\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime})=Z\Delta(x-x^{\prime},m^{2})+\int_{m^{2}_{1}}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\rho(\sigma^{2})\Delta(x-x^{\prime},\sigma^{2})}\ .

(10.13)

The lower limit on the integral is the smallest invariant mass of the
multi-particle continuum and
m^{2}_{1}>m^{2}
is assumed.

We can now derive a bound on
Z
. Observe that

\lim_{t^{\prime}\to t}(i\partial_{t}\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime}))=\langle 0|[\dot{\Phi}(x),\Phi(x^{\prime})]|0\rangle=-i\delta^{3}(x-x^{\prime})=(i\partial_{t}\Delta(x-x^{\prime},m^{2}))\ .

We are using the assumption that there are no derivative terms in
J(x)

or equivalently,
\Pi(x)=\dot{\Phi}(x)
and noting that the in/out
fields satisfy the same commutation relations.

Taking
-i\partial_{t}
on eq.(
10.13
) and taking
the limit
t^{\prime}\to t
, we deduce

\displaystyle-i\delta^{3}(\vec{x}-\vec{x}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle Z(-i\delta^{3}(\vec{x}-\vec{x}^{\prime}))+\int_{m_{1}^{2}}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\ \rho(\sigma^{2})\left[-i\delta^{3}(\vec{x}-\vec{x}^{\prime},\sigma)\right]

\displaystyle Or,~1

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle Z+\int_{m_{1}^{2}}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\ \rho(\sigma^{2})~~\Longrightarrow\boxed{0\leq Z<1.}

(10.14)

The inequalities on
Z
can be understood as follows. Since asymptotic
condition is needed to link
\Phi(x)
with
\Phi_{in/out}(x)
,
Z\neq 0
. To understand the upper limit, notice that the free fields can only
produce 1-particles states since it is linear in creation/annihilation
operators. The interacting field has no such restriction and can produce
multi-particle states as well. Hence the probability for it to produce
1-particle states is
less
than that for the free fields i.e.

|\langle 0|\Phi(x)|k\rangle|^{2}<|\langle 0|\Phi_{in/out}(x)|k\rangle|^{2}
. This results in
Z<1
.

In principle the
Z
factors for the in and out fields could have been
different in the asymptotic conditions. However, following identical
steps as above would lead us to the same relation
(
10.13
) implying equality of the
Z
’s.

An important point to note is that
Z<1
has a physical reason, quite
independent of any infinities and their renormalization that we will
encounter later on.

Remark:
In the Kallen-Lehmann spectral representation we
considered the vacuum expectation value of the commutator of the fully
interacting quantum field presumed to satisfy the usual canonical
commutation relations. Because of this, the interacting quantum field
gets identified with the so called “bare” quantum field in the
renormalized perturbation theory. We could instead use a
“renormalized” quantum field,
\Phi_{R}(x):=\Phi(x)/\sqrt{Z}
and
correspondingly define,
\Delta^{\prime}_{R}(x-x^{\prime}):=Z^{-1}\Delta^{\prime}(x-x^{\prime})
. It
follows that
\rho_{R}(q^{2})=Z^{-1}\rho(q^{2})
and

[\Phi_{R}(x),\dot{\Phi}_{R}(x^{\prime})]=iZ^{-1}\delta^{3}(x-x^{\prime})
. In terms of the
renormalized quantities, there is no factor of
Z
in equation
(
10.13
). The manipulations leading to the bound
on
Z
will now give,

\lim_{t^{\prime}\to t}(i\partial_{t}\Delta^{\prime}_{R}(x-x^{\prime}))=\langle 0|[\dot{\Phi}_{R}(x),\Phi_{R}(x^{\prime})]|0\rangle=-iZ^{-1}\delta^{3}(x-x^{\prime})=Z^{-1}(i\partial_{t}\Delta(x-x^{\prime},m^{2}))\ ,

and the eq.(
10.13
) will lead to
1=Z\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\rho_{R}(\sigma^{2})\right]
implying again
that
Z<1
. These bounds are true provided the spectral integral is

finite
. In perturbation theory, the two point functions
(commutator or the Feynman propagator) of the unrenormalized fields are
Ultra-Violet divergent and the bound cannot be inferred (See section
10.7 of
Weinberg
). The Kallen-Lehmann representation
eq.(
10.11
) itself does
not
depend on the
canonical commutation relations for the interacting field and can indeed
be derived for composite fields as well.

10.4
The
S
-matrix and its properties

Having the
\Phi_{in/out}(x)
and their corresponding mode expansions at
our disposal, we can now define the in/out states as,
|k\rangle_{in}:=a^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k})|0\rangle
and
|k\rangle_{out}:=a^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k})|0\rangle
. Similarly, multi-particle states
can be defined. We can form wave packets for normalizable states and
take limit of infinite sharpness at the end. We bypass these steps and
work with the momentum eigenstates. Note that these states are
time
independent
. While we can certainly define the general in/out states
and take their spans, we need to (and do) make a further assumption that
these spans generate the full Hilbert space of the interacting quantum
fields
10
10

10

This automatically precludes bound states in the
interacting system and amounts to postulating asymptotic completeness
property mentioned earlier.
. The sets of in and out states just
constitute two orthonormal bases, conveniently transforming by
representations of the Poincare group. This guarantees existence of a
unitary operator connecting the two orthonormal bases. This is our
scattering operator in this Heisenberg picture formulation. Taking the
basis elements to be generated by
monomials of
a^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k},\sigma,\dots)
and
a^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k},\sigma,\dots)
, the
S-
matrix is defined as,

S_{\beta\alpha}:=\langle\beta\ out|\alpha\ in\rangle~~=:~~\langle\beta\ in|S|\alpha\ in\rangle\

(10.15)

Note that
\alpha,\beta
label
basis states
which are created by

monomials
in
a^{\dagger}_{in},a^{\dagger}_{out}
. The
definition of
S
operator shows that it preserves the labels:

\langle\beta\ out|=:\langle\beta\ in|S
. We stipulate some conditions
on the
S-
matrix.

Stability of the vacuum and 1-particle states:
We expect vacuum
state to suffer no scattering spontaneously except may be acquiring a
phase (uniqueness of vacuum allows a phase since rays are defined unto
phases). We choose the phase to be 1, and stipulate
\boxed{S_{00}=1}
. Likewise presumed stability of single particle states also
disallows any spontaneous change (nothing to scatter against). Thus we
stipulate that
S_{k^{\prime},k}=\delta^{3}(\vec{k}^{\prime}-\vec{k})
. Scattering
takes place with multi-particle states.

Claim:

~\Phi_{out}(x)=S^{-1}\Phi_{in}(x)S
.

Proof:
Consider,
\langle\beta\ out|\Phi_{out}(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle
and evaluate in two ways.

\displaystyle\langle\beta\ out|\Phi_{out}(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\langle\beta\ in|S)\Phi_{out}(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle.

Next,
\langle\beta^{\prime}\ out|:=\langle\beta\ out|\Phi_{out}(x)
is a
linear combination of the out-basis elements. Each of this can be
expressed as corresponding in-basis element times
S
. And the in-basis
element is also obtained by action of
\Phi_{in}(x)
. In equation,

\displaystyle\langle\beta^{\prime}\ out|=\sum_{\gamma}C_{\gamma}\langle\gamma\ out|=\sum_{\gamma}C_{\gamma}\left(\langle\gamma\ in|S\right)=\hskip 170.71652pt

\displaystyle\left(\sum_{\gamma}C_{\gamma}\langle\gamma\ in|\right)S=:\langle\beta^{\prime}\ in|S=(\langle\beta\ in|\Phi_{in}(x))S.

Taking inner product of the two expressions with
|\alpha\ in\rangle

gives,

\langle\beta\ out|\Phi_{out}(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle=\langle\beta\ in|S\Phi_{out}(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle=\langle\beta\ in|\Phi_{in}(x))S|\alpha\ in\rangle\ \forall\ \alpha,\beta.

Completeness of the in-basis implies,
\boxed{\Phi_{out}(x)=S^{-1}\Phi_{in}(x)S\ .}
proving the claim.

Claim:

Covariance of the in/out fields gives
invariance of the scattering operator.

Proof:
We have,

\displaystyle U(\Lambda,a)\Phi_{in}(x)U^{-1}(\Lambda,a)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Phi_{in}(\Lambda x+a)

\displaystyle U(\Lambda,a)\Phi_{out}(x)U^{-1}(\Lambda,a)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Phi_{out}(\Lambda x+a)~~~~\mbox{and}~~~~\Phi_{out}(x)=S^{-1}\Phi_{in}(x)S

\displaystyle\therefore U(S^{-1}\Phi_{in}(x)S)U^{-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S^{-1}\Phi_{in}(\Lambda x+a)S~=~S^{-1}U\Phi_{in}(x)U^{-1}S

(10.16)

\displaystyle\therefore U^{-1}SUS^{-1}\Phi_{in}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Phi_{in}(x)U^{-1}SUS^{-1}~=>~

\displaystyle U^{-1}SUS^{-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}~or~\boxed{SU(\Lambda,a)=U(\Lambda,a)S}\ .

(10.17)

Question:
Are the Schrodinger picture definitions of the
scattering matrix element (
10.5
) and the Heisenberg
picture scattering matrix element defined using
\Phi_{out}=S^{-1}\Phi_{in}S
, related? If so, how?

We now relate the S-matrix elements to vacuum expectation values of time
ordered products of the interacting fields - the
Lehmann-Symanzik-Zimmermann (LSZ) reduction formulae. This is followed
by covariant perturbation series leading to Feynman rules. We will first
detail these steps for the notationally simpler case of a scalar field
and then summarize the corresponding steps for the Dirac and the Maxwell
fields.

10.5
Lehmann-Symanzik-Zimmermann Reduction of
S-
matrix

We have defined the
S-
matrix elements using the in and out states
which form the basis elements created by monomials in

a^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k},\dots)
and
a^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k},\dots)

acting on the unique vacuum. The in and out fields are not independent
or uncorrelated, they are linked through the interacting field
\Phi(x)

via the asymptotic condition. The LSZ reduction of the
S-
matrix
elements expresses them in terms of the interacting field explicitly.
For simplicity, let us first consider the case of an interacting
Hermitian scalar field.

10.5.1
LSZ reduction for Klein-Gordon field

Consider a matrix element of the form
\langle\beta\ out|\alpha,k\ in\rangle
where we have separated the
k
label in the in-state. The
definition gives,

\displaystyle\langle\beta\ out|\alpha,k\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle\beta\ out|a^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k})|\alpha\ in\rangle=\langle\beta\ out|\left(a^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k})-a^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k})+a^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k})\right)|\alpha\ in\rangle\ .

The
a^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k})
acting on the out-state will remove a
particle with label
\vec{k}
if it is present in the label set
\beta
,
or will annihilate the out-state. For simplicity, let us assume that
there is no such state in the
\beta
label. Then we have just added and
subtracted a 0. For the first two term in the brackets , use the
inversion formula (
10.2
).

\displaystyle\langle\beta\ out|\alpha,k\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle\beta\ out|\left[\frac{-i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}xe^{ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\Phi_{in}(x)\right.

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 42.67912pt}\left.+\frac{+i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}xe^{ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\Phi_{out}(x)\right]|\alpha\ in\rangle.

\displaystyle\left[\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\lim_{t\to+\infty}-\lim_{t\to-\infty}\right)\left\{\frac{+i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}x\frac{e^{ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\Phi(x)}{\sqrt{Z}}\right\}

\displaystyle\therefore\sqrt{Z}\left[\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{4}x\ \partial_{0}\left\{e^{ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\Phi(x)\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{4}x\ \left\{e^{ik\cdot x}{\partial^{2}_{0}}\Phi(x)-\partial^{2}_{0}(e^{ik\cdot x})\Phi(x)\right\}~,~(-\partial_{0}^{2}e^{ik\cdot x}=(-\nabla^{2}+m^{2})e^{ik\cdot x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{4}x\ e^{ik\cdot x}\left\{{\partial^{2}_{0}}\Phi(x)+(-\nabla^{2}+m^{2})\Phi(x)\right\}~,~(\nabla^{2}\ \mbox{flipped onto\ }\Phi(x)).

\displaystyle\therefore\langle\beta\ out|\alpha,k\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{-i}{\sqrt{Z}}\int\frac{d^{4}xe^{ik\cdot x}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}(\Box-m^{2})\langle\beta\ out|\Phi(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle\ .

Now let us separate a particle with label
k^{\prime}
from the out-state and
write
\langle\beta\ out|=\langle\gamma,k^{\prime}\ out|
the inner product on
the right hand side of the above equation. Consider,

\displaystyle\langle\gamma,k^{\prime}\ out|\Phi(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle\gamma\ out|a_{out}(\vec{k}^{\prime})\Phi(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle\gamma\ out|(a_{out}(\vec{k}^{\prime})\Phi(x)-\Phi(x)a_{in}(\vec{k}^{\prime})+\Phi(x)a_{in}(\vec{k}^{\prime}))|\alpha\ in\rangle

As before, for simplicity, assume
\alpha
-label does not contain
k^{\prime}

and thus drop the third term in the brackets. Notice that we have added
and subtracted the zero term with
a_{in}(\vec{k}^{\prime})
to the right of

\Phi(x)
while
a_{out}(\vec{k}^{\prime})
is naturally to the left of

\Phi(x)
. We need to maintain this order as we do not have the
commutation relations between the in/out field and the interacting
field. As before, using the inversion formula (
10.2
)
and using the asymptotic condition, we get

\displaystyle\langle\gamma,k^{\prime}\ out|\Phi(x)|\alpha\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle\gamma\ out|\left[\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}x^{\prime}e^{-ik^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}}\left\{\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}\Phi(x^{\prime})_{out}\Phi(x)\right.\right.

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 128.0374pt}\left.\left.-\Phi(x)\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}\Phi(x^{\prime})_{in}\right\}\right]|\alpha\ in\rangle

\displaystyle\therefore\sqrt{Z}\left[\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}x^{\prime}\left\{\lim_{t^{\prime}\to\infty}(e^{-ik^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}}\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}\Phi(x^{\prime}))\Phi(x)\right.

\displaystyle\left.\mbox{\hskip 85.35826pt}-\lim_{t^{\prime}\to-\infty}\Phi(x)(e^{-ik^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}}\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}\Phi(x^{\prime}))\right\}

It is convenient to define a time ordering instruction. Define a
time ordered product
as:
~\hfill\boxed{T\left\{A(t_{1},\vec{x})B(t_{2},\vec{y})\right\}:=\theta(t_{1}-t_{2})A(t_{1},\vec{x})B(t_{2},\vec{y})+\theta(t_{2}-t_{1})B(t_{2},\vec{y})A(t_{1},\vec{x}).}\hfill~

Notice that the two limits already have the time ordering incorporated.
Hence we can combine the terms and write,

\displaystyle\sqrt{Z}\left[\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}x^{\prime}\left(\lim_{t^{\prime}\to\infty}-\lim_{t^{\prime}\to-\infty}\right)e^{-ik^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}}\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}T\left\{\Phi(x^{\prime})\Phi(x)\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d4x^{\prime}\partial^{\prime}_{0}\left(e^{-ik^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}}\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}T\left\{\Phi(x^{\prime})\Phi(x)\right\}\right)

Proceeding exactly as before we get,

\displaystyle\langle\gamma,k^{\prime}\ out|\alpha,k\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{-i}{\sqrt{Z}}\right)^{2}\int d^{4}x^{\prime}\int d^{4}x\frac{e^{-ik^{\prime}\cdot x^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\frac{e^{ik\cdot x}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}

(10.18)

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 0.0pt}(\Box_{x^{\prime}}-m^{2})(\Box_{x}-m^{2})\langle\gamma,k^{\prime}\ out|T\left\{\Phi(x^{\prime})\Phi(x)\right\}|\alpha,k\ in\rangle

The generalization is immediate and we state the master formula for the

S-
matrix element as,

\displaystyle\langle k_{1},^{\prime}\dots,k^{\prime}_{n}\ out|k_{1},\dots,k_{m}\ in\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{-i}{\sqrt{Z}}\right)^{m+n}\int d^{4}x^{\prime}_{1}..d^{4}x^{\prime}_{n}\int d^{4}x_{1}..d^{4}x_{m}

(10.19)

\displaystyle~~~~\prod_{j}^{n}\frac{e^{-ik^{\prime}_{j}\cdot x^{\prime}_{j}}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\prod_{j}^{m}\frac{e^{+ik_{j}\cdot x_{j}}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}(\Box_{x^{\prime}_{1}}-m^{2})

\displaystyle~~~~\dots(\Box_{x^{\prime}_{m}}-m^{2})(\Box_{x_{1}}-m^{2})\dots(\Box_{x_{n}}-m^{2})

\displaystyle~~~~\langle 0|T\left\{\Phi(x^{\prime}_{1})\dots\Phi(x^{\prime}_{n})\Phi(x_{1})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\right\}|0\rangle

The vacuum expectation value of the time ordered product of
n
quantum
fields (interacting or free) is called an
n-
point function/Green
function/n-point correlation function
.

To get the
S-
matrix elements, the n-point function is operated by the
free field equation expression, multiplied by the in/out mode functions
and integrated over all the space-time points. Note that the time
ordering arises because the definition of
S-
matrix requires all the
creation operators,
a^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k})
, have to be on the right
while the annihilation operators,
a_{out}(\vec{k})
have to be on the
left. This will also naturally lead to the Feynman Green’s function
(free, 2-point function).

Let us note the steps that were followed to get the
S-
matrix elements
in terms of the n-point functions.

•

Mode decomposition of the free field and the inversion formulae;

•

Equation of motion for the interacting field with a ‘source’ term
on the right hand side;

•

Equal time(anti-)commutation relations for both the interacting
and the in/out fields;

•

Asymptotic conditions;

•

Reduction process;

10.5.2
LSZ reduction for Dirac field

We begin by recalling the mode decomposition.

\displaystyle\Psi(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(\pi)^{3}}}\left[b(\vec{k},\sigma)u(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{ik\cdot x}+d^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)v(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{-ik\cdot x}\right]

\displaystyle\Psi^{\dagger}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(\pi)^{3}}}\left[b^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)u^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{-ik\cdot x}+d(\vec{k},\sigma)v^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{ik\cdot x}\right]

We have used the
\Psi^{\dagger}
field instead of
\bar{\Psi}
because
the inversion formulae take a more convenient form.

We had defined the
u,v
spinors as,

\displaystyle({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+m)u(\vec{k},\sigma)=0~,~\bar{u}(\vec{k},\sigma)u(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})~=~

\displaystyle\delta_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}

\displaystyle~=~-\bar{v}(\vec{k},\sigma)v(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})~,~(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+m)v(\vec{k},\sigma)=0

\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma}u(\vec{k},\sigma)\bar{u}(\vec{k},\sigma)=\frac{-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+m}{2m}

,

\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma}v(\vec{k},\sigma)\bar{v}(\vec{k},\sigma)=-\frac{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+m}{2m}

We need to express these in terms of the adjoints rather than in terms
of the Dirac adjoints. This alternative for can be derived as follows.
We have,

\displaystyle\bar{u}(\vec{k},\sigma)\gamma^{\mu}u(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda^{\mu}_{~\nu}\bar{u}(\hat{k},\sigma)\gamma^{\mu}u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})~,~k^{\mu}=\Lambda^{\mu}_{~\nu}\hat{k}^{\nu}~,~\hat{k}^{\mu}=(m,\vec{0})~.~\mbox{For
$\mu=0,$}

\displaystyle u^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)u(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda^{0}_{~\nu}u^{\dagger}(\hat{k},\sigma)\gamma^{0}\gamma^{\nu}u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})~=~\Lambda^{0}_{~\nu}u^{\dagger}(\hat{k},\sigma)\gamma^{\nu}u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})~\because~\gamma^{0}u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})=u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda^{0}_{~0}u^{\dagger}(\hat{k},\sigma)\gamma^{0}u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})+\Lambda^{0}_{~i}u^{\dagger}(\hat{k},\sigma)\gamma^{i}u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})

\displaystyle\therefore u^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)u(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda^{0}_{~0}\bar{u}(\hat{k},\sigma)u(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})+0~=~\Lambda^{0}_{~0}\delta_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}+0

The second term in the last equation is zero because, for
\hat{k}

spinors
\gamma^{0}u(\hat{k},\sigma)=u(\hat{k},\sigma)
. This implies,

u^{\dagger}\gamma^{i}u=u^{\dagger}\gamma^{0}\gamma^{i}u=-u^{\dagger}\gamma^{i}\gamma^{0}u=-u^{\dagger}\gamma^{i}u\ .

Similarly,
v^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)v(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})=-\Lambda^{0}_{~0}\bar{v}(\hat{k},\sigma)v(\hat{k},\sigma^{\prime})=+\Lambda^{0}_{~0}\delta_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}
. But
\Lambda^{0}_{~0}
is defined
through,
k^{\mu}=\Lambda^{\mu}_{~\nu}\hat{k}^{\nu}
. For
\mu=0

this gives,
\Lambda^{0}_{~0}={\textstyle\frac{\omega_{\vec{k}}}{m}}
. Our
orthonormality relations then take the form,

\boxed{u^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)u(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})=\frac{\omega_{\vec{k}}}{m}\delta_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}=v^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)v(\vec{k},\sigma^{\prime})~~,~~u^{\dagger}v=0=v^{\dagger}u\ .}

We can use these relations to derive the inversion formulae. For
instance, multiplying the mode decomposition for
\Psi(x)
by

u^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{-ik\cdot x}
and integrating over
d^{3}x

yields,

b(\vec{k},\sigma)=\frac{2m}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}\int d^{3}xu^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{-ik\cdot x}\Psi(x)

It is convenient to define

U(\vec{k},\sigma):=2m\frac{u(\vec{k},\sigma)}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}~~,~~V(\vec{k},\sigma):=2m\frac{v(\vec{k},\sigma)}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}

The inversion formulae are,

\displaystyle b(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{3}xe^{-ik\cdot x}U^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)\Psi(x)

(10.20)

\displaystyle d^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{3}xe^{+ik\cdot x}V^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)\Psi(x)

(10.21)

\displaystyle b^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{3}xe^{+ik\cdot x}\Psi^{\dagger}(x)U(\vec{k},\sigma)

(10.22)

\displaystyle d(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{3}xe^{-ik\cdot x}\Psi^{\dagger}(x)V(\vec{k},\sigma)

(10.23)

In the reduction process, we will have for instance,

\displaystyle b^{\dagger}_{in}(\vec{k},\sigma)-b^{\dagger}_{out}(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d^{3}x\ e^{ik\cdot x}\left(\Psi^{\dagger}(x)_{in}-\Psi^{\dagger}_{out}(x)\right)U(\vec{k},\sigma)

and using asymptotic condition

\displaystyle\longrightarrow

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{Z}}\int d^{4}x\ \partial_{0}\left(e^{ik\cdot x}\Psi^{\dagger}(x)\right)U(\vec{k},\sigma)

Next,

\displaystyle\partial_{0}(e^{ik\cdot x}\Psi^{\dagger}(x))U(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ik\cdot x}(\partial_{0}\Psi^{\dagger}+ik_{0}\Psi^{\dagger})U;

\displaystyle ik_{0}\Psi^{\dagger}U

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle i\bar{\Psi}(k_{0}\gamma^{0})U=i\bar{\Psi}({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}-k_{i}\gamma^{i})U=i\bar{\Psi}(-mU)+\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{i}(-ik_{i}U)

\displaystyle\therefore e^{ik\cdot x}ik_{0}\Psi^{\dagger}U

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ik\cdot x}(-i\bar{\Psi}mU)+\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{i}(-\partial_{i}e^{ik\cdot x})U~=~e^{ik\cdot x}\left(-im\bar{\Psi}+\partial_{i}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{i}\right)U

\displaystyle\therefore\partial_{0}\left(e^{ik\cdot x}\Psi^{\dagger}\right)U(\vec{k},\sigma)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{ik\cdot x}\left\{\partial_{0}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{0}+\partial_{i}\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{i}-im\bar{\Psi}\right\}U~=~(-ie^{ik\cdot x})\left\{i\bar{\Psi}\overleftarrow{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}}+m\bar{\Psi}\right\}U

Hence, instead of
(-\Box_{x}+m^{2})
acting on
\Phi(x)
, we will have

(-2mi)(i\overleftarrow{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}}+m)
acting on
\bar{\Psi}(x)

and
(-2mi)(-i\overrightarrow{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}}+m)
acting on
\Psi(x)
.
The wavefunction factors will be:

\displaystyle\mbox{Particle in in-state:~}U(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{ik\cdot x}

,

\displaystyle\mbox{Particle in out-state:~}\bar{U}(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{-ik\cdot x}

(10.24)

\displaystyle\mbox{anti-Particle in in-state:~}\bar{V}(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{ik\cdot x}

,

\displaystyle\mbox{anti-Particle in out-state:~}V(\vec{k},\sigma)e^{-ik\cdot x}

(10.25)

For multi-particle case we will again have time ordering instruction. For
fermions, it is defined with an relative minus sign,

~\hfill\boxed{T\left\{\Psi_{\alpha}(x)\Psi_{\beta}(y)\right\}~:=~\theta(x^{0}-y^{0})\Psi_{\alpha}(x)\Psi_{\beta}(y)-\theta(y^{0}-x^{0})\Psi_{\beta}(y)\Psi_{\alpha}(x)}\hfill~
.

and
T\left\{\Psi_{\alpha}(x)\Psi_{\beta}(y)\right\}=-T\left\{\Psi_{\beta}(y)\Psi_{\alpha}(x)\right\}
. Thus for fermions,
changing the ordering inside the time ordering generates a minus sign
for each exchange. We summarize the general matrix element for
m

fermions going into
n
fermions as,

{}_{out}\langle..\vec{k}^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}\sigma^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}..|..\vec{k}_{j}\sigma_{j}..\rangle_{in}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{-i}{\sqrt{Z_{\Psi}}}\right)^{m+n}\prod_{j,j^{\prime}}\int d^{4}x^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}d^{4}x_{j}U(\vec{k}_{j},\sigma_{j})\bar{U}(\vec{k}^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}},\sigma^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}})

(10.26)

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 14.22636pt}e^{-i\sum_{j^{\prime}}k^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}\cdot x^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}}(-i{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}^{\prime}_{1}+m)\dots(-i{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}^{\prime}_{n}+m)

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 42.67912pt}\langle 0|T\left\{\Psi(x_{1}^{\prime})..\Psi(x^{\prime}_{n})\bar{\Psi}(x_{1})..\bar{\Psi}(x_{m})\right\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 71.13188pt}(-i\overleftarrow{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}_{1}}+m)\dots(-i\overleftarrow{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}_{m}}+m)e^{+i\sum_{j}k_{j}\cdot x_{j}}

For anti-fermions in the in/out states, the spinors
U,\bar{U}
are
changed to
V,\bar{V}
as appropriate.

10.5.3
LSZ reduction for Maxwell field

This is a bosonic field so there is no additional minus sign. Like the
Dirac field, it has two polarizations and thanks to the zero mass, these
are transverse polarizations. We begin by recalling the mode
decomposition.

\displaystyle A_{\mu}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k}{\sqrt{2\omega(2\pi)^{3}}}\sum_{\lambda=1,2}\left[a_{\vec{k},\lambda}\underline{\varepsilon}_{\mu}(\vec{k},\lambda)e^{ik\cdot x}+a^{*}_{\vec{k},\lambda}\underline{\varepsilon}^{*}_{\mu}(\vec{k},\lambda)e^{-ik\cdot x}\right]~~

\displaystyle\underline{\varepsilon}_{0}(\vec{k},\lambda)~:=~-\frac{\vec{k}\cdot\vec{\varepsilon}(\vec{k},\lambda)}{\omega_{\vec{k}}}~~,~~\underline{\varepsilon}_{i}(\vec{k},\lambda)~:=~\left(\delta_{i}^{~j}-\frac{k_{i}\ k^{j}}{\vec{k}^{2}}\right)\varepsilon_{j}(\vec{k},\lambda)~~,~~\omega_{\vec{k}}=|\vec{k}|

\displaystyle\underline{\vec{\varepsilon}}(\vec{k},\lambda)\cdot\underline{\vec{\varepsilon}}^{*}(\vec{k},\lambda^{\prime})~=~\delta_{\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}}~~,~~\sum_{\lambda}\underline{\varepsilon}_{i}(\vec{k},\lambda)\underline{\varepsilon}^{*}_{j}(\vec{k},\lambda)=~\left(\delta_{i}^{~j}-\frac{k_{i}\ k^{j}}{\vec{k}^{2}}\right)

This gives the inversion formulae as,

\displaystyle a(\vec{k},\lambda)~=~i\varepsilon_{i}(\vec{k},\lambda)\int d^{3}xe^{-ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}A^{i}(x)

,

\displaystyle a^{\dagger}(\vec{k},\lambda)~=~-i\varepsilon^{*}_{i}(\vec{k},\lambda)\int d^{3}xe^{+ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}A^{i}(x)

In the transverse/radiation/Coulomb gauge,

\underline{\varepsilon}_{\mu}(\vec{k},\lambda)=\varepsilon_{\mu}(\vec{k},\lambda)~,~\vec{k}\cdot\vec{\varepsilon}(\vec{k},\lambda)=0
and the equations of motion are

\Box A_{i}(x)=0
. The commutation relations are:

[A_{i}(t,\vec{x}),\pi_{j}(t,\vec{y})]~=~i\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{\partial_{i}\partial_{j}}{\nabla^{2}}\right)~:=~i\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{ik\cdot(x-y)}\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{k_{i}k_{j}}{\vec{k}^{2}}\right)

The reduction formula goes similar to the scalar. We will have
(-\Box_{x}+m^{2})\to-\Box_{x}
and the wave function factors would be
\boxed{\mathcal{E}_{\mu}(\vec{k},\lambda):={\textstyle\frac{\varepsilon(\vec{k},\lambda)}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}}.}
Then the general

S-
matrix element for
m\to n
particles takes the form,

{}_{out}\langle..\vec{k}^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}\lambda^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}..|..\vec{k}_{j}\lambda..\rangle_{in}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{-i}{\sqrt{Z_{A}}}\right)^{m+n}\prod_{j,j^{\prime}}\int d^{4}x^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}d^{4}x_{j}\mathcal{E}(\vec{k}_{j},\lambda)\mathcal{E}^{*}(\vec{k}^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}},\lambda^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}})

(10.27)

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 14.22636pt}e^{-i\sum_{j^{\prime}}k^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}\cdot x^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}}}(-\Box^{\prime}_{1})\dots(-\Box^{\prime}_{n})

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 42.67912pt}\langle 0|T\left\{A_{\mu^{\prime}_{1}}(x_{1}^{\prime})..A_{\mu^{\prime}_{n}}(x^{\prime}_{n})A_{\mu_{1}}(x_{1})..A_{\mu_{m}}(x_{m})\right\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 71.13188pt}(-\overleftarrow{\Box_{1}})\dots(-\overleftarrow{\Box_{m}})e^{+i\sum_{j}k_{j}\cdot x_{j}}

Having related the
S-
matrix elements to the
n-
point functions of
the interacting fields, out next task is to try see if these can be
expressed in terms of the free fields in some systematic, well defined
way. This is achieved in the so-called covariant perturbation series.

11
Covariant Perturbation Theory

In formulating the scattering theory for interacting fields, we
postulated the in/out fields satisfying the free field equations. More
importantly, we also postulated them to satisfy the same equal time
(anti-)commutation relations. With some assumptions of existence, these
suffice to develop a perturbation scheme to compute the
n-
point
functions.

Since the interacting and the free (in/out) fields satisfy the same
basic quantum conditions, it is plausible that they are related by some

unitary transformation
. For systems with finitely many degrees of
freedom, it is theorem that guarantees existence of canonical
transformations at the classical level and unitary transformations at
the quantum level (thanks to the Stone-von-Neumann theorem). For field
theories, there is no such guarantee and we need to postulate the
required existence. Their utility gives a post-facto justification for
the assumptions. Let,

~\hfill\boxed{\Phi(t,\vec{x})=U^{-1}(t)\Phi_{in}(t,\vec{x})U(t)~~,~~\Pi(t,\vec{x})=U^{-1}(t)\Pi_{in}(t,\vec{x})U(t)\ .}\hfill~
.

The fields satisfy the equations of motion in the form,

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Phi_{in}(x)=i[H_{in}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}),\Phi_{in}(x)]~

,

\displaystyle~\partial_{t}\Pi_{in}(x)=i[H_{in}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}),\Pi_{in}(x)]

(11.1)

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Phi(x)=i[H(\Phi,\Pi),\Phi(x)]~

,

\displaystyle~\partial_{t}\Pi(x)=i[H(\Phi,\Pi),\Pi(x)]

(11.2)

These enable us to derive an equation for
U(t)
.

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Phi_{in}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\partial_{t}[U(t)\Phi U^{-1}(t)]=\partial_{t}U\cdot U^{-1}\Phi_{in}+U(\partial_{t}\Phi)U^{-1}+\Phi_{in}\cdot U\partial_{t}U^{-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[\partial_{t}U\cdot U^{-1},\Phi_{in}]+iU[H(\Phi,\Pi),\Phi]U^{-1}~~\mbox{But,}

\displaystyle U[H(\Phi,\Pi),\Phi]U^{-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[UH(\Phi,\Pi]U^{-1},U\Phi U^{-1}]~=~[H(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}),\Phi_{in}]

\displaystyle\therefore\partial_{t}\Phi_{in}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle[\partial_{t}U\cdot U^{-1}+i\left\{H(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})-H_{in}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})+H_{in}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})\right\},\Phi_{in}]

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Phi_{in}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Phi_{in}+[\partial_{t}U\cdot U^{-1}+iH_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}),\Phi_{in}]~~~~\mbox{Similarly,}

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Pi_{in}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Pi_{in}+[\partial_{t}U\cdot U^{-1}+iH_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}),\Pi_{in}]~.

Since
\partial_{t}U\cdot U^{-1}+iH_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})
commutes with
both
\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}
, it must be a multiple of identity, say

E_{0}\mathbb{1}
. This gives the equation determining the
U(t)
as,

\boxed{i\partial_{t}U(t)~=~H^{\prime}_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})U(t)}~,~\boxed{H^{\prime}_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}):=H(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})-H_{in}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})+E_{0}(t)}

(11.3)

To solve the equation, it is convenient to define the combination

U(t,t^{\prime}):=U(t)U^{-1}(t^{\prime})
. It follows that this combination too
satisfies the same first order equation with the initial condition,

U(t,t)=\mathbb{1}
. The integral form of this equation is:

U(t,t^{\prime})~=~\mathbb{1}-i\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt^{\prime\prime}H^{\prime}_{I}(t^{\prime\prime})U(t^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime})\ .

This is solved by iteration.

Define:
U_{0}(t,t^{\prime})=\mathbb{1},
and for
n\geq 1,\ U_{n}(t,t^{\prime}):=\mathbb{1}-i\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}H^{\prime}(t_{n})U_{n-1}(t_{n},t^{\prime})
. Then
U(t,t^{\prime})=\sum_{n}U_{n}(t,t^{\prime})
is the formal solution of the integral equation.

It is trivial to verify the formal solution. It is formal because no
conditions are imposed for convergence of the series. The first few
terms are,

\displaystyle U_{0}(t,t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}

\displaystyle U_{1}(t,t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}-i\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{1}H^{\prime}(t_{1})\mathbb{1}

\displaystyle U_{2}(t,t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}-\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{2}H^{\prime}(t_{2})U_{1}(t_{2},t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}+(-i)\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{2}H^{\prime}(t_{2})+(-i)^{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{2}}dt_{1}H^{\prime}(t_{2})H^{\prime}(t_{1})

\displaystyle U_{3}(t,t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}+(-i)\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{3}H^{\prime}(t_{3})\left\{\mathbb{1}+(-i)\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{2}H^{\prime}(t_{2})\right.

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 128.0374pt}\left.+(-i)^{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{2}}dt_{1}H^{\prime}(t_{2})H^{\prime}(t_{1})\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}+(-i)\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{3}H^{\prime}(t_{3})+(-i)^{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{3}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{3}}dt_{2}H^{\prime}(t_{3})H^{\prime}(t_{2})

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 108.12054pt}+(-i)^{3}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{3}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{3}}dt_{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{2}}dt_{1}H^{\prime}(t_{3})H^{\prime}(t_{2})H^{\prime}(t_{1})~~~~

\displaystyle\therefore U_{n}(t,t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-i)^{k}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{k}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{k}}dt_{k-1}\dots\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{2}}dt_{1}H^{\prime}(t_{k})H^{\prime}(t_{k-1})\dots H^{\prime}(t_{1})

(11.4)

Consider the term
\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{n}}dt_{n-1}
. By
interchanging the order f integration we can write it as (
H^{\prime}_{n}:=H^{\prime}(t_{n})
),

\displaystyle\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{n}}dt_{n-1}H^{\prime}_{n}H^{\prime}_{n-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t}dt_{n}H^{\prime}_{n}H^{\prime}_{n-1}~=~\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t_{n}}^{t}dt_{n-1}H^{\prime}_{n-1}H^{\prime}_{n}

\displaystyle\therefore LHS=\frac{1}{2}(LHS+RHS)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left[\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{n}}dt_{n-1}H^{\prime}_{n}H^{\prime}_{n-1}+\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t_{n}}^{t}dt_{n-1}H^{\prime}_{n-1}H^{\prime}_{n}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left[\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t_{n}}dt_{n-1}T\left\{H^{\prime}_{n}H^{\prime}_{n-1}\right\}\right.

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 85.35826pt}\left.+\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t_{n}}^{t}dt_{n-1}T\left\{H^{\prime}_{n}H^{\prime}_{n-1}\right\}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n-1}T\left\{H^{\prime}_{n}H^{\prime}_{n-1}\right\}

Similarly, we can symmetrize the higher order terms to replace each
product by their time ordered products and then combine the integrals to
have the same limits of integrations. The
n^{th}
order term then takes
the form:
{\textstyle\frac{1}{n!}}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n-1}\dots\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{1}T\{H^{\prime}(t_{n})H^{\prime}(t_{n-1})\dots H^{\prime}(t_{1})\}
. We write the
iterated formal solution of the (
11.3
) as,

\displaystyle U(t,t^{\prime})

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle T\left(exp\left\{-i\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt^{\prime}H^{\prime}_{I}(\Phi_{in}(t^{\prime}),\Pi_{in}(t^{\prime}))\right\}\right)

(11.5)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{1}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-i)^{n}}{n!}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{1}\dots\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}dt_{n}\ T\left\{H^{\prime}_{I}(t_{1})\dots H^{\prime}_{I}(t_{n})\right\}

(11.6)

The solution is thus obtained entirely in terms of the ‘in’ fields. Note
that the solution gives
U(t,t^{\prime})
and
not

U(t)
. While the
equations satisfied by
U(t)
and
U(t,t^{\prime})
are the same, there is no
“initial” condition provided for
U(t)
and in a sense it is
ill-defined. There is no canonical way to deduce/define
U(t)
from

U(t,t^{\prime})
. Fortunately,
U(t,t^{\prime})
suffice.

Note:
From the definition it follows the useful composition
property that
U(t,t^{\prime})=U(t,t^{\prime\prime})U(t^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime})
, regardless of any
inequalities for
t^{\prime\prime}
. This may also be verified directly.

Let us see an implication of the existence of
U(t)
. Consider an

n-
point function for a scalar,
G(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\langle 0|T\left\{\Phi(x_{1})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\right\}|0\rangle
. Insert in this
\Phi(x)=U^{-1}(t)\Phi_{in}(x)U(t)
which gives,

\displaystyle\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\dots\Phi(x_{n})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U^{-1}(t_{1})\Phi_{in}(x_{1})U(t_{1})\cdot U^{-1}(t_{2})\Phi_{in}(x_{2})U(t_{2})..U^{-1}(t_{n})\Phi(x_{n})U(t_{n})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle U^{-1}(t)\left[U(t,t_{1})\Phi_{in}(x_{1})U(t_{1},t_{2})\Phi_{in}(x_{2})\dots\right.

\displaystyle\left.\mbox{\hskip 28.45274pt}U(t_{n-1},t_{n})\Phi_{in}(x_{n})U(t_{n},-t)\right]U(-t)~~,~~U(t,t^{\prime}):=U(t)U^{-1}(t^{\prime})

Observe that in the limit
t\to\infty
, the factor
U^{-1}(t)
goes to
the extreme left and
U(t)
to the extreme right. All other space-time
arguments being finite, we can take these factors outside the time
ordering symbol. The product of the fields
\Phi(x)
’s is already under
time ordering which then allows us to arrange all the factors within

T\{\dots\}
to be conveniently grouped. In particular, all the
U(t_{i},t_{j})
can be combined using their composition property noted above.

With the limit of
t\to\infty
implicit, we can write the
n-
point
function as,

G(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})~=~\langle 0|U^{-1}(t)T\left\{\Phi_{in}(x_{1})\dots\Phi_{in}(x_{n})\ exp\left(-i\int_{-t}^{t}dt^{\prime}H^{\prime}_{I}(t^{\prime})\right)\right\}U(t)|0\rangle\ .

(11.7)

Next, we evaluate the
U(-t)|0\rangle
in the limit
t\to\infty
and
its adjoint.

Claim:

U(-t)|0\rangle\to\lambda_{-}|0\rangle
as
t\to\infty
.

Proof:
Consider an in-state containing at least one particle
of momentum
k,|\alpha,k\rangle_{in}
. Then,

{}_{in}\langle\alpha,k|U(-t)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

{}_{in}\langle\alpha|a_{in}(\vec{k})U(-t)|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle i\int_{\Sigma_{t^{\prime}}}\frac{d^{3}x}{\sqrt{2\omega_{\vec{k}}(2\pi)^{3}}}e^{-ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial^{\prime}_{0}}_{in}\langle\alpha|\Phi_{in}(-t^{\prime},\vec{x})U(-t)|0\rangle

We have used the inversion formula for
a_{in}
by choosing an arbitrary

\Sigma_{t^{\prime}}
hyper-surface and
a_{in}
is of course independent of
this.

In the integrand above, substitute
\Phi_{in}(t^{\prime},\vec{x})=U(t^{\prime})\Phi(t^{\prime},\vec{x})U^{-1}(t^{\prime})
and evaluate the time derivative.

Integrand

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{-ik\cdot x}\langle\alpha|\left[\dot{U}(-t^{\prime})U^{-1}(-t^{\prime})\Phi_{in}(-t^{\prime},\vec{x})U(-t)+\Phi_{in}(-t^{\prime},\vec{x})U(-t^{\prime})\partial_{t^{\prime}}U^{-1}(t^{\prime})U(-t)\right.

\displaystyle\left.+U(-t^{\prime})\partial^{\prime}_{0}\Phi(-t^{\prime})U^{-1}(-t^{\prime})U(-t)-U(-t^{\prime})\Phi(-t^{\prime})U^{-1}(-t^{\prime})U(-t)(\partial^{\prime}_{0}(-ik\cdot x))\right]|0\rangle

Now take choose
t^{\prime}=t
. Then, the first two terms on the r.h.s.
combine as,

[\dot{U}(-t)U^{-1}(-t),\Phi_{in}(-t,\vec{x})]U(-t)~=~-i[H^{\prime}_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in}),\Phi_{in}(-t,\vec{x})]U(-t)~=~0\ .

In the usual theories, the interaction Hamiltonian has no
\Pi

dependence and hence at equal time, commutes with the field giving 0.

In the last two terms, the
U^{-1}(-t^{\prime})U(-t)
factor becomes

\mathbb{1}
for
t^{\prime}=t
. These terms combine to give,
{}_{in}\langle\alpha|U(-t)\left(e^{-ik\cdot x}\overleftrightarrow{\partial_{0}}\Phi(-t)\right)|0\rangle
. Taking the limit
t\to\infty
and invoking the asymptotic condition, converts
\Phi(x)
into

\sqrt{Z}\Phi_{in}(x)
. The spatial integration converts the expression
into
\sqrt{Z}_{in}\langle\alpha|U(-t)a_{in}(\vec{k})|0\rangle=0
.

Thus we conclude that
{}_{in}\langle\alpha,k|U(-t)|0\rangle\to 0
as
t\to\infty
for
all
states containing at least one particle.

U(-t)|0\rangle
must therefore be proportional to
|0\rangle
itself
thereby proving the claim.

By similar reasoning, we obtain
U(t)|0\rangle\to\lambda_{+}|0\rangle

as
t\to\infty
.

Corollary:

\lambda_{+}^{*}\lambda_{-}=\left[\langle 0|Texp\left(-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt^{\prime}H^{\prime}_{I}(t^{\prime})\right)|0\rangle\right]^{-1}

(11.8)

The proof is simple,

\displaystyle\lambda_{+}^{*}\lambda_{-}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\langle 0|U^{-1}(t)|0\rangle\langle 0|U(-t)|0\rangle

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\langle 0|U^{-1}(t)|U(-t)|0\rangle~~\mbox{since
intermediate states do not contribute by above result}

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\langle 0|U(-t)U^{-1}(t)|0\rangle~=~\langle 0|U(-t,t)|0\rangle

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\langle 0|(U(t,-t))^{-1}|0\rangle~=~(\langle 0|U(t,-t)|0\rangle)^{-1}\ .

The final expression follows by substituting the formal solution in the
limit
t\to\infty
.

Using the equations (
11.7
,
11.8
), we express the
n-

point function as,

\boxed{G(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})~=~\frac{\langle 0|T\left\{\Phi_{in}(x_{i})\dots\Phi_{in}(x_{n})exp-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt^{\prime}H_{I}(t^{\prime})\right\}|0\rangle}{\langle 0|T\left\{exp-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt^{\prime}H_{I}(t^{\prime})\right\}|0\rangle}}

(11.9)

Notice that the multiple of identity
E_{0}(t)\mathbb{1}
has been
canceled between the numerator and the denominator before taking the
limit
t\to\infty
.

Suffice it to say that analogous expressions exist for other fields as
well. However we will not write them explicitly.

The reduction formulae give
S-
matrix elements in terms of the

n-
point functions and the
n-
point functions have a perturbative
expansion in terms of the free fields alone. These two together are the
master formulae for computations.

A further simplification is provided by the
Wick’s Theorem
.

11.1
Normal ordering and Wick’s theorem

Recall that the mode expansion of the
free
quantum fields can be
grouped as
\Phi(x)=\Phi_{+}(x)+\Phi_{-}(x)
with
\Phi_{\pm}(x)

denoting the sum over positive/negative frequency modes. The positive
frequency part is made up of annihilation operators while the negative
frequency part is made up of creation operators alone. For a Hermitian
quantum field, the negative frequency part is the Hermitian adjoint of
the positive frequency part. A product of fields at different points
will mix these parts and the idea is to bring all annihilation operators
to the right and the creation operators to the left. The vacuum
expectation value of so ordered groups will of course be zero. In this
process, several commutators of fields at different space-time points
are generated, but
they all are c-numbers
. This leads to a
simplification.

We define
normal ordered products
of two
free
fields as:

\displaystyle\mbox{For bosons~ ~}:\Phi_{-}(x)\Phi_{+}(y):~=~\Phi_{-}(x)\Phi_{+}(y)~~

,

\displaystyle~~:a^{\dagger}a:~:=~a^{\dagger}a

(11.10)

\displaystyle:\Phi_{+}(x)\Phi_{-}(y):~=~\Phi_{-}(y)\Phi_{+}(x)~~

,

\displaystyle~~:aa^{\dagger}:~:=~a^{\dagger}a

(11.11)

\displaystyle\mbox{For fermions~ ~}:\Psi_{-}(x)\Psi_{+}(y):~=~\Psi_{-}(x)\Psi_{+}(y)~~

,

\displaystyle~~:b^{\dagger}b:~:=~b^{\dagger}b

(11.12)

\displaystyle:\Psi_{+}(x)\Psi_{-}(y):~=~-\Psi_{-}(y)\Psi_{+}(x)~~

,

\displaystyle~~:bb^{\dagger}:~:=~-b^{\dagger}b

(11.13)

For product of two or more positive (or negative) frequency fields, the
normal ordering does not change order. It is immediately obvious that

\langle 0|:Operator:|0\rangle=0
.

Note that the normal ordering are meaningful only for
products of free fields (in/out). Hence the
in/out
suffixes are
suppressed for these.

To get a general form for several bosonic as well as fermionic free
fields, notice that for a quantum field
Q(x)=Q_{+}(x)+Q_{-}(x)
a
product of
n
fields generates terms with the
k
number of
Q_{+}
’s
interspersed with
(n-k)
number of
Q_{-}
’s, with the order of the
space-time points maintained, with
k=0,\dots,n
. Under normal ordering
each of these terms will shift the
Q_{+}
’s to the right and
Q_{-}
’s to
the left, generating a permutation of the space-time points, say
p
. If

Q
is a fermionic field, the term with permutation
p
will get a
factor of
\sigma_{p}=sgn(p)
while a bosonic field will have
\sigma_{p}=1
. Note that for any given
k
, there will be several terms eg

Q_{1}Q_{2},Q_{3}Q_{7},\dots
etc. Each will generate its own permutation under
normal ordering. With this understood, we can write the general
expression for normal ordered product of
n-
fields as,

~\hfill\boxed{:Q(x_{1})\dots Q(x_{n}):~:=~\sum_{A,B}\sigma_{p}\prod_{i\in A}Q_{-}(x_{p(i)})\prod_{j\in B}Q_{+}(x_{p(j)})\ .}\hfill~

The
A,B
are two groups of space-time points corresponding to the
k,(n-k)
mentioned above and the sum refers to various possible groupings
of the space-time points within each class.

Exercise:
Verify for
n=4
.

Consider now the relation between time ordered products and normal
ordered products. For a single field, both orderings are trivial and
their vacuum expectation value vanishes:
\langle 0|T\{\phi_{in}(x)\}|0\rangle=0=\langle 0|:\phi(x):|0\rangle
.

For time ordered product of two fields, for any particular instances of
time they appear in a particular order which can be explicitly put in
the normal ordered form, eg.
a(\vec{k})a^{\dagger}(\vec{k}^{\prime})=``\mathbb{1}"+a^{\dagger}(\vec{k}^{\prime})a(\vec{k})=:a(\vec{k})a^{\dagger}(\vec{k}^{\prime}):+``\mathbb{1}"
. The last term is a
c-number (multiple of the identity operator). Similarly,
\Phi(x)\Phi(y)=:\Phi(x)\Phi(y):+\ c-
number. And the c-number is trivial to
evaluate by just taking the vev (vacuum expectation value):
c-
number =

\langle 0|\Phi(x)\Phi(y)|0\rangle
. Noting that
T\{\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\}=\theta(x^{0}-y^{0})\Phi(x)\Phi(y)+\theta(y^{0}-x^{0})\Phi(y)\Phi(x)
, we
get,
\boxed{T\{\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\}=:T\{\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\}:+\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\}|0\rangle}
. Notice that normal ordering and time
ordering commute:
:T\{A(x)B(y)\}:=T\{:A(x)B(y):\}
, for all
non-trivial
A(x),B(y)
operators i.e. for operators which are
polynomials in the basic field operators of degree greater that zero.
The generalization of this to product of arbitrary number of field is
the Wick’s theorem. We state it explicitly for a scalar field.

Wick’s Theorem:

\displaystyle T\{\Phi(x_{1})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle:T\{\Phi(x_{1})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\}:

\displaystyle+\left[\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\}|0\rangle:T\{\Phi(x_{3})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\}:+\mbox{~permutations}\right]

\displaystyle+\left[\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\}|0\rangle\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{3})\Phi(x_{4})\}|0\rangle\times\right.

\displaystyle\left.\mbox{\hskip 113.81102pt}:T\{\Phi(x_{5})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\}:+\mbox{~permutations}\right]

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 28.45274pt}\vdots~\vdots

\displaystyle+\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\left[\langle 0|T\{\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\}|0\rangle\dots\langle 0|T\{\Phi_{n-1}\Phi_{n}\}|0\rangle+\mbox{~permutations}\right]\\
\mbox{\hskip 227.62204pt ($n$ even)}\\
\left[\langle 0|T\{\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\}|0\rangle\dots\langle 0|T\{\Phi_{n-2}\Phi_{n-1}\}|0\rangle\Phi_{n}\right.\\
\left.\mbox{\hskip 139.41832pt}+\mbox{~permutations}\right]~\mbox{($n$ odd)}\end{array}\right.

In the last line we have used the abbreviation
\Phi_{i}:=\Phi(x_{i})
and
we will use the same when convenient.

Proof:

The proof is by induction and we have already seen the validity for
n=1,2.
Assume the theorem is true for
n=n
. Include an extra field

\Phi(x_{n+1})
and choose
t_{n+1}
to be the earliest instant so that
it stays on the extreme right. Then,

\displaystyle T\{\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n+1}\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle T\{\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}\}\Phi_{n+1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left[:T\{\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}\}:+\sum_{perm}\langle 0|T\{\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\}|0\rangle:T\{\dots\}:+\dots\right]\Phi_{n+1}~,

\displaystyle:\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}:\Phi_{n+1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left\{\sum_{A,B}\sigma_{p}\prod_{i\in A}\Phi^{-}_{i}\ \prod_{j\in B}\Phi^{+}_{j}\right\}\left(\Phi^{+}_{n+1}+\Phi^{-}_{n+1}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{A,B}\sigma_{p}\prod_{i\in A}\Phi^{-}_{i}\ \prod_{j\in B}\Phi^{+}_{j}\Phi^{+}_{n+1}\ +

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 28.45274pt}\sum_{A,B}\sigma_{p}\prod_{i\in A}\Phi^{-}_{i}\ \left\{\Phi_{n+1}^{-}\prod_{j\in B}\Phi^{+}_{j}+\left[\prod_{j\in B}\Phi^{+}_{j}\ ,\ \Phi_{n+1}^{-}\right]\right\}

The first two terms in the last equation have the requisite normal
ordered form for
n+1
fields. The third term has several commutators,

[\Phi^{+}_{j},\Phi^{-}_{n+1}]
which again are c-numbers and can be
evaluated by taking vev. That is,

\displaystyle[\Phi^{+}_{j},\Phi^{-}_{n+1}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|(\Phi^{+}_{j}\Phi^{-}_{n+1}-\Phi^{-}_{n+1}\Phi^{+}_{j})|0\rangle~=~\langle 0|\Phi^{+}_{j}\Phi^{-}_{n+1}|0\rangle+0

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|\Phi_{j}\Phi_{n+1}|0\rangle~=~\langle 0|T\left\{\Phi_{j}\Phi_{n+1}\right\}|0\rangle~~,~~\mbox{since
$t_{n+1}$ is the earliest.}

\displaystyle\therefore\ :\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}:\Phi_{n+1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle:\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}\Phi_{n+1}:+\sum_{j}\sigma_{p}:\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{j-1}\Phi_{j+1}\dots\Phi_{n}:\langle 0|T\left\{\Phi_{j}\Phi_{n+1}\right\}|0\rangle

Thus, inserting the time ordering, the first term,
:T\{\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}\}:\Phi_{n+1}
gets expressed as
:T\{\Phi_{1}\dots\Phi_{n}\Phi_{n+1}\}:+\ \mbox{\lx@text@lbrace terms which have a structure similar to
the second term\lx@text@rbrace}
and so on. Hence the induction hypothesis allows the
expression to hold for
n+1
and the theorem is proved by induction.

Exercise:
Verify the theorem for
n=3,4
.

Observe that
G(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\dots\Phi(x_{n})\}|0\rangle
vanishes for odd
n
and equals

\sum_{perm}\sigma_{p}\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\}|0\rangle\dots\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{n-1})\Phi(x_{n})\}|0\rangle
for even
n
.

Thus,
2n-
point function of free fields is the sum of products of

n
,
2-
point functions of free fields. We denote:

\boxed{\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x)\Phi(y)\}|0\rangle=:i\Delta_{F}(x-y)=:\mbox{(Feynman
propagator)}}
.

We have the
S-
matrix elements in terms of the
n-
point functions of
interacting quantum fields, expressed in terms of vev of time ordered
products of free fields and thanks to Wick’s theorem these are expressed
in terms of
2-
point functions of free fields. In short, the
S-
matrix
elements are obtained from a bunch of
2-
point functions of free
fields, together with some integrations and operations of
(\Box-m^{2})
. It remains to have a convenient algorithm for computations.

A few remarks are in order. The normal ordering is introduced here as a
simplification step. It works because the postulated
unique

Poincare invariant vacuum state is annihilated by all (free field)
annihilation operators. This also
requires
the Poincare
generators of the free fields to be normal ordered
11
11

11

Note that
while abelian symmetries could allow a non-zero multiple of
identity for invariance (i.e.
P^{\mu}|0\rangle=\alpha^{\mu}|0\rangle
), non-abelian symmetry generators have to
annihilate the vacuum. Hence the Lorentz generators must
annihilate the vacuum and then the commutator of
M^{\mu\nu}

with
P^{\lambda}
shows that the
\alpha^{\mu}=0
must also hold.
Poincare group being non-abelian must have its generators being normal
ordered for the vacuum to be invariant.
. The Poincare generators of the
interacting fields also need to annihilate the vacuum. Thanks to the
assumed unitary operator linking the free and the interacting fields,
these generators too are expressed in terms of the free field
creation-annihilation operator. These expressions, in particular the
Hamiltonian, must also be normal ordered for Poincare invariance. We
will make this explicit for the interaction Hamiltonian
H_{I}(\Phi_{in},\Pi_{in})
.

In the quantum optics context, the normal ordering was used since the
detectors worked by absorbing a quantum from the field and in principle,
for a detector working by emission of a quantum would require
anti-normal ordering. Such an option is not available with manifest
Poincare invariance
with a unique invariant vacuum state
.

An explicit example of evaluation of an
n-
point function will be
useful. Consider
G_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})
computed to second order in
H_{I}
.
Consider the numerator first.
All fields are ‘in’ fields and the
‘in’ subscript is suppressed below.

\displaystyle G_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})|_{Nr}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\left(\mathbb{1}-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt^{\prime}H_{I}(t^{\prime})\right.

\displaystyle\left.\mbox{\hskip 85.35826pt}+\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2!}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt_{1}dt_{2}T\{H_{I}(t_{1})H_{I}(t_{2})\}\right)\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\{\phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\}|0\rangle-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt_{1}\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})H_{I}(t_{1})\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 56.9055pt}+\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt_{1}dt_{2}\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})H_{I}(t_{1})H_{I}(t_{2})\}|0\rangle

Now let us take a specific interaction Hamiltonian, simplest non-trivial
being
H_{I}(t):=g\int d^{3}y:\Phi(t,\vec{y})^{3}:
. As noted above, for
the case of Poincare invariant vacuum, the Poincare generators and hence
in particular the Hamiltonian must be normal ordered. The time
integrations combine with these spatial integration to give a space time
integral. Thus, we get,

\displaystyle G_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})|_{Nr}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\{\phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})\}|0\rangle-ig\int\ d^{4}y\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2}):\Phi^{3}(y):\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 14.22636pt}+\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}g^{2}\int\ d^{4}y_{1}\int d^{4}y_{2}\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2}):\Phi^{3}(y_{1})::\Phi^{3}(y_{2}):\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle i\Delta_{F}(x_{1}-x_{2})-\frac{g^{2}}{2}\int\ d^{4}y_{1}\int d^{4}y_{2}\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2}):\Phi^{3}(y_{1})::\Phi^{3}(y_{2}):\}|0\rangle

The first term is just the Feynman propagator and the
o(g)
term
vanishes since it is a 5-point function. The non-trivial term is the

o(g^{2})
term. This is not in the form of the Wick’s theorem, in that
there are normal ordered factors. We can replace the normal ordered
product in terms of unordered product minus the product of two point
functions i.e. using the Wick’s theorem in reverse form. For instance,
consider (for three distinct points)

\displaystyle:\Phi(y_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime}_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime\prime}_{1}):

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Phi(y_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime}_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime\prime}_{1})-\langle 0|\Phi(y_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime}_{1})|0\rangle\Phi(y^{\prime\prime}_{1})

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 56.9055pt}-\langle 0|\Phi(y^{\prime}_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime\prime}_{1})|0\rangle\Phi(y_{1})-\langle 0|\Phi(y_{1})\Phi(y^{\prime\prime}_{1})|0\rangle\Phi(y^{\prime}_{1})

And likewise for the second factor of
:\Phi(y_{2})^{3}:
. If we now
substitute these in the
o(g^{2})
term and eventually take the
coincidence limit of the primed arguments, we see that the two point
functions of coincident points cancel out. The net result result is that
in writing the permutation terms, we omit the Feynman propagators of
coincident points and this holds because we use the normal ordered
interaction Hamiltonian. If we did not normal order the interaction
Hamiltonian then these terms, which are formally divergent, will remain
and will have to be handled differently. This is what will happen in the
functional integral method which will be discussed later. Keeping this
in mind, the
o(g^{2})
term under vev becomes,

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2}):\Phi^{3}(y_{1})::\Phi^{3}(y_{2}):\}|0\rangle~\mbox{\hskip 227.62204pt$~$}

\displaystyle=i\Delta_{F}(x_{1}-x_{2}).i\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2}).i\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2}).i\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2})+\mbox{~permutations}

\displaystyle=(i^{4})\left[\Delta_{F}(x_{1}-x_{2})\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2})^{3}+\Delta_{F}(x_{1}-y_{1})\Delta_{F}(x_{2}-y_{2})\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}\right.

\displaystyle\left.+\Delta_{F}(x_{1}-y_{2})\Delta_{F}(x_{2}-y_{1})\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2})^{2}\right]

There are no other ‘pairings’ of space-time points as they would involve
Feynman propagators with coincident arguments.

The denominator of the
n-
point function has the same structure as the
numerator except for the
\Phi(x_{1})\Phi(x_{2})
fields i.e.

\displaystyle G_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})|_{Dr}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle 0|0\rangle-ig\int\ d^{4}y\langle 0|T\{:\Phi^{3}(y):\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 14.22636pt}+\frac{(-i)^{2}}{2}g^{2}\int\ d^{4}y_{1}\int d^{4}y_{2}\langle 0|T\{:\Phi^{3}(y_{1})::\Phi^{3}(y_{2}):\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1-\frac{g^{2}}{2}\int\ d^{4}y_{1}\int d^{4}y_{2}\langle 0|T\{:\Phi^{3}(y_{1})::\Phi^{3}(y_{2}):\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1+\frac{(-ig)^{2}}{2}(CF)\int\ d^{4}y_{1}\int d^{4}y_{2}\ (i\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2}))^{3}

Here,
CF
is the
combinatorial factor
- number of distinct ways
of effecting the same pairings - and equals
3!
in the example above.

The generalization is fairly obvious. For definiteness consider the
interaction Hamiltonian
density
to be
H_{I}(\Phi(y)):={\textstyle\frac{g}{k!}}:\Phi^{k}(y):
. Then, it is apparent that the numerator of a
general
n-
point function is a sum of the
m^{th}
order contributions,

m=0,1,\dots
. The
m^{th}
order contribution has the form:

\bullet~{\textstyle\frac{(-ig)/k!)^{m})}{m!}}\int d^{4}y_{1}\dots d^{4}y_{m}\langle 0|T\{\Phi(x_{1})\dots\Phi(x_{n}):\Phi^{k}(y_{1}):\dots:\Phi^{k}(y_{m}):\}|0\rangle\ ;

\bullet~
The Wick’s theorem gives a sum of terms, each of which is a
product of a total of
(n+km)/2
Feynman propagators,

i\Delta_{F}(x_{j}-y_{k})
, whose arguments give the ‘pairing’ of space-time
points from the set:
x_{1},\dots,x_{n},k-\mbox{copies of}\ y_{1},\dots,k-\mbox{copies of}\ y_{m}
. The normal ordered form of interaction
Hamiltonian ensures that the paired points are necessarily
distinct
. The
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}
points are assumed to be distinct. A
‘pairing’ is also called a ‘Wick contraction’. The sum of terms is
generated from any particular one by permutations. If
n+km
is odd,
the contribution vanishes;

\bullet~
There would also be combinatorial factor counting distinct
ways of getting the same set of pairing (or Feynman propagators). The
denominator has similar contributions except the
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}
points.

There is a convenient diagrammatic representation to keep track of the
generated terms as well as associating specific factors and integrals
with them. The diagrams are the
Feynman Diagrams
while the
prescription to construct associated integral is given by the
Feynman rules
.

Procedure to generate Feynman diagrams for Green’s function:

\bullet~
For each distinct
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}
, draw a
vertex
with
a single edge. Call these vertices as
external vertices
;

\bullet~
For normal ordered monomial of order
k
, draw a vertex
y_{j}

with
k
edges sticking out. Call these as the
internal vertices
;

\bullet~
Wick contract or pair, by joining two edges from two distinct
vertices, internal or external. If the pair has one or both vertices to
be external vertices, the line is called an
external line
while a
pairing with both vertices being internal, is called an
internal
line
. This constructs a Feynman diagram with vertices and
internal/external lines.

Procedure to associate integral with a Feynman diagram:

\bullet~
With each contraction, associate a Feynman propagator,

i\Delta_{F}(z^{\prime}-z^{\prime\prime})
.

\bullet~
With each internal vertex, associate a factor of
(-i)\times
coefficient of the monomial of the fields in
H_{I}(\Phi(y))
and an
integral over its space-time location,
\int d^{4}y
.

\bullet~
Associate a numerical factor as a ratio. In the numerator,
count the number of
distinct
ways of generating the same diagram
(or the same contractions). In the denominator, put
m!
if
m
is the
total number of internal vertices.

For the above example of
G_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})
to second order for
H_{I}=g:\Phi(y)^{3}:
, here is a summary:

o(g)

Has one loose end and vev is zero.

x_{1}
x_{2}

y_{2}

(b)

(-ig)^{2}\left(\frac{3.3.2.1}{2!}\right)\int d^{4}y_{1}d^{4}y_{2}\ (i\Delta_{F}(x_{1}-y_{2}))\times(i\Delta_{F}(x_{2}-y_{1}))(i\Delta_{F}(y_{1}-y_{2}))^{2}

(c)

x_{1}
x_{2}
y_{1}
y_{2}
3
2
