\displaystyle-64p\cdot p^{\prime}+32(k\cdot p-k\cdot p^{\prime})-Tr(\gamma^{\nu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{\nu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}\gamma_{\mu})

(14.25)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-64p\cdot p^{\prime}+32(k\cdot p-k\cdot p^{\prime})+0

To simplify the expression further, we need to use:
p\cdot p^{\prime}=-m^{2}+k\cdot p-k\cdot p^{\prime}
which follows from
0=(k^{\prime})^{2}=(p+k-p^{\prime})^{2}
.
For comparison with
PeskinSchroder
, it is useful to note:
k\cdot p=k^{\prime}\cdot p^{\prime}\ ,\ p\cdot k^{\prime}=p^{\prime}\cdot k
.

The final expression is,

\frac{1}{4}\sum_{spin/Pol}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}=2e^{4}\left[\left(\frac{p\cdot k^{\prime}}{p\cdot k}+\frac{p\cdot k}{p\cdot k^{\prime}}\right)+2m^{2}\left(\frac{1}{p\cdot k^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{p\cdot k}\right)+m^{4}\left(\frac{1}{p\cdot k}-\frac{1}{p\cdot k^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right]

(14.26)

Exercise:
Check the algebra!

The Compton cross-section is usually presented in the lab frame with the
electron initially at rest, i.e.
p^{\mu}=(m,\vec{0}),k^{\mu}=(\omega,\omega\hat{z}),(p^{\prime})^{\mu}=(E^{\prime},\vec{p}]),(k^{\prime})^{\mu}=(\omega^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}sin{\theta},0,\omega^{\prime}cos(\theta))
. The final
electron and photon momenta define a plane which is taken to be the

z-x
plane with the final photon making an angle
\theta
to the

z-
axis. These choices give:
p\cdot k^{\prime}=-m\omega^{\prime},p\cdot k=-m\omega
and,

\sum_{spin/Pol}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}=2e^{4}\left[\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}+\frac{\omega}{\omega^{\prime}}+2m\left(-\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{\omega}\right)+m^{2}\left(-\frac{1}{\omega}+\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right]

(14.27)

Next,
(p^{\prime})^{2}=(p+k-k^{\prime})^{2}
implies,

-m^{2}=-m^{2}+2p\cdot(k-k^{\prime})+(k-k^{\prime})^{2}\Rightarrow 0=m(\omega-\omega^{\prime})-\omega\omega^{\prime}(1-cos(\theta)),

leading to the Compton formula for shift in the photon wavelength with
the scattering angle:

\mbox{Compton Formula:~ ~}\boxed{\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{\omega}=\frac{1-cos\theta}{m}}~\leftrightarrow~\omega^{\prime}=\frac{\omega}{1+{\textstyle\frac{\omega}{m}}(1-cos\theta)}\ .

(14.28)

To get the differential cross-section, we simplify the phase space
integral as,

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}}{2\omega^{\prime}(2\pi)^{3}}\int\frac{d^{3}p^{\prime}}{2E^{\prime}(2\pi)^{3}}(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{4}(p;+k^{\prime}-p-k)=\mbox{\hskip 85.35826pt}

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\omega^{\prime}(\omega^{\prime})^{2}d\Omega}{2\omega^{\prime}(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{2E^{\prime}(2\pi)^{3}}(2\pi)^{4}\delta(\omega^{\prime}+E^{\prime}-m-\omega)

We have used up a
\delta^{3}
to get
\vec{p}^{\prime}=\vec{k}^{\prime}-\vec{k}-\vec{p}=(\omega^{\prime}sin\theta,0,\omega^{\prime}cos\theta-\omega)
which gives

(E^{\prime})^{2}-(\omega^{\prime})^{2}+\omega^{2}-2\omega^{\prime}\omega cos\theta+m^{2}
.
Hence

\int d\omega^{\prime}\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{4E^{\prime}(\omega^{\prime})}\delta(\omega^{\prime}+E^{\prime}(\omega^{\prime})-m-\omega)=\frac{\omega^{\prime}_{*}}{4E^{\prime}(\omega^{\prime}_{*})}\frac{1}{|1+{\textstyle\frac{dE^{\prime}}{d\omega^{\prime}_{*}}}|}~~,~~\frac{dE^{\prime}}{d\omega^{\prime}}=\frac{\omega^{\prime}-\omega cos\theta}{E^{\prime}}\ .

Inserting in the phase space integral,

\displaystyle\int_{\Gamma_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{dcos\theta}{2\pi}\frac{\omega^{\prime}_{*}}{4E^{\prime}_{*}}\frac{1}{|1+\frac{\omega^{\prime}-\omega cos\theta}{E^{\prime}}|_{*}}~~,~~\omega^{\prime}_{*}+E^{\prime}(\omega^{\prime}_{*})=m+\omega

(14.29)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{8\pi}\int dcos\theta\frac{\omega^{\prime 2}}{m\omega}\ .~~\mbox{\hskip 56.9055pt We have,}

\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{dcos\theta}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{4m\omega}\frac{1}{8\pi}\frac{(\omega^{\prime})^{2}}{m\omega}[\sum|\mathcal{M}|^{2}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{e^{4}}{16\pi}\frac{1}{m^{2}}\left(\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}\right)^{2}\left[\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}+\frac{\omega}{\omega^{\prime}}+\left\{2m\frac{-1+cos\theta}{m}+m^{2}\frac{(1-cos\theta)^{2}}{m^{2}}\right\}\right]

This give the differential cross-section for the Compton scattering,
known as
Klein-Nishina formula
,

\boxed{\left(\frac{d\sigma}{dcos\theta_{lab}}\right)=\frac{\pi\alpha^{2}}{m^{2}}\left(\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}\right)^{2}\left[\frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}+\frac{\omega}{\omega^{\prime}}-sin^{2}\theta_{lab}\right]\ ,\ \mbox{with}\ \frac{\omega^{\prime}}{\omega}=\frac{1}{1+{\textstyle\frac{\omega}{m}}(1-cos\theta)}.}

(14.30)

Remarks:

(a) There has been no approximation at the
\alpha^{2}
level computation. It
can now be used for various limits. At
\theta=0
, forward scattering,
there is no frequency change and the cross-section equaling

{\textstyle\frac{\pi\alpha^{2}}{m}}
is independent of the photon energy. For a
massive charged particle
, one defines its
Compton length
to be

\lambda_{c}:=h/(mc)=2\pi/m
in the natural units,
\hbar=1=c
.
The forward scattering cross-section is then
\alpha^{2}(\pi{\mathchar 22\mkern-9.0mu{\lambda}}^{2})
, where
{\mathchar 22\mkern-9.0mu{\lambda}}:=\lambda/(2\pi)
.

(b) There are two scales in the problems:
m,\omega
. This gives two
natural limits: (i)
\omega\to 0\leftrightarrow\omega/m\ll 1
and
(ii)
\omega\to\infty\leftrightarrow\omega/m\gg 1
.

For a generic
\theta
, consider
\omega\to 0
. Then
\omega/\omega^{\prime}\to 1+(\omega/m)(1-cos\theta)
and

\left.\frac{d\sigma}{dcos\theta}\right|_{\omega/m\ll 1}=\frac{\pi\alpha^{2}}{m^{2}}\left[1+cos^{2}\theta-4sin^{2}(\theta/2)\ \frac{\omega}{m}+\dots\right]~,~\sigma_{tot}=\frac{8\pi\alpha^{2}}{3m^{2}}+\dots

(14.31)

The leading term is the
Thomson cross-section
for classical
radiation scattering off free electrons.

In the opposite limit,
m/\omega\ll 1
, we have

\omega^{\prime}/\omega=\frac{m}{\omega}\frac{1}{1-cos\theta}\left(1-\frac{m}{\omega}\frac{1}{1-cos\theta}+\dots\right)~:=~\epsilon(1-\epsilon\dots)~~,~~\epsilon(\theta):=\frac{m}{\omega}\frac{1}{1-cos\theta}.

In this limit,

\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{dcos\theta}

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\frac{\pi\alpha^{2}}{m^{2}}\epsilon(\theta)~=~\frac{\pi\alpha^{2}}{m^{2}}\frac{m}{\omega(1-cos\theta)},

(14.32)

\displaystyle\sigma_{tot}(\delta):=\int_{-1}^{1-\delta}dcos\theta\frac{d\sigma}{dcos\theta}

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\frac{\pi\alpha^{2}}{m\omega}\left[-\ell n(\delta/2)\right]~\to\infty\ ,\ \mbox{as $\theta\to 0$}.

(14.33)

For the
\epsilon(\theta)\ll 1
condition to hold so that the expansion
is meaningful,
\theta\gg\sqrt{2m/\omega}
must hold. At
\theta=0

we know the exact answer which is finite.

14.3
Electron-Positron Annihilation:

Having evaluated the Compton scattering amplitude, this is actually
simple to evaluate. From the table giving the amplitudes (notice the use
of
p^{\prime}-k
and
k-p^{\prime}
momenta in the crossed diagrams), we can see that
the annihilation diagrams expressions are obtained by making the
substitutions:
\boxed{p\to p,k\to-k,p^{\prime}\to-p^{\prime},k^{\prime}\to k^{\prime}\ \mbox{and}\ \bar{u}\to\bar{v}.}
These substitutions preserve the
momentum conservations appropriate for the processes:
p+k=p^{\prime}+k^{\prime}\to p-k=-p^{\prime}+k^{\prime}
. The photon polarizations are insensitive to the ‘sign’ of
momentum and will give
\eta_{\mu\nu}
as before. One of the spin sums
however changes from
[-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}+m]\to[-(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}+m)]=[{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}-m]

which generates an
overall minus sign in the summed, squared
amplitude
. This is actually an example of what is known as the
crossing symmetry
of the
S-
matrix:
A scattering amplitude for a
particle with momentum
k
in the initial state is the same as the
amplitude with the initial particle moved to the final state
anti-particle with momentum
-k
.

Without any explicit calculation we can write down the summed squared
amplitude for the annihilation process as,

\sum_{spin/Pol}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}=(-)2e^{4}\left[-\left(\frac{p\cdot k^{\prime}}{p\cdot k}+\frac{p\cdot k}{p\cdot k^{\prime}}\right)+2m^{2}\left(\frac{1}{p\cdot k^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{p\cdot k}\right)+m^{4}\left(\frac{1}{p\cdot k}+\frac{1}{p\cdot k^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right]

(14.34)

It is more convenient to express the cross-section in the center of mass
frame:

\displaystyle p^{\mu}=(E,p\hat{z})

,

\displaystyle(p^{\prime})^{\mu}=(E,-p\hat{z})~,~E^{2}=p^{2}+m^{2}~~,~~s=-(p+p^{\prime})^{2}=4E^{2}

\displaystyle k^{\mu}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(E,Esin\Theta,0,Ecos\Theta)~,~(k^{\prime})^{\mu}=(E,-Esin\Theta,0,-Esin\Theta)

This gives,

\displaystyle p\cdot k

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-E^{2}+pEcos\Theta=-E(E-pcos\Theta)~,

\displaystyle p\cdot k^{\prime}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-E^{2}-pEcos\Theta=-E(E+pcos\Theta),

\displaystyle\frac{|k^{\prime}|_{cm}}{|k|_{cm}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{s^{2}-0+0^{2}}{s^{2}-2s(2m^{2})+0}}~=~\frac{1}{1-m^{2}/E^{2}}~=~\frac{E}{\sqrt{E^{2}-m^{2}}}=\frac{E}{p}

The differential cross-section takes the form,

\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega_{cm}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{64\pi^{2}}\frac{1}{4E^{2}}\frac{E}{|p|}\left(\sum_{spin/Pol}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}\right)\mbox{\hskip 56.9055ptwith}

\displaystyle\sum_{spin/Pol}|\mathcal{M}|^{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-2e^{4})\left[-\left(\frac{E+pcos\Theta}{E-pcos\Theta}+\frac{E-pcos\Theta}{E+pcos\Theta}\right)\right.

(14.36)

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 42.67912pt}+\frac{2m^{2}}{-E}\left(\frac{1}{E+pcos\Theta}+\frac{1}{E-pcos\Theta}\right)

\displaystyle\left.\mbox{\hskip 85.35826pt}+\frac{m^{4}}{E^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{E+pcos\Theta}+\frac{1}{E-pcos\Theta}\right)^{2}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4e^{4}\left[\frac{E^{2}+p^{2}cos^{2}\Theta}{E^{2}-p^{2}cos^{2}\Theta}+\frac{2m^{2}}{E^{2}-p^{2}cos^{2}\Theta}-\frac{2m^{4}}{(E^{2}-p^{2}cos^{2}\Theta)^{2}}\right]

(14.37)

The differential cross-section for unpolarized,
e^{+}e^{-}
annihilation
process is then given by,

\boxed{\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega_{cm}}=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{s}\frac{E}{|p|}\left[\frac{E^{2}+p^{2}cos^{2}\Theta+2m^{2}}{m^{2}+p^{2}sin^{2}\Theta}-\frac{2m^{4}}{(m^{2}+p^{2}sin^{2}\Theta)^{2}}\right]~~,~~s=4E^{2}\ .}

(14.38)

In the high energy limit,
E\gg m
, this reduces to,

\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega_{cm}}~\to~\frac{\alpha^{2}}{s}\left(\frac{1+cos^{2}\Theta}{sin^{2}\Theta}\right)

(14.39)

To obtain the total cross-section, we need to integrate over the final
state. Since the two photons a identical,
\Theta
needs to be
integrated between
0,\pi/2
. The Bose factor of 2 (which we did not
include in the amplitude) cancels the factor of 2 from the angular
integration. We get,

\sigma_{tot}~=~\frac{\alpha^{2}}{s}(2\pi)\int_{0}^{1}dx\frac{1+x^{2}}{1-x^{2}}

(14.40)

The integral is clearly divergent from the ‘forward’ direction (
\Theta=0
). This is artificial since we set
m=0
in the integrand. Split
the integration as
\int_{0}^{1-\Delta}+\int_{1-\Delta}^{1}
. The first
term is a finite number and this contribution falls off as
s^{-1}
. For
the second term, we go back to the exact differential cross-section,
approximate the integrand for
1-\Delta\leq cos(\Theta)\leq 1
. Then,
the factors of
E
all cancel and second term
\sim\alpha^{2}(1-\Delta)m^{-2}
where,
\Delta\ll m^{2}/p^{2}
so that the denominator can
be approximated. Thus, the total cross-section does
not
diverge
but is bounded by
m^{-2}
. This is an example of bounds satisfied by
total cross-sections at very high energies.

15
Numerical Estimates of Cross-sections and
Applications

We have obtained examples of cross-sections for some of the basic
processes in quantum electrodynamics. We also saw how they relate to
non-relativistic versions of the processes eg potential scattering and
inferred the modification due to relativistic effects as well as
estimate ‘strengths’ of interactions. Before we study the higher order
corrections, it is useful to have a sense of order of magnitudes of
cross-sections and how these numbers are used in applications. We will
focus on the QED processes.

What is the value of the fine structure constant?

This is related to the electric charge, the Planck constant due to
quantum framework and the speed of light due to special relativity. We
first obtain the expression in terms of “engineering units” and then
use the measured values to compute the fine structure constant.

Observe that the Feynman rules are derived from the Lagrangian density
which has properly normalized kinetic (quadratic) terms,

-{\textstyle\frac{1}{4}}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+i\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\Psi-m\bar{\Psi}\Psi
and the interaction term
introduces ‘
e
’ as
e\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\mu}\Psi A_{\mu}
and thus is
dimensionless. This definition gives the equation of motion,

\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=-e\bar{\Psi}\gamma^{\nu}\Psi\leftrightarrow\partial_{i}E^{i}=e\Psi^{\dagger}\Psi
, using the
identifications:
F^{0i}:=E^{i},\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=-J^{\nu},J^{\mu}=(\rho,J^{i})
. Furthermore, the Hamiltonian and hence the
energy density is
\vec{E}^{2}/2
.

The MKSA (SI) units has the Gauss law in the form:
\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{E}_{SI}=\rho_{SI}/\epsilon_{0}
. The field energy density (as
inferred from the Poynting theorem) is
\epsilon_{0}\vec{E}_{SI}^{2}/2
.
Comparing the energy densities, we introduce the identification,
E:=\sqrt{\epsilon_{0}}E_{SI}
Then
\rho=\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{E}=\sqrt{\epsilon_{0}}\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{E}_{SI}:=\sqrt{\epsilon_{0}}{\textstyle\frac{\rho_{SI}}{\epsilon_{0}}}
. This leads to the identification,

\boxed{e:={\textstyle\frac{e_{SI}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{0}}}}.}
Thus, we identify the
variables used in the action with those used in engineering variables by
comparing the equations of motion
and
the energy densities.

In the natural units,
\hbar=1=c
used in writing the action, the
fine structure constant was defined as
\alpha:=e^{2}/(4\pi)
which is
dimensionless as noted above. Substituting
e
in terms of
e_{SI}
and
introducing
\hbar,c
, we write
\alpha:={\textstyle\frac{e^{2}_{SI}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}}\hbar^{a}c^{b}
and determine the powers
a,b
by
requiring
\alpha
to be dimensionless. For this, we need the dimensions
of
e_{SI}
and
\epsilon_{0}
! Now we also use the SI expression of the
Lorentz force,
F=e_{SI}E_{SI}
. Hence,
dimensionally

(Force)
2
/(energy density)
\sim e^{2}_{SI}/\epsilon_{0}\sim M^{1}L^{3}T^{-2}
. This and
\alpha
being dimensionless gives
a=b=-1

and
\boxed{\alpha={\textstyle\frac{e^{2}_{SI}}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}\hbar c}}\simeq 1/137\ ,}
using the values:
(4\pi\epsilon_{0})^{-1}=c^{2}10^{-7},e_{SI}=1.6\times 10^{-19}
Coulomb,
\hbar\simeq 1.05\times 10^{-34}

Joules.sec and
c\simeq 3\times 10^{8}
m/sec.

An Aside:
Another set of units are commonly used in gravitational
physics, the so called
geometrized units
. These are defined by
setting
G=c=1
. The choice of
c=1
gives: 1 sec = 3
\times 10^{8}

meters. Newton’s constant in SI units is,
G\approx 6.67\times 10^{-11}kg^{-1}meter^{3}sec^{-2}
. Hence setting
G=1
along with
c=1
, gives
1 kg =
7.4\times 10^{-28}
meters.

It is conventional in gravitational physics to use the Gauss law in the
form
\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{E}=4\pi\rho
and the electric field energy
density as
E^{2}/(8\pi)
. This gives the identifications:
E_{geom}=\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}E_{SI}\ ,\ q_{geom}=q_{SI}/\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}
. As before, the Lorentz force equation gives the dimensions as:

[q^{2}_{SI}{\epsilon_{0}}]=[4\pi q^{2}_{geom}]=M^{1}L^{3}T^{-2}=L^{2}
.

Setting
q_{geom}={\textstyle\frac{q_{SI}}{\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}}}G^{\alpha}c^{\beta}
must have dimensions of
L
, we infer
\alpha=1/2
and

\beta=-2
and
\boxed{q_{geom}={\textstyle\frac{q_{SI}}{\sqrt{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}}}G^{1/2}c^{-2}=q_{SI}\sqrt{c^{2}\times 10^{-7}}G^{1/2}c^{-2}\approx(8.6\times 10^{-18})q_{SI}}
meters.

Looking at the expressions for the cross-sections and noting that in the
natural units energy
\sim
length
-1
, we see that the
cross-sections are of the form
\alpha/E^{2}
. This gets more and more
accurate at ultra relativistic energies where masses can be neglected.
Since the cross-section has dimensions of area while energies are
typically given in MeV/GeV/TeV etc, it is useful to have a conversion
between energy units and length units. As already notes,
c=1\Rightarrow 1
second
=3\times 10^{8}
meters.
\hbar=1\Rightarrow 1
Joule
=10^{34}sec^{-1}\simeq 3.3\times 10^{25}meter^{-1}
.
Next,
\boxed{100MeV=1.6\times 10^{-19+8}J\simeq 5\times 10^{14}meter^{-1}}
. (This is also expressed as
200MeV.fermi=1
). Clearly,
a cross-section at 100 MeV (electron mass being 0.5 Mev) is
approximately equal to
\boxed{\sigma_{100Mev}\simeq\alpha^{2}/E^{2}\simeq 2\times 10^{-33}m^{2}.}
The conventional unit for these
cross-sections is
1 barn := 100 fermi
2
=
10^{-28}m^{2}
.
Typical
numbers encountered in high energy processes (around 1 GeV) dominated by
strong interactions
\sim 10^{-30}m^{2}
, electromagnetic interactions

\sim 10^{-36}m^{2}
and weak interactions
\sim 10^{-42}m^{2}
.

So, scattering experiments will provide us with such numbers. How are
they
useful
?

In many applications, say passage of a collimated set of particles
through some medium, we have the estimate of the cross-section of
scattering of individual particles comprising the ‘beam’ and the medium.
Intuitively, a cross-section may be viewed as a target disk of area

\sigma
which is bombarded by ‘marbles’ which get reflected from the
disk. They are reflected if they hit the disk or pass by if not. Thus,

\sigma
gives the likelihood of a scattering interaction. Suppose we
have multiple targets (medium) and multiple beam particles. The
probability of interaction is clearly proportional to the ratio of the
effective area of the target particles and the area exposed to the beam

Target
Beam
Total Area

Thus, probability of scattering = (number of target particles exposed o
the beam)
\times\sigma
/Total area presented by the medium). Let
n
be
the number of target particles exposed per unit area perpendicular to
the beam. Then the number of particles exposed = n
\times
total area
and the
\boxed{\mbox{probability of scattering\ }=n\cdot\sigma.}

Let
\rho
be the number density of the target particles i.e. number per
unit volume. Let
d
be the thickness of the medium. Then the areal
density
n=\rho\cdot d
. The probability of scattering is
1n\sigma=\rho\cdot d\cdot\sigma
for
d=\hat{d}=(\rho\cdot\sigma)^{-1}
. Let

\langle v\rangle
be the average speed of the beam particles. Then the
average
reaction time :=

\tau_{r}:=\hat{d}/\langle v\rangle=1/(\rho\langle v\rangle\sigma)
.

Thus, if we have a confined plasma of say electrons and we bombard it
with a beam of positrons and look for production of
\mu^{\pm}
pairs,
then we should expect to wait for a time
\tau=1/(\rho\langle v\rangle\sigma_{e^{+}e^{-}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}})
. This type of use of microscopic
cross-sections is required in discussing bulk processes eg in
nuclear physics or astrophysics and are useful in estimating
thermalization times.

Sometimes, we aren’t interested in tracking individual processes, any
interaction may suffice. In such cases we need to sum over
all
possible final states
,
\sigma_{tot}=\sum_{f}\sigma_{i\to f}
. The

\sigma_{i\to f}\sim|\mathcal{M}_{i\to f}|^{2}
. We already have
expressions using phase space integration for fixed number of final
state particles. Now we have to sum over the number of particles and the
labels,

\sigma_{tot}=\frac{1}{4E_{k}E_{p}}v_{lab}\sum_{f,\alpha}\int\prod_{i=1}^{N_{f}}\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}_{j}}{2\omega_{k^{\prime}}(2\pi)^{3}}(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{4}(\Sigma k^{\prime}-P_{in})|\mathcal{M}|^{2}\ .

This can be related to the forward scattering amplitude via the
“Optical Theorem”.

We have
S^{\dagger}S=\mathbb{1}\Rightarrow\sum_{f}\langle i|S^{\dagger}|f\rangle\langle|S|i\rangle=1=\sum_{f}|S_{fi}|^{2}
.
Substituting for
S_{fi}
we get,

|S_{fi}|^{2}=\delta_{fi}\delta_{fi}+(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{4}(P_{f}-P_{i})\delta_{fi}[i(\mathcal{M}_{fi}-\mathcal{M}_{fi}^{*})]+(2\pi)^{8}[\delta^{4}(P_{f}-P_{i})]^{2}|\mathcal{M}_{fi}|^{2}\ .

Summing over
f
and using unitarity gives,

(2\pi)^{4}\sum_{f}\delta^{4}(P_{f}-P_{i})\delta_{fi}[i(\mathcal{M}_{fi}-\mathcal{M}_{fi}^{*})]=-(2\pi)^{8}\sum_{f}\delta^{4}(P_{f}-P_{i})\delta^{4}(P_{f}-P_{i})|\mathcal{M}_{fi}|^{2}

Or,

\boxed{2Im(\mathcal{M}_{ii})=(2\pi)^{4}\sum_{f}\delta^{4}(P_{f}-P-i)|\mathcal{M}_{fi}|^{2}.}

(15.1)

Substituting the rhs in the expression for
\sigma_{tot}
gives,

\sigma_{tot}=\frac{2Im(\mathcal{M}_{ii})}{4k\sqrt{s}}~~,~~\mbox{where, $k=k_{CM}$ and $s=-(\sum P_{i})^{2}$ \ .}

The
\mathcal{M}_{ii}
is the forward scattering,
i\to i
,
amplitude
and
\sigma_{tot}
is the inclusive cross-section for
i\to\mbox{any}f
processes. This could also be used to estimate the total
cross-section.

Remark:
Let us note that we defined the scattering matrix in
the basis of number states or Fock basis. Further, we chose the
idealization of plane waves for both in and out states. This is
convenient but looses the information about
spatial
locations of
the scattering particles. This also looses any notion of “impact
parameter” - how far the projectile particle is from the target
particle or equivalently the ‘orbital angular momentum’ of the
projectile about the target particle. The information about the
transverse position is of course contained in the parameters of the
outgoing particles. This should be kept in mind while interpreting some
of the divergences of cross-sections.

16
Radiative corrections in QED

Consider now corrections due to higher powers of interaction
Hamiltonian, also called
radiative corrections
. Having seen the
correspondence between the correction terms and Feynman diagrams, we can
list the corrections directly in terms of the diagrams. A Feynman
diagram is made up of lines (free propagators) and vertices. In QED,
there are two types of propagators and one types of vertex. So consider
corrections to two point functions and the three point function.

16.1
The fermion propagator: self-energy

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}}~+~\cdots

(16.2)

Here is a graphical expansion of the exact two point function of the
fermions. In the second line, the diagrams have been grouped into a
series of terms involving
1-particle irreducible (1PI)
blobs,
connected by free propagators. The 1PI blob represents the sum of all
diagrams with two external legs and which cannot be disconnected by
removing a single fermion line. The 2nd and the 3rd diagrams in the
first line are 1IP (their extreme propagators being the external lines)
while the last diagram is 1-particle reducible. The second line follows
from first one by inspection.

Let
iS^{\prime}_{F}(p)
denote the lhs - the full 2-point function or full
propagator - and
iS_{F}(p)
denote the free propagator. Let the 1PI blob
be denoted by
i\Sigma(p)
. Then the series is:

\displaystyle-iS^{\prime}_{F}(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-iS_{F}(p)+-iS_{F}\cdot i\Sigma(p)\cdot-iS_{F}+-iS_{F}\cdot i\Sigma\cdot-iS_{F}\cdot i\Sigma\cdot-iS_{F}+\dots

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-iS_{F}+-iS_{F}\cdot i\Sigma(-iS_{F}--iS_{F}\cdot i\Sigma\cdot-iS_{F}\dots)

\displaystyle\therefore-iS^{\prime}_{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-iS_{F}+-iS_{F}\cdot i\Sigma\cdot-iS^{\prime}_{F}

\displaystyle\therefore S_{F}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(1-S_{F}\Sigma)S^{\prime}_{F}~\leftrightarrow~\mathbb{1}=S^{-1}_{F}(-\Sigma)S^{\prime}_{F}~~~~\mbox{and}~~S_{F}^{-1}={\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m,

\displaystyle\therefore

\displaystyle\boxed{S_{F}^{\prime}(p)=\frac{\mathbb{1}}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m-\Sigma(p)}~,~~~\mbox{$\Sigma(p)$ is called the fermion
self energy.}}

The
S^{\prime}_{F}(p),\Sigma(p)
are matrices with the Dirac spinor indices
though we may not always be explicit about it. What can we say about its
singularities?

We can appeal to Lorentz covariance and decompose
\Sigma(p)=a(p^{2}){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+b(p^{2})\mathbb{1}+c(p^{2})\gamma_{5}
. With parity
conserving interactions such as qed, we can take
c(p^{2})=0
.
Furthermore,
to the leading order
,
a(p^{2})=0=b(p^{2})
. Thus the
denominator of the exact propagator is,

\displaystyle[S^{\prime}_{F}(p)]^{-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(1-a(p^{2})){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+(m-b(p^{2}))=(1-a(p^{2}))\left[{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+\frac{m-b(p^{2})}{1-a(p^{2})}\right]~~~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle S^{\prime}_{F}(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{1-a(p^{2})}\left[\frac{-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+\frac{m-b(p^{2})}{1-a(p^{2})}}{p^{2}+\left(\frac{m-b(p^{2})}{1-a(p^{2})}\right)^{2}}\right]

Clearly, the denominator vanishes for
p^{2}=-m_{ph}^{2},m_{ph}:={\textstyle\frac{m-b(-m_{ph}^{2})}{1-a(-m{ph}^{2})}}
. Since the numerator has the
form
-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m_{ph}
, we can regard the pole to be defined by

{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}
. Since
a,b
are functions of
p^{2}=-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}
, we may regard the self energy as a function of

{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}
and define the pole by the condition:
\boxed{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}=0.}
Clearly,
m_{ph}\neq m
.

The exact propagator can be expanded about its pole as,

\displaystyle{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0+({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m_{ph})\left[1-\frac{d\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})}{d{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}\right]+o(({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m_{ph})^{2})

\displaystyle\therefore S^{\prime}_{F}(p)

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\frac{1}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m_{ph}}\left[\frac{1}{1-\frac{d\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})}{d{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}}\right]~:=~\frac{Z_{2}}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m_{ph}}

The shift of the position of the pole in the exact propagator from that
of the free propagator,
\boxed{\delta m:=m_{ph}-m=-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph})}
is important in an
S-
matrix element which
has the spinors on the external lines. These spinors satisfy the
equation of motion with
physical mass
(=
m_{ph}
) and
not

the mass parameter in the free propagator inferred from the Lagrangian.
In particular this means that in the LSZ formula for
S-
matrix element,
the amputation of external fermion legs is to be done with

(-i{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.65451pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.13524pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.8724pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\partial}}}}+m_{ph})
. This in turn means that in the Green’s
functions with external fermion legs, the external lines must include
the self-energy corrections i.e. should have
S^{\prime}_{F}
propagator instead
of the free propagator
S_{F}
(and of course no more self energy
corrections on the external lines). We will return to this point later
again while discussing renormalized perturbation series.

We also see that the residue at the pole in the exact propagator is not
1 and we identify it with the
Z_{2}
which we know from the
Kallen-Lehmann representation to be
less than 1
.

(16.4)

Here is a graphical representation of the exact photon propagator. As
before, we group together the 1-PI diagrams connected by free
propagators. Let the exact propagator be denoted by
-iD^{\prime}_{\mu\nu}(q)

and the free propagator by
-iD_{\mu\nu}(q)
. Let the 1PI blob be
denoted by
i\Pi_{\mu\nu}(q)
. In the Lorentz gauge, the free propagator
is:
D_{\mu\nu}(q)=\eta_{\mu\nu}/(q^{2}-i\epsilon)
. While the series
can be formally summed as before, it is more convenient to separate the
tensor indices in the
\Pi_{\mu\nu}(q)
tensor.

Lorentz covariance implies,
\Pi_{\mu\nu}(q)=\eta_{\mu\nu}A(q^{2})+q_{\mu}q_{\nu}B(q^{2})
. The
\Pi_{\mu\nu}
tensor may be thought of as

\gamma\to\gamma
process, although
q^{2}\neq 0
. We now appeal to a

Ward identity:

q^{\mu}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(q)=0
. This is done
separately below. Presently, it implies
A(q^{2})=-q^{2}B(q^{2})
and we
define:
\boxed{\Pi_{\mu\nu}(q):=[\eta_{\mu\nu}q^{2}-q_{\mu}q_{\nu}]\Pi(q^{2})}
. With this notation, the exact 2-point
function takes the form,

\displaystyle-iD^{\prime}_{\mu\nu}(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\nu}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}+-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\alpha}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\cdot[i(q^{2}\eta^{\alpha\beta}-q^{\alpha}q^{\beta})\Pi(q)]\cdot-i\frac{\eta_{\beta\nu}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}+

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 85.35826pt}-iD_{\mu\alpha}\cdot[i(\dots)^{\alpha\beta}]\cdot-iD_{\beta\rho}\cdot[i(\dots)^{\rho\sigma}]\cdot-iD_{\sigma\nu}+\dots

Define,

i(q^{2}\eta^{\alpha\beta}-q^{\alpha}q^{\beta})(-i\eta_{\beta\nu}q^{-2})=\left(\delta^{\alpha}_{~\nu}-\frac{q^{\alpha}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right)=:\Delta^{\alpha}_{~\nu}~\Rightarrow~\Delta^{\alpha}_{~\nu}\Delta^{\nu}_{~\beta}=\Delta^{\alpha}_{~\beta}\ .

Then the exact propagator series takes the form,

\displaystyle-iD^{\prime}_{\mu\nu}(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\nu}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}+-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\alpha}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\Delta^{\alpha}_{~\nu}\Pi(q^{2})+-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\alpha}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\Delta^{\alpha}_{~\beta}\Delta^{\beta}_{~\nu}\Pi(q^{2})+\dots

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\nu}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}+-i\frac{\eta_{\mu\alpha}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\Delta^{\alpha}_{~\nu}(\Pi+\Pi^{2}+\Pi^{3}+\dots)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{-i}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\left[\left\{\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}+\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right\}+\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right)(\Pi+\Pi^{2}+\Pi^{3}\dots)\right]

\displaystyle\therefore D^{\prime}_{\mu\nu}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{q^{2}(1-\Pi(q^{2}))}\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right)+\frac{1}{q^{2}}\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}.

In any
S-
matrix calculation, the
D^{\prime}
propagator will land on a
fermion line and thanks to the Ward identity, the terms proportional to

q^{\mu},q^{\nu}
will vanish. Hence, for
S-
matrix element
computations
, we can take
\boxed{D^{\prime}_{\mu\nu}(q)={\textstyle\frac{\eta_{\mu\nu}}{(q^{2}-i\epsilon)(1-\Pi(q^{2}))}}}
. The
\Pi(q^{2})
is called the photon
self energy. To the leading order, the self energy vanishes and hence in
perturbation theory, it can never equal 1 and cause another pole at some
other
q^{2}
. As long as it is regular at
q^{2}=0
, the exact propagator

continues to have a simple pole at

q^{2}=0
, just like the free
propagator. Hence, the photon wavefunction,
\epsilon_{\mu}(\vec{k})

continues to be transverse and longitudinal polarizations will decouple.

Unlike the fermion self energy which shifts the mass, the photon self
energy does
not
shift the photon mass from zero thanks to the Ward
identity. However, like the fermion self energy, the residue at the
pole does shift away from 1,
\boxed{(Z_{3})^{-1}:=1-\Pi(q^{2}=0).}

16.2.1
The Ward identity claim:
q^{\mu}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(q)=0
:

\gamma_{1}
\gamma_{2}
\gamma_{i}
\gamma_{j}
\gamma_{i+1}
\gamma_{n}
p_{1}
p_{i}
p_{i}+q
p_{n}+q

Proof:
Recall that
\Pi_{\mu\nu}
is defined without
external propagators i.e. it is an amputated 2-point function. The
momentum
q
however, need not be on-shell and hence it does
not

correspond to an
S-
matrix element (even if we disregard the
polarization factors). Consider diagrams contributing to the photon self
energy with some fixed number of vertices (or order in the coupling).
The set of these diagrams will be generated by vertex injecting momentum

q^{\mu}
at various points on the available fermion lines. The fermion
lines will necessarily be loops as there are no external fermions
contributing to the photon self energy. Consider the subset of diagrams
wherein the
q^{\mu}
vertex is on some particular loop which
contributes a factor of the form: (the fermion arrow points from
i=1

to
i=n
and so do the fermion momenta)

Tr\left[S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{n}}\dots S_{F}(p_{i+1}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{i+1}}\left\{S_{F}(p_{i}+q){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}S_{F}(p_{i})\right\}\gamma^{\mu_{i}}\dots S_{F}(p_{1})\gamma^{\mu_{1}}\right]

The
q^{\mu}
vertex is inserted between the
i^{th}
and
(i+1)^{th}

vertices and adds the propagator
S_{F}(p_{i}+q)
. All momenta from

p_{i+1}
to
p_{n}
are shifted by
q
. We have also contracted with

q^{\mu}
. The expression between the braces simplifies as

13
13

13

This identity holds as long as both the fermion propagators
have the same mass,
m_{ph}
or
m
. This is relevant while dealing with
external fermion lines.
,

\frac{1}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}_{i}+{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}+m}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}\frac{1}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}_{i}+m}=\frac{1}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}_{i}+m}-\frac{1}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}_{i}+{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}+m}=S_{F}(p_{i})-S_{F}(p_{i}+q)\ .

The trace thus becomes,

\displaystyle Tr\left[S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{n}}\dots S_{F}(p_{i+1}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{i+1}}\left\{S_{F}(p_{i})\right\}\gamma^{\mu_{i}}\dots S_{F}(p_{1})\gamma^{\mu_{1}}\right]\mbox{\hskip 56.9055pt}

\displaystyle-Tr\left[S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{n}}\dots S_{F}(p_{i+1}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{i+1}}\left\{S_{F}(p_{i}+q)\right\}\gamma^{\mu_{i}}\dots S_{F}(p_{1})\gamma^{\mu_{1}}\right]

Note that the momenta after
i
(and
i-1
) have
q
added to them.
Summing over the diagrams where the
q^{\mu}
vertex is on this fermion
loop i.e from
i=1,\dots,n
, there is a pairwise cancellation. The
first term at
i
cancels the second term at
i+1
and so on. We are
left with the second term at
i=1
and the first term at
i=n
, i.e.

\sum_{i=1}^{n}Tr\left[\dots\right]=Tr\left[S_{F}(p_{n})\gamma^{\mu_{n}}\dots S_{F}(p_{1})\gamma^{\mu_{1}}\right]-Tr\left[S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{n}}\dots S_{F}(p_{1}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{1}}\right]

Because we have a fermion loop, there is an integration over say
p_{1}
.

Provided the integral is finite, we can shift the integration
variable and absorb away the
q
. The integrals of the two traces, then
cancel out and the claim is proved.

Remark:
We have not yet introduced loop diagrams. The above
fermion loop, before the
q
insertion, has
n
vertices and
n
momenta
entering at those vertices. The conservation of momenta, taking out the
overall conservation, thus leaves one momentum undetermined and this is
to be integrated.

Remark:
As an extension of the result, consider an open
fermion line with incoming momentum
p_{0}
, outgoing momentum
p_{n}
and
insertions on it.

\gamma_{1}
\gamma_{2}
\gamma_{i}
\gamma_{j}
\gamma_{i+1}
\gamma_{n-1}
\gamma_{n}
p_{0}
p_{1}
p_{i}
p_{i}+q
p_{n-1}+q
p_{n}+q

For the insertion between the
i,i+1
vertices, we will have a string
of factors as,

S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{n}}S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\dots\gamma^{\mu_{i+1}}\left\{S_{F}(p_{i}+q){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}S_{F}(p_{i})\right\}\gamma^{\mu_{i}}\dots S_{F}(p_{1})\gamma^{\mu_{1}}S_{F}(p_{0})

Replacing
S_{F}(p_{i}+q){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}S_{F}(p_{i})=S_{F}(p_{i})-S_{F}(p_{i}+q)
and
summing over the insertions from
i=0,\dots,n
, we get

\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}\left[\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle S_{F}(p_{n})\gamma^{\mu_{n}}S_{F}(p_{n-1})\dots S_{F}(p_{1})\gamma^{\mu_{1}}S(p_{0})

\displaystyle\mbox{\hskip 56.9055pt}-S_{F}(p_{n}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{n}}S_{F}(p_{n-1}+q)\dots S_{F}(p_{1}+q)\gamma^{\mu_{1}}S(p_{0}+q)

To get an
S-
matrix contribution, we have to multiply by

\bar{u}(p_{n}+q)[S_{F}(p_{n}+q)]^{-1}]
on the left and by

[S_{F}(p_{0})]^{-1}u(p_{0})
on the right and take the limits
p_{0}^{2}\to-m^{2},(p_{n}+q)^{2}\to-m^{2}
. Now we see that each of the two terms has
only one of the poles which can cancel the inverse propagator. In the
on-shell limit then, each of the terms vanishes, thereby proving that

for
S-
matrix elements with external fermion lines, sum over
insertion of photon lines followed by contraction with the photon
momentum gives zero.

Note:
There is one subtlety here. For external lines, we
should be using the exact propagator as per the LSZ rules. The

S{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}S
identity requires both propagators to have the same mass,
the physical mass. This would require all internal fermion lines to use the
exact propagator (and then do not consider the fermion self energy
correction). For fermion loop, this issue does not arise. Notice however
that
S^{\prime}_{F}(p)^{-1}=S_{F}(p)^{-1}-\Sigma(p)
and
\sigma(p)
is always
of order
\alpha
and higher. Thus, in using free inverse propagator
instead of exact inverse propagator, we are dropping a higher order
contribution which we can do in a perturbation theory.

The conclusion is then that
q_{\mu}\mathcal{M}^{\mu}(q,\dots)=0

which is a statement of Ward identity.

}}~+~\cdots

(16.6)

Notice that some corrections on the fermion lines and the photon line
are just self-energy corrections. The remaining corrections have photon
lines necessarily connecting the two fermion lines and these diagrams
are already 1PI. The last diagram in the second equation is 1PR.

We can simplify the form of the exact vertex function,

\Gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime})
by appealing to Lorentz covariance.

\Gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime})=\gamma^{\mu}A(q^{2})+(p^{\mu}+p^{{}^{\prime}\mu})B(q^{2})+(p^{{}^{\prime}\mu}-p^{\mu})C(q^{2})\ .

With two independent momenta, we have 3 Lorentz scalars,
p^{2},(p^{\prime})^{2},p\cdot p^{\prime}
. The first two equal
-m^{2}_{ph}
while the third is traded
for
q^{2}
for convenience.

Claim:

~\bar{u}(p^{\prime})q_{\mu}\Gamma^{\mu}u(p)=0
.

Proof:
This is the Ward identity argument given above.

The above form for
\Gamma^{\mu}
then implies,

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\bar{u}(p^{\prime}){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}u(p)A(q^{2})+(-m^{2}_{ph}+m^{2}_{ph})\bar{u}(p^{\prime})B(q^{2})iu(p)+q^{2}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})C(q^{2})u(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 0+0+q^{2}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})C(q^{2})u(p)~\Rightarrow~\bar{u}(p^{\prime})C(q^{2})u(p)=0~.

The
A,B
terms can be rewritten using “Gordon identity”,

\boxed{\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)=\frac{1}{2m_{ph}}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\left[(p+p^{\prime})^{\mu}-2i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}\right]u(p)}

This can be established as follows (
m_{ph}\to m
for convenience):

We have,
u(p)=-{\textstyle\frac{1}{m}}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}u(p)\ ,\ \bar{u}(p^{\prime})=-{\textstyle\frac{1}{m}}\bar{u}(p^{\prime}){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}
. Therefore

\displaystyle\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2m}(\gamma^{\mu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}\gamma^{\mu})~~\mbox{But,}~~\gamma^{\mu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=p_{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}=p_{\nu}\left(-\eta^{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}[\gamma^{\mu},\gamma^{\nu}]\right)

\displaystyle\therefore\gamma^{\mu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-p^{\mu}-2i\Sigma^{\mu\nu}p_{\nu}~~,~~{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}\gamma^{\mu}=-(p^{\prime})^{\mu}-2i\Sigma^{\nu\mu}p^{\prime}_{\nu}~~,~~\Sigma^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{i}{4}[\gamma^{\mu},\gamma^{\nu}]\ ;

\displaystyle\therefore\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2m}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\left[-p^{\mu}-(p^{\prime})^{\mu}-4i\Sigma^{\mu\nu}(p_{\nu}-p^{\prime}_{\nu})\right]u(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2m}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})[(p+p^{\prime})^{\mu}-2i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}]u(p)~~~,~~~\sigma^{\mu\nu}:=2\Sigma^{\mu\nu}~,~q:=p^{\prime}-p\ .

Eliminating the
(p+p^{\prime})^{\mu}
from the
B(q^{2})
term, and identifying

A+2m_{ph}B=:F_{1}(q^{2})
and
4\Sigma^{\mu\nu}B(q^{2})=:{\textstyle\frac{\sigma^{\mu\nu}}{2m_{ph}}}F^{2}(q^{2})
, we take the general form of

\Gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime})
as,

\boxed{\Gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime})=\gamma^{\mu}F_{1}(q^{2})+i\frac{\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}}{2m_{ph}}F_{2}(q^{2})~,~q:=p^{\prime}-p\ .}

The
F_{i}(q^{2})
are called
form factors.
To the lowest order,

F_{1}(q^{2})=1,F_{2}(q^{2})=0
. These get corrected at higher orders.

16.4
Electric Charge and Anomalous Magnetic Moment

The form factor decomposition helps us identify the
electric
charge
and the
anomalous magnetic moment
of electron (and other
charged fermions). This is seen as follows.

Consider the scattering of an electron off a heavy charged particle. We
imagine the scattering to be effected by exchanging a single photon
between the heavy charge and the electron. Schematically the amplitude
can be written as,

i\mathcal{M}=ie^{2}\ [\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\Gamma^{\mu}(p^{\prime},p)u(p)]\ \frac{1}{q^{2}}\ [\bar{u}(k^{\prime})\gamma_{\mu}u(k)]

The first factor is from electron, second is the single photon
propagator and the third factor is from the heavy charge. The
\Gamma

vertex has only 1PI diagrams and excludes the photon self energy on the
propagator. This represents the modification of the electron response
due to the 1PI corrections, the photon self energy would indicate
modification in the electromagnetic field felt by the electron and hence
is also referred to as
vacuum polarization
. This is ignored in
this calculation.

In the limit of infinitely heavy fermion, the second
and third factors are replaced by an external classical potential

A_{\mu}(q)
and the amplitude is defined as,

i\mathcal{M}\ (2\pi)\ \delta((p^{\prime}-p)^{0})=-ie\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\Gamma^{\mu}u(p)\tilde{A}^{cl}_{\mu}(p^{\prime}-p)

We consider two cases - Coulomb potential and magnetic field, and
consider non-relativistic limit of the scattering.

Coulomb potential:

A^{cl}_{\mu}(x)=(\phi(x),\vec{0})
.
Coulomb field is static and we also assume it to be slowly varying
spatially. This means that we take
\tilde{A}^{cl}_{\mu}(q)=2\pi\delta(q^{0})(\tilde{\phi}(q),\vec{0})
with the

\tilde{\phi}(q)
having support near
q\simeq 0
. We can thus take the
limit
q\to 0
of the first factor. This in turn means that only the

F_{1}
term contributes. In the non-relativistic limit,

\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)\to\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{0}u(p)=2mu^{\dagger}(p)u(p)
and the amplitude takes the form,
i\mathcal{M}\to-ieF_{1}(0)\tilde{\phi}(q)(2mu^{\dagger}(p)u(p))
. Comparing with the
Born approximation for scattering off a potential leads to
the identification,
V(x)=eF_{1}(0)\phi(\vec{x})
. Thus,

\boxed{\mbox{electric charge}=eF(0).}
Since
F_{1}(0)=1
at the
leading order, the radiative corrections to
F_{1}(q^{2})
should vanish as

q^{2}\to 0
.

Magnetic field:

A_{\mu}^{cl}=(0,\vec{A}^{cl}_{i}(x))
.
Again this is taken to be time independent and spatially slowly varying.
Thus we consider the limit
q\to 0
. Earlier, we dropped the
F_{2}

term, because
F_{1}
term was non-zero. Now however
\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{i}u(p)\simeq o(p/m)
in the non-relativistic limit which is
comparable to the
F_{2}
term.

Recall from the NR limit of the Dirac spinors,
u^{T}:=(u_{1}^{T},u_{2}^{T}),\ ({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m)u(p)=0\Rightarrow u_{2}(p)\simeq-{\textstyle\frac{\vec{p}\cdot\vec{\sigma}}{2m}}u_{1}
and we have the normalization
u^{\dagger}u(p)=2m
. We also had,

\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{i}u(p)\simeq u_{1}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\sigma^{i}u_{2}(p)+u_{2}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\sigma^{i}u_{1}(p)\simeq-\frac{1}{2m}u_{1}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\{\sigma^{i}\vec{p}\cdot\vec{\sigma}+\vec{p}^{\prime}\cdot\vec{\sigma}\sigma^{i}\}u_{1}(p).

Using
\sigma^{i}\sigma^{j}=\delta^{ij}+i\epsilon^{ij}_{~k}\sigma^{k}
, we
get,

\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\vec{\gamma}\cdot\vec{A}^{cl}u(p)=-\frac{1}{2m}u_{1}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\left(\vec{p}\cdot\vec{A}^{cl}+\vec{p}^{\prime}\cdot\vec{A}^{cl}-iA_{i}^{cl}\epsilon^{ij}_{~k}q_{j}\sigma^{k}\right)u_{1}(p)

Noting that
q^{0}=0
, the
F_{2}
term has
\sigma^{ij}q_{j}
. Going over
to the two component spinors, we get

\displaystyle\frac{i}{2m}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\sigma^{ij}u(p)q_{j}

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\frac{i}{2m}\epsilon^{ij}_{~k}[u_{1}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\sigma^{k}u_{1}(p)]

The contribution of the
u_{2}
spinors is negligible in the NR limit.

Combining the terms we get in the NR limit,

\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\Gamma^{i}u(p)\tilde{A}_{i}^{cl}(q)\approx u_{1}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\left[\frac{(\vec{p}+\vec{p}^{\prime})\cdot\vec{A}^{cl}}{2m}F_{1}(0)-\frac{i}{2m}\epsilon^{ij}_{~k}q_{j}A^{cl}_{i}\sigma^{k}(F_{1}(0)+F_{2}(0))\right]u_{1}(p)

In the non-relativistic Hamiltonian,
(p-eA)^{2}/(2m)
we have the

e(p\cdot+A\cdot p)
terms which are recovered. The remaining terms
however are new. Focusing only on those, we write the amplitude as,

i\mathcal{M}=-ieu_{1}^{\dagger}(p^{\prime})\left[-\frac{1}{2m}(F_{1}(0)+F_{2}(0))\sigma^{k}B_{k}\right]u_{1}(p)~~,~~B_{k}:=-i\epsilon_{k}^{~ij}q_{i}\tilde{A}_{j}^{cl}(q)\ .

This amplitude is interpreted as the Born approximation to a potential
scattering with potential,
V(x)=-\langle\vec{\mu}\rangle\cdot\vec{B}(\vec{x})
, with the effective magnetic moment,

\boxed{\langle\vec{\mu}\rangle=\frac{e}{m_{ph}}[F_{1}(0)+F_{2}(0)]u_{1}^{\dagger}(p)\frac{\vec{\sigma}}{2}u_{1}(p):=g\frac{e}{2m_{ph}}\vec{S}~,~g:=2[F_{1}(0)+F_{2}(0)]=2[1+F_{2}(0)].}

g
is called the
Lande’s g-factor
, its value being
2
is
prediction of Dirac equation while
F_{2}(0)\neq 0
is a prediction of
QED. It is called the
anomalous magnetic moment
.

Without actually calculating the higher order corrections, we noted what
they mean for 2-point functions (self-energies). We used Lorentz
covariance to get a form factor decomposition and interpreted them by
appealing to the NR limit. One of the immediate prediction was the
anomalous magnetic moment.

We also note that to the leading order (see diagrams), we have
Z^{-1}_{2}=1,Z^{-1}_{3}=1,F_{1}(q^{2})=1,F_{2}(q^{2})=0
. This is the reason that
at the tree level calculations that we did, did not have any factors of

Z
’s. This will change when we do explicit evaluations of the leading
corrections in the next section.

17
Radiative corrections at 1-loop: Divergences

We now calculate the leading radiative corrections to the self energies
and the QED vertex function i.e. the 1-loop contributions to

\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}),\Pi(q^{2}),F_{1}(q^{2}),F_{2}(q^{2})

diagrams and the corresponding invariant amplitudes.

QED Vertex function,
\delta\Gamma^{\mu}:=\Gamma^{\mu}-\gamma^{\mu}

q
p^{\prime}-k
k
