p^{\prime}
p

\displaystyle\delta\Gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(ie)^{2}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{-i\eta_{\alpha\beta}}{(k)^{2}+\mu^{2}-i\epsilon}\times

\displaystyle\left[\gamma^{\alpha}\frac{-i(-({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}})+m)}{(p^{\prime}-k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\gamma^{\mu}\frac{-i(-({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}})+m)}{(p-k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\gamma^{\beta}\right]

In the photon self energy expression, the
(-1)
is due to the fermion
loop. The photon propagator is added a small mass
\mu^{2}
in
anticipation. In the vertex correction, the expression is understood to
be sandwiched between
\bar{u}(p^{\prime})
and
u(p)
.

There are some new points to be noted.

\bullet
There is a momentum integration over
k
, unrelated to the
external momenta. This
k
can be space-like, time-like or light-like.
In any frame, we may consider the region where
k^{\mu}\to\infty
,
then: (i) the electron self-energy
\sim\int d^{4}kk^{\alpha}/k^{4}\sim\int dk
which is naively
linearly divergent
; (ii) the photon
self-energy
\sim\int d^{4}k/k^{2}\sim\int kdk
which is naively

quadratically divergent
and (iii) the vertex correction
\sim d^{4}kk^{2}/k^{6}\sim\int dk/k
which is naively
logarithmically
divergent
.

\bullet
There are also other regions of integration space which give
divergent contributions, but these will be visible after the integrand
is put in a convenient form.

\bullet
The
i\epsilon
in the denominator is quite significant now.
It implies that the 4-dimensional integration must be defined with the

k^{0}
integration being done first and the spatial integrations done
subsequently.

\bullet
The naively divergent integrals need to be
regularised

i.e. a prescription for the integration must be supplied which will
manifest the divergence in an explicit form. The divergent contribution
so obtained, must be
subtracted
to obtain finite answers. This is
the process of
renormalization
.

\bullet
The integrand has a numerator which has tensor/spinor indices
while the denominator is a product of scalar factors. One combines the
denominator factors into a single factor form using the so called
Feynman parameters
. This is followed by the momentum integration with a
regularization and a finite part is identified. The integration over the
Feynman parameters is done last to get the answer. We explain these
steps now.

The Feynman/Schwinger trick:

\mbox{Claim:\hskip 14.22636pt}\frac{1}{A_{1}\dots A_{n}}=(n-1)!\int_{0}^{\infty}dx_{1}\dots dx_{n}\frac{\delta(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}-1)}{(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}A_{i})^{n}}.

Proof: Observe that
A^{-1}=\int_{0}^{\infty}d\alpha e^{-\alpha A}~,~Re(A)>0
. Therefore,

\displaystyle\frac{1}{A_{1}\dots A_{n}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}d\alpha_{1}\dots d\alpha_{n}e^{-\Sigma_{i}\alpha_{i}A_{i}}\cdot 1~~,~~1=\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\delta(t-\Sigma_{i}\alpha_{i})~~\mbox{and}~~\alpha_{i}\to tx_{i},

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\int_{0}^{\infty}dx_{1}\dots dx_{n}\ t^{n}e^{-t\Sigma_{i}x_{i}A_{i}}\ \frac{1}{t}\ \delta(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}-1)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dx_{1}\dots dx_{n}\delta(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}-1)\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\ t^{n-1}e^{-t(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}A_{i})}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(n-1)!\int_{0}^{\infty}dx_{1}\dots dx_{n}\frac{\delta(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}-1)}{(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}A_{i})^{n}}~~\because~\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\ t^{n-1}e^{-t\Lambda}=\Lambda^{-n}\Gamma(n)\ .

Note:
Since each of the denominator factors are of the form

A_{i}=(p_{i}-k)^{2}+m_{i}^{2}-i\epsilon
, we see that

\displaystyle\Sigma_{i}x_{i}A_{i}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle k^{2}-2k\cdot(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}p_{i})+\Sigma_{i}x_{i}(p_{i}^{2}+m_{i}^{2})-i\epsilon

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(k-\Sigma_{i}x_{i}p_{i})^{2}+M^{2}-i\epsilon~~,~M^{2}(x_{i},p_{i},m_{i}):=\Sigma_{i}x_{i}(p_{i}^{2}+m_{i}^{2})-(\Sigma_{i}x_{i}p_{i})^{2}\ .

The obvious step is to shift the integration variable,
k\to k+\Sigma_{i}x_{i}p_{i}
which simplifies the denominator - it has the same
form of a single propagator with the same
-i\epsilon
.

Let us begin with the fermion self energy.

17.1
Isolation of Divergence: Fermion Self Energy

i\Sigma(p)=(ie)^{2}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\gamma^{\mu}\frac{-i(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+m)}{k^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\gamma^{\nu}\frac{-i\eta_{\mu\nu}}{(p-k)^{2}+\mu^{2}-i\epsilon}

The Feynman trick gives,

\frac{1}{(k^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon)((p-k)^{2}+\mu^{2}-i\epsilon)}=\int_{0}^{1}dx\frac{1}{[(k-xp)^{2}+M^{2}-i\epsilon]^{2}}~,

with,
M^{2}:=x(1-x)p^{2}+(1-x^{2})m^{2}+x\mu^{2}
. Shifting
k\to k+xp
, and using
\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{\mu}=-4\mathbb{1},\gamma^{\mu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}\gamma_{\mu}=2{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}
, gives

i\Sigma=e^{2}\int_{0}^{1}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{-4m-2({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+x{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 4.46007pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{)p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 4.46007pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{)p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.62367pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{)p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.20345pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{)p}}}}}{[k^{2}+M^{2}(x,p)-i\epsilon]^{2}}

Recalling that the
k^{0}
integration is to be done first and that the
poles are at
k^{0}=\pm\sqrt{\vec{k}^{2}+M^{2}}\mp i\epsilon
, we rotate
the contour anti-clockwise without crossing any singularity. This is
equivalent to putting
k^{0}=i\underline{k}^{0}
and
k^{2}\to(\underline{k}^{0})^{2}+\vec{k}^{2}=
Euclidean vector norm. This sends
\int d^{4}k\to i\int d^{4}\underline{k}
. For Euclidean integrals
\int d^{4}\underline{k}{\textstyle\frac{\underline{k}^{\alpha}\gamma_{\alpha}}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M^{2})^{2}}}=0
, since the integrand is odd under
k\to-k
. We are left with,

i\Sigma=-ie^{2}\int_{0}^{1}dx\int\frac{d^{4}\underline{k}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{4m+2x{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M^{2})^{2}}~~,~~M^{2}:=x(1-x)p^{2}+(1-x^{2})m^{2}+x\mu^{2}

The
k-
integral is logarithmically divergent and needs to be regulated.
There are several ways of doing this. One is the
Pauli-Villars

regularization which subtracts from the photon propagator, another
identical piece with arbitrarily large mass squared,
\Lambda^{2}
, i.e.

\frac{1}{(p-k)^{2}+\mu^{2}}\to\frac{1}{(p-k)^{2}+\mu^{2}}-\frac{1}{(p-k)^{2}+\Lambda^{2}}.

For large
\underline{k}
, both terms go as
\underline{k}^{-2}
and
cancel each other leaving a finite answer. Thus
i\Sigma\to i\Sigma_{reg}:=i\Sigma(\Lambda=\infty)-i\Sigma(\Lambda)
. The same
combining of denominators will produce identical terms with
M^{2}(\mu^{2})\to M^{2}(\Lambda^{2})
. The momentum integration becomes,

\int\frac{d^{4}\underline{k}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\left[\frac{1}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M_{\mu}^{2})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M_{\Lambda}^{2})^{2}}\right]=\int\frac{d\Omega_{3}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dk|k|^{3}\left[\dots\right]

The angular integration gives:
\Omega_{n-1}={\textstyle\frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}}=2\pi^{2}
for
n=4
and the integral becomes,

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{4}\underline{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\left[\dots-\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dy}{2}\left[\frac{y}{(y+M_{\mu}^{2})^{2}}-\frac{y}{(y+M_{\Lambda}^{2})^{2}}\right]~~,~~k^{2}=:y~\mbox{substituted.}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{16\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dy\left[\frac{1}{y+M_{\mu}^{2}}-\frac{1}{y+M^{2}_{\Lambda}}-\frac{M^{2}_{\mu}}{(y+M_{\mu}^{2})^{2}}+\frac{M^{2}_{\Lambda}}{(y+M^{2}_{\Lambda})^{2}}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{16\pi^{2}}\left[ln\left(\frac{y+M_{\mu}^{2}}{y+M^{2}_{\Lambda}}\right)_{0}^{\infty}+\left(\frac{M_{\mu}^{2}}{y+M^{2}_{\mu}}-\frac{M_{\Lambda}^{2}}{y+M^{2}_{\Lambda}}\right)_{0}^{\infty}\right]

\displaystyle\therefore\int\frac{d^{4}\underline{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\left[\dots-\dots\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{16\pi^{2}}ln\left(\frac{M_{\Lambda}^{2}}{M_{\mu}^{2}}\right)\ .

In the limit
\Lambda\to\infty,M^{2}_{\Lambda}\to x\Lambda^{2}
and we
get,

\boxed{i\Sigma(p)=-i\frac{e^{2}}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ (2m+x{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})ln\left[\frac{x\Lambda^{2}}{x(1-x)p^{2}+(1-x)m^{2}+x\mu^{2}}\right]}

(17.1)

Recall that the mass shift as well as the
Z_{2}
are obtained from the
self energy as,
\delta m:=m_{ph}-m=-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}),Z_{2}^{-1}=1-{\textstyle\frac{\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})}{d{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}}|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}
.
Since the self energy already has an explicit factor of
e^{2}
, in the
integrand, we can use
{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}\approx-m
. The derivative of

\Sigma
is obtained as,

\displaystyle\left.\frac{d\Sigma}{d{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}\right|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ \left[xln\left(\frac{x\Lambda^{2}}{-x(1-x)m^{2}+(1-x)m^{2}+x\mu^{2}}\right)+\right.

\displaystyle\left.(2m-x\cdot m)\frac{-1}{-x(1-x)m^{2}+(1-x)m^{2}+x\mu^{2}}(-2x(1-x)(-m))\right]

Simplification leads to,

\boxed{\left.\frac{d\Sigma}{d{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}\right|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}=\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ \left[-xln\left(\frac{x\Lambda^{2}}{(1-x)^{2}m^{2}+x\mu^{2}}\right)+2(2-x)\frac{x(1-x)m^{2}}{(1-x)^{2}m^{2}+x\mu^{2}}\right]}

(17.2)

\boxed{\delta m=-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph})=\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ (2-x)ln\left(\frac{x\Lambda^{2}}{(1-x)^{2}m^{2}+x\mu^{2}}\right)}

(17.3)

The integrands are well behaved at both end points so the integrals are
finite and the leading contribution is given by the
\Lambda^{2}

dependent part alone and for dimensional reasons we divide by the
fermion mass. Thus, the
divergent contributions
as
\Lambda\to\infty
take the form,

\displaystyle\delta m

\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx(2-x)ln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2})=\frac{3\alpha}{4\pi}ln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2})

\displaystyle Z_{2}^{-1}

\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow

\displaystyle 1-\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(-xln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2}))=1+\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}ln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2})\Rightarrow Z_{2}\approx 1-\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}ln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2})

The logarithmic divergence is thus manifested in terms of

ln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2})
. There are of course finite pieces, but until we
take care of the divergent parts the finite parts are irrelevant.

17.2
Isolation of Divergence: Photon Self-Energy

i\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)=-e^{2}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{Tr[\gamma^{\mu}(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+m)\gamma^{\nu}(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}}+m)]}{(k^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon)((k+q)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon)}

Using the trace formulae for the Dirac matrices (
14.4
), we
get

Numerator:

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle Tr[\gamma^{\mu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}\gamma^{\nu}({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}+{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.41145pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.95816pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.73698pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{q}}}})+m^{2}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4[k^{\mu}(k+q)^{\nu}-\eta^{\mu\nu}k\cdot(k+q)+(k+q)^{\mu}k^{\nu}-m^{2}\eta^{\mu\nu}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4[2k^{\mu}k^{\nu}-\eta^{\mu\nu}(k^{2}+m^{2})+(k^{\mu}k^{\nu}+k^{\nu}q^{\mu}-\eta^{\mu\nu}k\cdot q)]

Denominator:

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{k^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\frac{1}{(k+q)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dx\ \frac{1}{[(k+xq)^{2}+x(1-x)q^{2}+m^{2}]^{2}}~~~~\mbox{shift~}k\to k-xq,

The shift generates additional terms linear in
k
in the numerator.
Under integration, these terms drop out and we are left with,

\displaystyle i\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-4e^{2})\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{\left\{2k^{\mu}k^{\nu}+2x^{2}q^{\mu}q^{\nu}-\eta^{\mu\nu}(k^{2}+x^{2}q^{2}+m^{2})-x(2q^{\mu}q^{\nu}-\eta^{\mu\nu}q^{2})\right\}}{(k^{2}+M^{2}-i\epsilon)^{2}}

where,
\boxed{M^{2}=x(1-x)q^{2}+m^{2}}
. Doing Wick rotation as before,

\displaystyle i\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-4e^{2})i\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{\left\{2\underline{k}^{\mu}\underline{k}^{\nu}-2x(1-x)q^{\mu}q^{\nu}+x(1-x)\eta^{\mu\nu}q^{2}-\eta^{\mu\nu}(\underline{k}^{2}+m^{2})\right\}}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M^{2}-i\epsilon)^{2}}

The tensorial integral,

\int\frac{d^{4}\underline{k}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{\underline{k}^{\mu}\underline{k}^{\nu}}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M^{2})^{2}}=A\delta^{\mu\nu}~~,~~\mbox{with}~~A=\frac{1}{4}\int\frac{d^{4}\underline{k}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{\underline{k}^{2}}{(\underline{k}^{2}+M^{2})^{2}}

There are several problems to be faced now. First, the integral is
quadratically divergent and shift in the momentum variable is
unjustified. Second, we have now
\delta^{\mu\nu}
and
\eta^{\mu\nu}

in the numerator, confusing Lorentz covariance. Third, naively we see a
quadratically divergent piece with coefficient
\eta^{\mu\nu}
but only
logarithmically divergent one with coefficient
q^{\mu}q^{\nu}
casting
doubts on possibility of gauge invariance. We could try the
Pauli-Villars regulation, but we will introduce a different one, the

dimensional regularization
. The Pauli-Villars may be seen in

PeskinSchroder
. The dimensional regularization has the main
virtue of keeping the Ward identity satisfied, even for non-abelian
gauge theories.

The idea is to think of the perturbation theory to be a member of a
class of similar theories formulated in general
n
dimensions. One
chooses a value of
n
where the integrals are well defined (
n<4
)
and analytically continues
n\to 4
. This isolates the original
divergence in a particular form (poles) providing the needed
regularization. Since the mass/length dimensions also depend on
space-time dimensions we need the coupling constants to be
dimensionfull. To maintain space-time covariance, we need to regard the
external momenta and the
\gamma
matrices etc also to be

n-
dimensional. We set
\epsilon:=4-n
and consider the limit

\epsilon\to 0
. Since the integrals are over Euclidean momenta due to
the Wick rotation,
the external momenta and the metric tensor need to
continue back to Minkowski signature at the end of the calculations
.

In this regularization scheme, the following rules are adopted.

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{n}k}{(2\pi)^{n}}f(|k|^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\Omega_{n-1}}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int dk|k|^{n-1}f(|k|^{2})~~,~~\boxed{\int d\Omega_{n-1}=\frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}}

(17.4)

\displaystyle\therefore\int\frac{d^{n}k}{(2\pi)^{n}}f(|k|^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left[\frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}\right]\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int dkk^{n-1}f(k^{2})

(17.5)

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}dk\frac{k^{n-1}}{(k^{2}+M^{2})^{\alpha}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}dx\frac{x^{{\textstyle\frac{n}{2}}-1}}{(x+M^{2})^{\alpha}}~~,~~\mbox{put}~y=\frac{M^{2}}{x+M^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{M^{n-2\alpha}}{2}\int_{0}^{1}dyy^{\alpha-1-{\textstyle\frac{n}{2}}}(1-y)^{{\textstyle\frac{n}{2}}-1}=\frac{M^{n-2\alpha}}{2}\beta(\alpha-n/2,n/2)

\boxed{\therefore\int_{0}^{\infty}dk\frac{k^{n-1}}{(k^{2}+M^{2})^{\alpha}}=\frac{M^{n-2\alpha}}{2}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha-n/2)\Gamma(n/2)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}}

(17.6)

and

\boxed{\int\frac{d^{n}k}{(2\pi)^{n}}\frac{1}{(k^{2}+M^{2})^{\alpha}}~=~\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{n/2}}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha-n/2)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}(M^{2})^{n/2-\alpha}}

(17.7)

The
\Gamma
function has isolated poles at
\alpha-n/2=0,-1,-2,\dots
i.e. at
n=2(\alpha+m),m=0,1,\dots.
The Gamma

\Gamma(\epsilon/2)=2/\epsilon-\gamma+o(\epsilon)
where,
\gamma=0.57721\dots
is the
Euler-Mascheroni Constant
.

Since finite parts can be affected we need to keep
\epsilon
in various
place too eg
\{\gamma^{\mu},\gamma^{\nu}\}=-2\delta^{\mu\nu}\mathbb{1},Tr(\mathbb{1})=n=4-\epsilon,\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}\gamma_{\mu}=(2-\epsilon)\gamma^{\nu}

terms will give contributions from the
1/\epsilon
terms. The coupling
constant dimensions work as follows.
[\Psi]=(n-1)/2,[A_{\mu}]=(n-2)/2\Rightarrow[e]=n-(n-1)-(n/2-1)=\epsilon/2
. Therefore
we write
e\to e\mu_{0}^{\epsilon/2}
where
\mu_{0}
is an arbitrary mass
scale which should disappear from physical quantities. The dimensions
are in mass units. The tensorial integral will now follow from

k^{\mu}k^{\nu}\to{\textstyle\frac{1}{n}}\delta^{\mu\nu}k^{2}
. We use these in
evaluating the
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)
.

\displaystyle\Pi(q^{2})

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle-ne^{2}\mu_{0}^{\epsilon}\int_{0}^{1}dx\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{2}}\left(\frac{M^{2}}{4\pi}\right)^{-\epsilon/2}\Gamma(\epsilon/2)(2x)(1-x)

\displaystyle-\frac{2(4-\epsilon)e^{2}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)\left\{\frac{2}{\epsilon}-\gamma\right\}\left\{ln\left(\frac{4\pi\mu_{0}^{2}}{M^{2}}\right)\frac{\epsilon}{2}+1\right\}

Using
a^{\epsilon/2}=1+{\textstyle\frac{\epsilon}{2}}ln(a)+o(\epsilon^{2})
, we

\boxed{\Pi(\underline{q}^{2})=-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)\left(\frac{2}{\epsilon}-\gamma\right)\left(1+\frac{\epsilon}{2}ln\left(\frac{4\pi\mu_{0}^{2}}{M^{2}}\right)\left(1-\frac{\epsilon}{4}\right)\right)}

(17.8)

Notice that for
\underline{q}^{2}

and

\boxed{\Pi(0)=-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\frac{2}{\epsilon}\int_{0}^{1}dx(x-x^{2})+\mbox{constant}\ =-\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}\frac{1}{\epsilon},}~\Rightarrow~\boxed{Z_{3}=1-\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi\epsilon}\ }

(17.9)

We see the divergence in
\Pi(0),Z_{3}
and there is of course no mass
shift. We return to the interpretation of
\Pi(q^{2})
later.

Remark:
The
\epsilon^{-1}
pole in dimensional
regularization corresponds to logarithmic divergence in Pauli-Villars.
this is indicated by comparing the regulated integral

\int[(k^{2}+M^{2})^{-2}-(k^{2}\Lambda^{2})^{-2}]
in Pauli-Villars, which
goes over to
{\textstyle\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}}ln(x\Lambda^{2}/M^{2})
. In the dimensional
regularization, our integral
2
goes as

{\textstyle\frac{1}{4\pi^{2}}}{\textstyle\frac{2}{\epsilon}}
. Hence,
\epsilon^{-1}\leftrightarrow ln(\Lambda/M)
. Thanks to the dimensional regularization
maintaining the Ward identity, the
q^{2}\delta^{\mu\nu}-q^{\mu}q^{\nu}

got pulled out and the superficially quadratically divergent integral go
converted to a logarithmically divergent one.

17.3
Isolation of Divergence: Vertex function

We compute
\delta\Gamma^{\mu}=\Gamma^{\mu}-\gamma^{\mu}
, with
p^{2}=(p^{\prime})^{2}=-m^{2}
and sandwiching by
\bar{u}(p^{\prime}),u(p)
is implicit.

\delta\Gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime})=-ie^{2}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\frac{\eta_{\alpha\beta}}{k^{2}+\mu^{2}-i\epsilon}\left[\gamma^{\alpha}\frac{(-({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}})+m)}{(p^{\prime}-k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\gamma^{\mu}\frac{(-({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}})+m)}{(p-k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\gamma^{\beta}\right]

We have three denominators and the Feynman trick leads to,

\displaystyle\frac{1}{k^{2}+\mu^{2}-i\epsilon}\frac{1}{(p-k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\frac{1}{(p^{\prime}-k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\hskip 85.35826pt

\displaystyle M^{2}:=x(p^{2}+m^{2})+y((p^{\prime})^{2}+m^{2})+z\mu^{2}-(xp+yp^{\prime})^{2}

\displaystyle\therefore M^{2}=0+0++z\mu^{2}+m^{2}(x+y)^{2}+q^{2}xy\hskip 65.44142pt

q^{2}>0
(space-like) for this diagram,
\boxed{M^{2}=(x+y)^{2}m^{2}+xyq^{2}+z\mu^{2}}
is manifestly positive. As usual shifting the momentum

k\to k+xp+xp^{\prime}

\displaystyle\gamma^{\alpha}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{\alpha}

\displaystyle-2\eta^{\alpha\mu}\gamma_{\alpha}-\gamma^{\mu}(-4)=2\gamma^{\mu}

(17.10)

\displaystyle\gamma^{\alpha}\gamma^{\rho}\gamma^{\sigma}\gamma_{\alpha}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4\eta^{\rho\sigma}

(17.11)

\displaystyle\gamma^{\alpha}\gamma^{\rho}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\sigma}\gamma_{\alpha}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\gamma^{\sigma}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\rho}

(17.12)

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle-2p^{\mu}-(-m)\gamma^{\mu}~,~\gamma^{\mu}{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}\to-2(p^{\prime})^{\mu}+m\gamma^{\mu}~~\mbox{between the spinors}.

Thus we see that, between the spinors, all the terms in the numerator
can be put in the form of
(p+p^{\prime})^{\mu}[\dots]+\gamma^{\mu}[\dots]

and therefore the integral can be arranged as contributing to the form
factors
F_{1},F_{2}
. The intermediate steps, including the Pauli-Villars
regularization, are left as an exercise. The result is (from

\delta\Gamma^{\mu}
):

\displaystyle F_{1}(q^{2})-1

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\left[ln\left(\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}\right)+\right.

(17.16)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\left.\frac{1}{M^{2}}\left((1-x)(1-y)q^{2}+(1-4z+z^{2})m^{2}\right)\right]

\displaystyle F_{2}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\left[\frac{2m^{2}z(1-z)}{M^{2}}\right],~~~\mbox{with}

(17.17)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\boxed{M^{2}:=q^{2}xy+m^{2}(1-z)^{2}+z\mu^{2}}

Note:

(i) In the
\delta F_{1}
, there is a UV divergence (
\Lambda\to\infty
) coming
from the large
k
region, even for
q^{2}=0
. This violates the

\delta F_{1}(0)=0
condition and thus changes the electric charge. The
condition can be naturally restored by defining
\boxed{\delta F_{1,ren}(q^{2}):=\delta F_{1}(q^{2})-\delta F_{1}(0).}
This is a
renormalization prescription
.

(ii) The
\delta F_{1}
also has an “infrared divergence” (
\mu^{2}\to 0
) at
q^{2}=0
coming from the
M^{-2}(0)=m^{-2}(1-z)^{-2}
from the

z\to 1
region.

(iii) The
F_{2}(q^{2})
has no divergences. Its value at
q^{2}=0
gives the
anomalous magnetic moment and can be evaluated explicitly as,

\displaystyle F_{2}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\frac{2z}{1-z}~=~\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz\int_{0}^{1-z}\frac{z}{1-z}~=~\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}

(17.18)

\displaystyle\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\boxed{\frac{g-2}{2}=\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}}~~\hskip 71.13188pt\mbox{One of the triumphs of QED!}

The
renormalized

F_{1}(q^{2})
is obtained as,

\displaystyle F_{1,ren}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1+\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\left[ln\left(\frac{m^{2}(1-z)^{2}}{m^{2}(1-z)^{2}+q^{2}xy}\right)\right.

(17.19)

\displaystyle\left.\hskip 42.67912pt+\frac{m^{2}(1-4z+z^{2})+q^{2}(1-x)(1-y)}{m^{2}(1-z)^{2}+q^{2}xy+\mu^{2}z}-\frac{m^{2}(1-4z+z^{2})}{m^{2}(1-z)^{2}+\mu^{2}z}\right]

We have to face the divergences now. All three radiative corrections
have UV divergence while the vertex function has IR divergence as well.
For dealing with the IR divergence, we need to look at another process
called “Bremsstrahlung” (breaking radiation in German).

17.4
Bremsstrahlung Cross-section to
o(\alpha)

We know from the classical electrodynamics that accelerated charge
radiates. A quantum mechanical view of such a radiation is depicted in
the diagrams below.

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}\hskip 14.22636pt+\hskip 14.22636pt\mbox{emission of any number of
photons}

The diagrams depict a scattering process which causes the top electron
to ‘accelerate’ and ‘emit’ a (on-shell) photon. This is the QFT view of
‘radiation from an accelerated charge’. The bottom charged line
represents some heavy fermion/boson/source, while the connecting wavy
line denotes mediation of the interaction. The first diagram suggests
photon emission
before
the kick while the second diagram suggests
photon emission
after
the kick. As per the rules of the
relativistic QFT, both contributions are to be added and mod-squared to
get to the cross-section. To the leading order - single photon emission
- the cross-section is order
\alpha
. This cross-section also has a an
IR divergence as
k\to 0
. An on-shell photon with arbitrarily small
momentum is called a ‘soft photon’.
To isolate the divergence, focus on the following diagrams:

}

We are computing the amplitude for the process
e\to e+\gamma
. Let

\mathcal{M}_{0}(k^{\prime},l^{\prime})
denote the part of the amplitude of electron
interacting with the external source, it is depicted as the blob. Here

k^{\prime},l^{\prime}
denote the out-going and in-coming momenta respectively. The
full amplitude is then given by (polarizations

\varepsilon(\vec{k},\lambda)
taken to be real),

\displaystyle i\mathcal{M}(p^{\prime},p,k)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(ie)\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\left[\mathcal{M}_{0}(p^{\prime},p-k)\frac{-i(-({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}})+m)}{(p-k)^{2}+m^{2}-\epsilon}\gamma^{\mu}\varepsilon_{\mu}\right.

\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\left.\varepsilon_{\mu}\gamma^{\mu}\frac{-i(-({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}+{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}})+m)}{(p^{\prime}+k)^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\mathcal{M}_{0}(p^{\prime}+k,p)\right]u(p)

To compare with the classical radiation formula, consider the limit
wherein the external source interaction approximates as,

\mathcal{M}_{0}(p^{\prime},p-k)\approx\mathcal{M}_{0}(p^{\prime}+k,p)\approx\mathcal{M}_{0}(p^{\prime},p)
. Next, since the photon is soft, we neglect the

{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.76042pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.21008pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.93578pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{k}}}}
in the fermion numerators. The denominators simplify as,

(p-k)^{2}+m^{2}=-m^{2}-2p\cdot k+0=m^{2}=-2p\cdot k
and likewise,

(p^{\prime}+k)^{2}+m^{2}=+2p^{\prime}\cdot k
. Furthermore,
(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m)\gamma^{\mu}u(p)\to 2p^{\mu}u(p)
, and

\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}+m)\to\bar{u}(p^{\prime})(p^{\prime})^{\mu}
. Thus
the amplitude takes the form,

i\mathcal{M}(p^{\prime},p,k)=e\underbrace{\left[\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\mathcal{M}_{0}(p^{\prime},p)u(p)\right]}_{\mbox{elastic scattering
amplitude}}\times\underbrace{\left(-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{p\cdot k}+\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}\right)}_{\mbox{extra $k$
dependent factor}}

The total, unpolarized cross-section is obtained as,

d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime}+k)=d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime})\int\frac{d^{3}k}{2|k|(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\lambda=1,2}e^{2}\left|\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{\varepsilon\cdot p}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}\right|^{2}

(17.20)

The integration is over soft photons i.e.
|\vec{k}|<k_{max}
. Notice
that The integral is dimensionless.

The integrand is the probability density of radiating a photon of
momentum
k
within
d^{3}k
and any transverse polarization, accompanying
the electron scattering with
p\to p^{\prime}
(“acceleration kick”,
p^{\prime}\neq p+k
) while
the integral is the total probability of emission of a
soft photon with energy up to

k_{max}
.

Multiplying the integrand by the photon energy,
|\vec{k}|
gives the

expectation value of the energy carried away by soft photons up to
energy

k_{max}
,

\mathcal{E}_{soft}(k_{max}):=\langle E\rangle=\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\lambda}\frac{e^{2}}{2}\left|\vec{\varepsilon}\cdot\left(\frac{\vec{p}^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{\vec{p}}{p\cdot k}\right)\right|^{2}

The polarization sum in the cross-section can be done as follows. Noting
that
k\cdot({\textstyle\frac{p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}}-{\textstyle\frac{p}{p\cdot k}})=0
, we can
drop the
k\tilde{k}
terms in the completeness relation for the
polarizations, effectively taking
\Sigma_{\lambda}\varepsilon_{\mu}\varepsilon_{\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}
. Hence,

\sum_{\lambda}\left[\left(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{p}{p\cdot k}\right)^{\mu}\varepsilon_{\mu}\right]\left[\left(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{p}{p\cdot k}\right)^{\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}\right]=\left(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{p}{p\cdot k}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{p^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{p}{p\cdot k}\right),

and the expectation value of energy carried by soft photons is given by,

\boxed{\mathcal{E}_{soft}(k_{max})=\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\lambda}\frac{e^{2}}{2}\left[-\frac{m^{2}}{(p^{\prime}\cdot k)^{2}}-\frac{m^{2}}{(p\cdot k)^{2}}-2\frac{p\cdot p^{\prime}}{(p\cdot k)(p^{\prime}\cdot k)}\right]}

(17.21)

Note that the integral represents average radiated energy inferred from
the quantum mechanical probability distribution for emission of a

single
soft photon with
|\vec{k}|<k_{max}
.

An Aside:
Incidentally, integrand in the r.h.s. is also the

classical
formula for energy carried away by the
k^{th}
Fourier
mode of the electromagnetic field. To see this, consider a classical
trajectory
z^{\mu}(\tau)=p^{\mu}/m
for
\tau<0
and equals

(p^{\prime})^{\mu}/m
for
\tau>0
. The corresponding current is,

\displaystyle J^{\mu}(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}d\tau\frac{(p^{\prime})^{\mu}}{m}\delta^{4}(x-z(\tau))+\int_{-\infty}^{0}d\tau\frac{p^{\mu}}{m}\delta^{4}(x-z(\tau))~~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle A^{\mu}(\vec{k})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{e}{|\vec{k}|}\left(\frac{(p^{\prime})^{\mu}}{p^{\prime}\cdot k}-\frac{p^{\mu}}{p\cdot k}\right)~~~~\mbox{(using the
Retarded Green function.)}

The energy of the above radiation field is the precisely as given by the
integrand in the r.h.s. of eq.(
17.21
)
PeskinSchroder
.
The integral now represents
the total energy carried by Fourier modes
with momenta

|\vec{k}|<k_{max}
.

The integral,
\mathcal{E}_{soft}(k_{max})
, thus has two
different interpretations.

Returning to the evaluation of the integral in eq.(
17.21
), let
us choose a frame in which the initial and final energies of the
electron are the same:
E^{\prime}=E\Rightarrow(p^{\prime})^{0}=p^{0}
and we write
p=E(1,\vec{v}),\ p^{\prime}=E(1,\vec{v}^{\prime}),\ k=(k:=|k|,\vec{k})
. This is
equivalent to
p^{2}=-m^{2}
and
m^{2}/E^{2}=1-\vec{v}^{2}
. With this
choice,
p\cdot k=Ek(-1+\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}),\ p^{\prime}\cdot k=Ek(-1+\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})
and
p\cdot p^{\prime}=E^{2}(-1+\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})
. The
k^{2}
from the
d^{3}k
cancels and the
integrated emitted energy takes the form,

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{soft}(k_{max})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{e^{2}}{2}\int dk\int\frac{d\Omega}{8\pi^{3}}\left[\frac{m_{0}^{2}}{E^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})^{2}}+\frac{1}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})^{2}}\right)-\frac{2(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}\right]

\displaystyle I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\Omega_{\hat{k}}}{4\pi}\left[\frac{2(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}-\frac{m^{2}}{E^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})^{2}}+\frac{1}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})^{2}}\right)\right]~~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{soft}(k_{max})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}\int dkI(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})~~\approx~~\frac{\alpha}{\pi}k_{max}I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})

The integral is actually divergent at the upper end. It has been cut off
at
k_{max}
which is provided by the
inverse of the duration over
which the electron receives the kick
. This is given by
k_{max}\sim|\vec{p}-\vec{p}^{\prime}|:=|\vec{q}|
. This is a physical cutoff.

The angular integration receives the maximum contribution from when
\hat{k}
is parallel to
\vec{v}
or
\vec{v}^{\prime}
depending upon if it is
the initial or the final state bremsstrahlung. Given the directions
v\hat{v},\ \hat{v}^{\prime}
, the
\hat{k}
varies between these two directions
(smaller angle). Thus, to pick up contribution when
\hat{k}
is
parallel to
\vec{v}
, we define
cos\theta
by
\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}=vcos\theta
which varies between
|\vec{v}|cos\theta=\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}
and
cos\theta=1
. Similarly for contribution
from nearly parallel to
\vec{v}^{\prime}
, we define
cos\theta
by

\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}=|\vec{v}^{\prime}|cos\theta
which varies from

|\vec{v}^{\prime}|cos\theta=\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}
to
\cos\theta=1
.

Additionally, in the extreme relativistic limit where we can neglect the

m^{2}/E^{2}
terms, we can approximate

(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})\approx(1-|\vec{v}|cos\theta)(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})\ or\ \approx(1-|\vec{v}^{\prime}|cos\theta)(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})
. The angular integral
then approximates as,

\displaystyle I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\int^{1}_{|\vec{v}|cos\theta=\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}}dcos\theta\frac{1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}}{(1-vcos\theta)(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}+\int^{1}_{|\vec{v}^{\prime}|cos\theta=\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}}dcos\theta\frac{1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}}{(1-v^{\prime}cos\theta)(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle ln\left(\frac{1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}}{1-|\vec{v}|}\right)+ln\left(\frac{1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime}}{1-|\vec{v}^{\prime}|}\right)\approx ln\left(\frac{(p\cdot p^{\prime})^{2}}{E^{2}(E-p)(E-p^{\prime})}\right)~~

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle 2ln\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}~~\mbox{where}~~q:=p^{\prime}-p

We have used:
(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})=-p\cdot p^{\prime}/E^{2}\ ,(1-|\vec{v}|)=(E-|\vec{p}|)/E,\ (E-|\vec{p}|)(E-|\vec{p}^{\prime}|)\approx(E-|\vec{p}|)^{2}
and
E(E-|\vec{p}|)\approx E^{2}-\vec{p}^{2}=m^{2}
in
getting to the last equation.

Thus the radiated energy in the soft modes is given by,

\mathcal{E}_{soft}(k_{max})~=~\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{k_{max}}dkI(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})~\xrightarrow[E\gg m]{}~\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{k_{max}}dk\ ln(q^{2}/m^{2})\ .

(17.22)

Interpreting the above energy classically, what would be the total
number of photons emitted,
N_{\gamma}
? Notice that
I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})dk
is the contribution to the radiated energy from the Fourier
modes with energy,
|\vec{k}|
. The equivalent number of photons would
be
{\textstyle\frac{I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})dk}{|\vec{k}|}}
and the total number

N_{\gamma}
is obtained by integrating over the energies:

N_{\gamma}=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{k_{max}}\frac{dk}{k}I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})\approx\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{k_{max}}\frac{dk}{k}\ ln(q^{2}/m^{2})

This is clearly divergent from the lower limit.

But this is the same expression for the total quantum mechanical
probability for emission of a soft photon up to energy
k_{max}
and thus
is divergent.

This is the IR divergence of the QED cross-section for
the bremsstrahlung process.

If the photon is given a small mass
\mu
, then the
\int dk/k
will
give
ln((|q|\simeq k_{max})/\mu)
while
I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})
gives
the
ln(q^{2}/m^{2})
. Hence,

\boxed{d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime}+k)=d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime})\cdot\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\underbrace{\left[ln(q^{2}/\mu^{2})\cdot ln(q^{2}/m^{2})\right]}_{\mbox{Sudakov double log}}}

(17.23)

18
Treatment of Divergences:

At the first non-trivial attempt at computing radiative corrections, we
encounter divergences of the UV type (from large loop momentum) and of
IR type (from small loop momentum in massless propagators). How do we
understand the physical origin of these? How do we adjust the
computational procedure so as to make
unambiguous predictions
to
be confronted with observations? Let us recapitulate what we have got.

\bullet
Quite generally, using only Poincare covariance and assumption
about the possible spectrum of a theory with mass gap, the
Kallen-Lehmann representation gave us,

\displaystyle\Delta^{\prime}_{F}(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle Z\Delta_{0}(p,m_{ph})+\int_{m^{2}_{th}}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\rho(\sigma^{2})\Delta_{0}(p,\sigma)~~,~~0<Z<1

\displaystyle\Delta_{0}(p,\sigma)~:=~\frac{-i}{p^{2}+\sigma^{2}-i\epsilon}\hskip 42.67912pt\mbox{(Free propagator of
mass $\sigma$)}

\displaystyle S^{\prime}_{F}(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle Z_{2}S_{0}(p,m_{ph})+\int_{m^{2}_{th}}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\frac{-i\{\rho_{1}(\sigma^{2}){\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+\rho_{2}(\sigma^{2})\}}{p^{2}+\sigma^{2}-i\epsilon}

\displaystyle S_{0}(p,\sigma)~:=~-i\frac{(-{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+\sigma)}{p^{2}+\sigma^{2}-i\epsilon}\hskip 28.45274pt\mbox{(Free
propagator of mass $\sigma$)}

\displaystyle(D^{\prime}_{F})_{\mu\nu}(q)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right)\left\{\frac{Z_{3}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}+\int_{0}^{\infty}d\sigma^{2}\frac{\Pi(\sigma^{2})}{q^{2}+\sigma^{2}-i\epsilon}\right\}

The
Z
’s are the field (or wavefunction) renormalization constants.
They are determined as the residues at the (isolated) pole at the
physical mass
,
m_{ph}
. This is without any perturbation series.

In perturbation series though we obtained (for fermion and photon),

S^{\prime}_{F}(p)=\frac{1}{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}+m-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})}~~~\&~~~D^{\prime}_{F}(q)=\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}-\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\right)\left[\frac{1}{q^{2}}\ \frac{1}{1-\Pi(q^{2})}\right]

This is consistent with the general expectation that the physical masses
are determined by the poles in the exact propagator while the
corresponding residues determine the
Z
’s. Thus,

\delta m:=m_{ph}-m=-\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph})~,~Z_{2}^{-1}=1-\frac{d\Sigma({\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})}{d{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}}|_{{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.20757pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.23265pt\kern-3.04367pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 0.88046pt\kern-2.49922pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}}~,~Z_{3}^{-1}=1-\Pi(0).

and of course the photon physical mass is zero.

\bullet
The vertex function for on shell fermion masses takes the
form,

\gamma^{\mu}(p,p^{\prime}):=\gamma^{\mu}F_{1}(q^{2})+i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}F_{2}(q^{2})~,~\sigma_{\mu\nu}:=\frac{i}{2}[\gamma{\mu},\gamma_{n}]~,~{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}=-m_{ph}={\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}}^{\prime}\ .

This decomposition is understood to be sandwiched between
\bar{u}(p^{\prime})

and
u(p)
. Since
m_{ph}=m+\delta m=m+o(\alpha)
, for the first
order corrections, we can take
m_{ph}=m
. Here are the expressions we
obtained:

\displaystyle(I)\hskip 36.98866pt\Sigma(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ (2m+x{\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.51563pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.06117pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.84927pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{p}}}})ln\frac{x\Lambda^{2}}{x(1-x)p^{2}+(1-x)m^{2}+x\mu^{2}-i\epsilon}

(18.1)

\displaystyle\delta m

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ (2-x)ln\frac{x\Lambda^{2}}{(1-x)^{2}m^{2}+x\mu^{2}},

(18.2)

\displaystyle Z_{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1+\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}ln(\Lambda^{2}/m^{2})~~

(18.3)

\displaystyle(II)\hskip 31.2982pt\Pi(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)\left\{\frac{2}{\epsilon}-\gamma-ln\left(\frac{m^{2}+q^{2}x(1-x)}{\mu_{0}^{2}}\right)\right\}

(18.4)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}\frac{1}{\epsilon}+o(\epsilon^{0})~\Rightarrow~Z_{3}=1-\frac{2\alpha}{3\pi}\frac{1}{\epsilon}

(18.5)

\displaystyle(III)\hskip 25.6073ptF_{1}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1+\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int dx\ dy\ dz\ \delta(1-x-y-z)\left\{ln\left(\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}\right)\right.

(18.6)

\displaystyle\left.\hskip 56.9055pt\frac{-(1-x)(1-y)q^{2}+(1-4z+z^{2})m^{2}}{M^{2}}\right\}

\displaystyle F_{2}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\left\{\frac{2m^{2}z(1-z)}{M^{2}}\right\}~,

(18.8)

\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826ptM^{2}:=q^{2}xy+m^{2}(1-z)^{2}+\mu^{2}z

\displaystyle\therefore F_{1}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 1+\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\left\{ln\left(\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}m^{2}}\right)\right.

(18.9)

\displaystyle\left.\hskip 113.81102pt+\frac{1-4z+z^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}}\right\}

\displaystyle F_{2}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int dx\ dy\ dz\delta(1-x-y-z)\left(\frac{z}{1-z}\right)=\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}~=:~\frac{g-2}{2}

(18.10)

\displaystyle(IV)\hskip 14.22636ptd\sigma_{p\to p^{\prime}+k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d\sigma_{p\to p^{\prime}}\int\frac{d^{3}k}{2k(2\pi)^{2}}\sum_{\lambda}e^{2}\left(\frac{\vec{\varepsilon}\cdot\vec{p}^{\prime}}{\vec{p}^{\prime}\cdot\vec{k}}-\frac{\vec{\varepsilon}\cdot\vec{p}}{\vec{p}\cdot\vec{k}}\right)^{2}

(18.11)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d\sigma_{p\to p^{\prime}}\left[\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}\int\frac{dk}{k}I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})\right]~~\mbox{where,}

(18.12)

\displaystyle I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\Omega}{4\pi}\left\{\frac{2(1-\vec{v}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})}-\frac{m^{2}/E^{2}}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v})^{2}}-\frac{m^{2}/E^{2}}{(1-\hat{k}\cdot\vec{v}^{\prime})^{2}}\right\}\hskip 22.76228pt

(18.14)

\displaystyle\mbox{where}~p^{\mu}=(E,E\vec{v})\ ,\ (p^{\prime})^{\mu}=(E,E\vec{v}^{\prime})\ ,\ k^{\mu}(|\vec{k}|,\vec{k})~\mbox{is used.}

\displaystyle\mbox{For $|\vec{v}|\approx|\vec{v}^{\prime}|\approx 1\ $},I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})\approx 2ln(\vec{q}^{2}/m^{2}),\ q:=p^{\prime}-p~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle d\sigma_{p\to p^{\prime}+k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle d\sigma_{p\to p^{\prime}}\left[\frac{\alpha}{\pi}ln(q^{2}/\mu^{2})\ ln(q^{2}/m^{2})\right]

(18.15)

18.1
Treatment of the IR divergences

Let us consider the IR problem first. Since
F_{1}
has both the UV and
the IR divergence, we will separate these by using the UV renormalized

F_{1,ren}
which was defined through,
\delta F_{1,ren}(q^{2}):=\delta F_{1}(q^{2})-\delta F_{1}(0)
. This guarantees that the renormalized
F_{1}

satisfies the condition
F_{1}(0)=1
. Using the expressions above, we
see that,

\displaystyle\delta F_{1,ren}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int dx\ dy\ dz\ \delta(1-x-y-z)\left\{\frac{-(1-x)(1-y)q^{2}+(1-4z+z^{2})m^{2}}{M^{2}(q^{2})}\right.

\displaystyle\left.\hskip 113.81102pt-\frac{(1-4z+z^{2})m^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}m^{2}+z\mu^{2}}\right\}

The IR divergence comes from
z\to 1\leftrightarrow x\sim y\sim 0\leftrightarrow M(q^{2},x,y)
would vanish but for the photon mass

\mu^{2}
. To isolate the divergence, it suffice to take
x=y=0,\ z=1
in
the numerator. Doing the
x
integration using the delta function gives

x=1-y-z>0\Rightarrow y<1-z
and leads to,

\delta F_{1,ren}\approx\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz\int_{0}^{1-z}dy\left\{\frac{-2m^{2}-q^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}m^{2}+y(1-y-z)q^{2}+\mu^{2}}\frac{2m^{2}}{(1-z)^{2}m^{2}+\mu^{2}}\right\}

Substituting
y:=(1-z)u,v:=1-z
, the leading contribution in the
limit
\mu\to 0
is expressed as
PeskinSchroder
,

\displaystyle\boxed{F_{1,ren}(q^{2})\approx 1-\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}f_{IR}(q^{2})\ ln\left(\frac{m^{2}\ or\ q^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)}~~~\mbox{where,}

(18.16)

\displaystyle\boxed{f_{IR}(q^{2})\ =\ \int_{0}^{1}du\left[\frac{m^{2}+q^{2}/2}{m^{2}+u(1-u)q^{2}}\right]-1~}

(18.17)

Since
F_{1}
is the coefficient of the
\gamma^{\mu}
term, we can
replace
e\to eF_{1,ren}
in the electron scattering off a
classical potential
. The cross-section is then given by,

\left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\sigma}\right)\simeq\left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\sigma}\right)_{tree}\left[1-\frac{\alpha}{\pi}f_{IR}(q^{2})ln\left(\frac{m^{2}\ or\ q^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)\right].

Notice that
e\to eF_{1}\Rightarrow e^{2}\to e^{2}F_{1}^{2}\Rightarrow\alpha/(2\pi)\to\alpha/(\pi)
.

Not only is this divergent as
\mu\to 0
, for non-zero
\mu
it is
actually
negative
implying negative cross-section! In the limit of

q^{2}\to\infty
(
q^{2}
is space-like and hence positive),
f_{IR}(q^{2})\to ln(q^{2}/m^{2})\Rightarrow F_{1,ren}(q^{2})\simeq 1-{\textstyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}}ln(q^{2}/m^{2})\,ln(q^{2}/\mu^{2})
and hence,

\boxed{d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime})\simeq d\sigma_{tree}(p\to p^{\prime})\left[1-\frac{\alpha}{\pi}ln(q^{2}/m^{2})\ ln(q^{2}/\mu^{2})\right]~~,~~q^{2}\to\infty\ ,\ \mu^{2}\to 0.}

(18.18)

The Bremsstrahlung cross-section on the other hand is,

\boxed{d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime}+k)=d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime})\left[\frac{\alpha}{\pi}ln\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}\,ln\frac{q^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right]=d\sigma(p\to p^{\prime})_{tree}\left[\frac{\alpha}{\pi}ln\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}\,ln\frac{q^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right].}

(18.19)

Both the cross-sections above are IR divergent and both suffer from
ambiguity from contamination of soft photons.

We already noted that detectors are unable to distinguish a charged
particle accompanied by soft photons below detector sensitivity. What is
the appropriate theoretically computed quantity which reflects this
limitation of the detection process?

When an experimenter reports a detection of a scattered electron, he/she
is actually giving an estimate of the probability that
an electron,

e(p^{\prime})
is detected
and
a photon is not detected.
This
probability is the probability for a process with no emitted photon plus
the probability that there are accompanying soft photons with energies
below the detection threshold,
\varepsilon_{th}
. In equation,

\boxed{(d\sigma)_{measured}=d\sigma\ (\ p\to p^{\prime}\ )+d\sigma\ (\ p\to p^{\prime}+k\ ;\ |\vec{k}|<\varepsilon_{th}\ )\ .}

(18.20)

But this is precisely the sum of the two cross-sections given in
eqns.(
18.18
,
18.19
). We see that the leading
contribution as
q^{2}\to\infty,\mu^{2}\to 0
is exactly canceled out in
the observed cross-section!

Note:
For a general
q^{2}
, the sum of the two cross-sections
is given by
PeskinSchroder
,

(d\sigma)_{measured}=d\sigma_{tree}(\ p\to p^{\prime}\ )\left\{1-\frac{\alpha}{\pi}f_{IR}(q^{2})ln\left(\frac{q^{2}\ or\ m^{2}\ }{\mu^{2}}\right)+\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\ I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})\ ln(\varepsilon_{th}/\mu^{2})\right\}

It turns out that without the limit
q^{2}\to\infty
, it still holds that

I(\vec{v},\vec{v}^{\prime})\to 2f_{IR}

PeskinSchroder
. For general

q^{2}
, the coefficient of
f_{IR}
is
ln(q^{2})
or
ln(m^{2})
. For large

q^{2}
we can of course drop
m^{2}
. Furthermore, experimentally it is
easier to track the behavior of the cross-section as a function of

q^{2}
, so taking
q^{2}\gg m^{2}
, we write the unambiguous and measurable
prediction as,

\boxed{\left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right)_{measured}=\left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right)_{tree}(p\to p^{\prime})\left[1-\frac{\alpha}{\pi}ln\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}\ ln\frac{q^{2}}{\varepsilon_{th}^{2}}+o(\alpha^{2})\right]_{q^{2}\gg m^{2}}}

(18.21)

Appreciate that we had parametrised the IR divergence in terms of the
photon mass
\mu^{2}
; we used the renormalized
F_{1,ren}(q^{2})
to
separate the IR from the UV and finally, identified the quantity which
is actually reported by experiments which is the sum of the two
cross-sections.

This has been a demonstration at the 1-loop. It is non-trivial result of
a great deal of work, that the basic mechanism of cancellation works to
all orders in
\alpha
. There are other types of divergences analogous
to the IR divergences, the so called “mass singularities” which do not
cancel but can be factorised in a convenient form and then eliminated
from the observed cross-sections. See the book by G. Sterman

Sterman
.

UV divergences is a different ball game and needs a different procedure.

18.2
Treatment of the UV divergences

All the three radiative corrections in,
\Sigma,\Pi
and
F_{1}
have the
UV divergences parametrised in terms of the Pauli-Villars cut-off

\Lambda
or the dimensional regularization
\epsilon^{-1}
pole. Note
that the bremsstrahlung process does not have a UV divergence as there
is physical cut-off for the energy of the “soft photons”. We need to
pay attention to the
Z
factors now.

Recall that the
S-
matrix element definition, via the LSZ reduction
procedure, had a factor of
{\textstyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{Z}}}
for each external line.
There was also an amputation of the external line, effected by the
equation of motion operator eg
\Box-m^{2}
acting on the Feynman
propagator
\Delta_{F}
for the external line. The
\sqrt{Z}
entered from
the asymptotic condition relating the interacting field to the in/out
fields. The in/out fields satisfy their respective field equations with

physical masses
and also have the normalization factors with

\omega_{k}
which also contain the physical masses. In the momentum
space, these factors associated with external lines are of the form

{\textstyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{Z}}}(p^{2}+m^{2})\Delta^{\prime}_{F}(p)
where the
\Delta_{F}

contains the self-energy giving it the form
\Delta^{\prime}_{F}(p)=(p^{2}+m^{2}-\Pi(p^{2}))^{-1}
(for scalars).

In perturbative computation of the self-energy however, the
m
is the
mass parameter in the
\mathpzc{L}
which is not the physical mass. In fact
from the Kallen-Lehmann representation, we know that the physical mass
is determined from
p^{2}+m^{2}-\Pi(p^{2})|_{p^{2}=-m_{ph}^{2}}=0\leftrightarrow-m^{2}_{ph}+m^{2}=\Pi(-m^{2}_{ph})
. Expanding
\Pi(p^{2})

about
-m^{2}_{ph}
gives us,

\displaystyle\Pi(p^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\pi(-m^{2}_{ph})+(p^{2}+m^{2}_{ph})\Pi^{\prime}(-m^{2}_{ph})+\dots~~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle(\Delta^{\prime}_{F})^{-1}(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle p^{2}+m^{2}-\Pi(-m^{2}_{ph})-(p^{2}+M^{2}_{ph})\Pi^{\prime}(-m^{2}_{ph})+\dots

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(p^{2}+m^{2}_{ph})\left\{1-\Pi^{\prime}(-m^{2}_{ph})+\dots\right\}~=~(p^{2}+m^{2}_{ph})\left\{Z_{\Phi}^{-1}+\dots\right\}

\displaystyle\therefore\frac{1}{\sqrt{Z_{\Phi}}}(p^{2}+m^{2}_{ph})\Delta^{\prime}_{F}(p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sqrt{Z_{\Phi}}\left\{1+o(\ (p^{2}+m^{2}_{ph})^{2}\ )\right\}

Since we evaluate the
S-
matrix elements on shell, all the higher order
terms vanish. The net result is that:

In an
S-
matrix element, for each external line
introduce a factor of
\sqrt{Z_{field}}\times\
appropriately
normalized wavefunction and now do
not
include self-energy
corrections on the external lines.

Consider the electron scattering off external potential. The
corresponding invariant amplitude is given by
e(\sqrt{Z_{2}})^{2}\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\Gamma^{\mu}(p^{\prime},p)u(p)
with
\Gamma^{\mu}=\gamma^{\mu}F_{1}+(\dots)F_{2}
. The
F_{2}
has no divergences while
Z_{2},F_{1}
both
are divergent. Thus we write,
Z_{2}=1+\delta Z_{2},F_{1}=1+\delta F_{1}
with the
\delta
’s representing the
o(\alpha)
divergent
corrections. Thus we write,

\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{e\to e}(p^{\prime},p)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e(1+\delta Z_{2})\left\{\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)\ (1+\delta F_{1}(q^{2}))+\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\frac{i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}}{2m_{ph}}u(p)\ \delta F_{2}(q^{2})\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e\left[\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)\right]\left\{1+\delta F_{1}+\delta Z_{2}\right\}+\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\frac{i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}}{2m_{ph}}u(p)\ \delta F_{2}(q^{2})~~\mbox{But,}

\displaystyle\delta Z_{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz\left[-zln\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}+2(2-z)\frac{z(1-z)m^{2}}{M^{2}}\right]~,~M^{2}=(1-z)^{2}m^{2}+z\mu^{2}

\displaystyle\delta F_{1}(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz(1-z)\left[ln\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}+(1+z^{2}-4z)\frac{m^{2}}{M^{2}}\right]

\displaystyle\therefore\delta F_{1}(0)+\delta Z_{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz\left[(1-2z)ln\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}+\frac{m^{2}}{M^{2}}\times\right.

\displaystyle\left.\hskip 113.81102pt\left\{(4-2z)(1-z)z+(1-z)(1+z^{2}-4z)\right\}\right]

Integrate the first term by parts,

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}dz(1-2z)ln\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(z-2z^{2})\left.ln\frac{z\Lambda^{2}}{M^{2}}\right|_{0}^{1}-\int_{0}^{1}dz(z-z^{2})\left\{\frac{1}{z}-\frac{2(1-z)(-1)m^{2}+\mu^{2}}{M^{2}}\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dz\frac{1-z}{M^{2}}\{M^{2}+2z(1-z)m^{2}-z\mu^{2}\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{1}dz\frac{1-z}{M^{2}}\{m^{2}(1-z)(1+z)\}=-\int_{0}^{1}dz\frac{m^{2}(1-z)^{2}(1+z)}{m^{2}\left((1-z)^{2}+z\frac{\mu^{2}}{m^{2}}\right)}

\displaystyle\therefore\delta F_{1}(0)+\delta Z_{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz\left[-\frac{m^{2}(1-z)(1-z^{2})}{M^{2}}+\frac{m^{2}}{M^{2}}(1-z)\{4z-2z^{2}+1+z^{2}-4z\}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dz\frac{m^{2}}{M^{2}}(1-z)(1-z^{2})\{-1+1\}=0~\mbox{(!)}

Thus not only has the
ln\Lambda^{2}
divergence canceled, we have got

\delta Z_{2}=-\delta F_{1}(0)
and thus the entire correction takes the
form,

\mathcal{M}_{e\to e}(p^{\prime},p)=e\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\gamma^{\mu}u(p)\left\{1+\underbrace{\delta F_{1}(q^{2})-\delta F_{1}(0)}_{\delta F_{1,ren}}\right\}+i\bar{u}(p^{\prime})\frac{i\sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}}{2m_{ph}}u(p)\delta F_{2}(q^{2})

We recover the
ad hoc
prescription of using
\delta F_{1,ren}

introduced earlier while discussing the IR divergences. Note that the
subtracted term was crucial for the IR divergence cancellation. It was
of course physically expected since
\delta F_{1}(q^{2}=0)=0
should
actually hold to all orders. Note that the UV divergence in the vertex
function,
\delta F_{1}(q^{2})
, is canceled against the divergence in

\delta Z_{2}
coming from electron self-energy.

Now we are left with the divergence in
Z_{3}
from the
\Pi(q^{2}=0)
for
the photon self-energy. We still have the electron mass-shift
\delta m

which is divergent.

18.2.1
1-Loop Renormalization: Charge Screening and Lamb shift

Consider charged particle scattering by exchanging a photon, necessarily
off-shell (space-like in fact). Replace the free propagator

(D_{F})_{\mu\nu}(q^{2})
by the exact propagator which includes the photon
self-energy,
(D^{\prime}_{F})_{\mu\nu}(q^{2})
. The exact propagator has additional
terms
q_{\mu}q_{\nu}
. But thanks to the Ward identity, these do not
contribute to
S-
matrix elements and effectively,
(D^{\prime}_{F})_{\mu\nu}(q^{2})=-i\eta_{\mu\nu}[q^{2}(1-\Pi(q^{2}))]^{-1}
. This has a pole at
q^{2}=0

with residue
Z_{3}=[1-\Pi(0)]^{-1}
. The replacement thus gives a
factor of
Z_{3}
. The photon internal line connects two vertices
contributing
e^{2}
. Thus, if we
identify

\boxed{e^{2}Z_{3}=:e^{2}_{ph}}
, then all divergences coming from the photon self-energy
can be neatly absorbed in the
physical, measured charge
which is
finite. For the mass parameter too, we identified
m^{2}_{ph}=m^{2}+\delta m
, which absorbs the divergence in
\delta m
into the
Lagrangian parameter
m
. The identification
e_{ph}:=e\sqrt{Z_{3}}
is
called
charge renormalization
while
m^{2}_{ph}:=m^{2}+\delta m
is called
mass renormalization
. For external photon line, we
will just have
\sqrt{Z_{3}}
factor and no self-energy corrections and of
course no mass shift.

Thus the exact photon propagator may be replaced by the free propagator
by simultaneously replacing
\alpha
by
\alpha_{eff}
defined below.

\displaystyle\alpha(D^{\prime}_{F})_{\mu\nu}(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(D_{F})_{\mu\nu}(q^{2})\frac{\alpha}{1-\Pi(q^{2})}=\frac{\eta_{\mu\nu}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\left[\frac{\alpha_{ph}(1-\Pi(0))}{1-\Pi(q^{2})}\right]:=\alpha_{eff}(q^{2})\left[\frac{\eta_{\mu\nu}}{q^{2}-i\epsilon}\right]

\displaystyle\mbox{with,}\hskip 28.45274pt\boxed{\alpha_{eff}(q^{2})=\frac{\alpha_{ph}}{1-(\Pi(q^{2})-\Pi(0))}}

To appreciate the implication of the above procedure, recall the
discussion of the effective potential inferred from the tree level
scattering for both the Yukawa and the QED coupling. Let us use the same
formula (for QED), but include the self-energy correction for the photon
propagator. The inferred potential is,

\displaystyle V(\vec{x})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{x}}\frac{-e^{2}_{ph}}{\vec{q}^{2}(1-\Pi(q^{2})+\Pi(0))}

(18.22)

\displaystyle\Pi(q^{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)\left\{\frac{2}{\epsilon}-\gamma-ln\left(\frac{m^{2}+q^{2}x(1-x)}{\mu_{0}^{2}}\right)\right\}

(18.23)

\displaystyle\Pi(q^{2})-\Pi(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)\left\{ln\left(\frac{m^{2}}{m^{2}+q^{2}x(1-x)}\right)\right\}

(18.24)

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\vec{q}^{2}\ll m^{2}}

\displaystyle\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x^{2}(1-x)^{2}\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}=\frac{\alpha}{15\pi}\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}}~~\mbox{(NR limit)}

(18.25)

\displaystyle\therefore V(\vec{x})

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{x}}\frac{-e^{2}_{ph}}{\vec{q}^{2}(1-\frac{\alpha}{15\pi}\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}})}

(18.26)

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle-\frac{\alpha_{ph}}{r}\underbrace{-\frac{4\alpha^{2}_{ph}}{15m^{2}}\delta^{3}(\vec{x})}_{\mbox{perturbation}}

(18.27)

The perturbed Coulomb potential induces a shift in the energy levels of
the Coulomb potential, say in Hydrogen atom. The first order
perturbation theory gives the shift as,

\boxed{\Delta E=-\frac{4\alpha^{2}_{ph}}{15m^{2}}\frac{\alpha^{3}_{ph}m^{3}}{8\pi}=-\frac{\alpha^{5}_{ph}m}{30\pi}\simeq-1.123\times 10^{-7}\mathrm{eV}(\mbox{Lamb Shift})}

(18.28)

This is the contribution of the photon self-energy to the famous Lamb
shift. The photon self-energy
\leftrightarrow\alpha_{eff}
is thus an
observable and observed effect. More exact calculation may be seen in

PeskinSchroder
.

We can also consider the ultra-relativistic regime
q^{2}\gg m^{2}
. Now

\displaystyle\Pi(q^{2})-\Pi(0)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)\left\{ln(\frac{m^{2}}{q^{2}})-ln\left(x(1-x)+\frac{m^{2}}{q^{2}}\right)\right\}

(18.29)

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle-\frac{2\alpha}{\pi}\left[\frac{1}{6}ln(m^{2}/q^{2})-\int_{0}^{1}dx\ x(1-x)ln\{x(1-x)+o(m^{2}/q^{2})\}\right]

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\frac{\alpha}{3\pi}\left[ln(q^{2}/m^{2})-5/3+o(m^{2}/q^{2})\right]

\displaystyle\boxed{\therefore\alpha_{eff}~=~\frac{\alpha_{ph}}{1-\frac{\alpha}{3\pi}ln\left(\frac{q^{2}}{m^{2}e^{5/3}}\right)}\xrightarrow{q^{2}\gg m^{2}}-\frac{3\pi}{ln(q^{2}e^{-5/3}/m^{2})}}

Note that the denominator is less than 1 and hence effective coupling is

larger
than the physical coupling. Thus, the effective coupling
gets stronger at shorter distances. This is interpreted as saying that
the photon self-energy correction polarizes the space between say the
nucleus and the electron, shielding the nuclear charge. As the shielding
cloud is penetrated, higher nuclear charge is seen and hence

\alpha_{eff}
is larger. For this reason, the photon self-energy

\Pi(q^{2})
is also called the
vacuum polarization
.

To summarize:

1.

The UV divergences in the self energies and the vertex
correction are absorbed away by introducing the physical
mass for electron, physical charge for the electron and
electron wavefunction renormalization constant to cancel
the divergence in
F_{1}(q^{2})
;

2.

The IR divergences in the amplitudes, imply IR divergence
in the cross-section. For the
e-e
scattering, the IR
divergence is canceled against the bremsstrahlung
process, once the measured quantity is correctly
identified taking into account the finite detector
resolution;

3.

The hiding of divergences in
\alpha_{ph}
and
m^{2}_{ph}

imply that
\alpha_{eff},\delta m^{2}
acquire
q^{2}

dependence - they “run” with
q^{2}
.

This seems satisfactory within the context of the
o(\alpha)

corrections and the magic of the Ward identity. But it raises more
questions.

\bullet
Are the divergences generic? What are the mathematical and
physical reasons for their existence?

\bullet
Can we sometimes/always take care of the divergences and make
unambiguous predictions?

\bullet
What kind of predictions can be made?

\bullet
What are the effective/running parameters?

\bullet
Are the divergences an artifact of perturbation theory? Etc,
etc ….

Addressing these questions is the genesis of the renormalization theory.

As a matter of strategy, we will stay within perturbative framework and
try to make sense of the divergences. After all, despite divergences,
we could obtain prediction from QED at 1-loop which have been well
tested!

We begin with a comment that the UV divergences persist at higher loops
as well and have to be faced. Can we always absorb them away in
physical masses, couplings and the field renormalizations in
S-
matrix
elements/cross-sections automatically and make finite, unambiguous
predictions? Indeed it is so for QED and for the class of
(super-)renormalizable theories. The proof needs a somewhat modified
procedure, introducing additional diagrams, representing the so called
‘counter terms’ and adjusting its coefficients/Feynman rules to
systematically absorb the divergences. We discuss this procedure in the
context of a scalar field theory, specifically the
\Phi^{4}
theory in 4
dimensions and
\Phi^{3}
theory in 6 dimensions.

18.3
The Method of Counter terms

Consider the
\Phi^{4}
theory given by,

\mathpzc{L}=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\mu}\Phi_{0}\partial^{\mu}\Phi_{0}-\frac{1}{2}m_{0}^{2}\Phi_{0}^{2}-\frac{\lambda_{0}}{4!}\Phi_{0}^{4}

The corresponding Feynman rules would be,

The suffix
0
quantities are called “bare quantities”. Define:

\Phi_{0}:=\sqrt{Z}\Phi
, arbitrary scaling of the field. This expresses
the Lagrangian density as,

\displaystyle\mathpzc{L}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{Z}{2}\partial_{\mu}\Phi\partial^{\mu}\Phi-\frac{Z}{2}m_{0}^{2}\Phi^{2}-\frac{\lambda_{0}Z^{2}}{4!}\Phi^{4}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\mu}\Phi\partial^{\mu}\Phi-\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\Phi^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{4!}\Phi^{4}

\displaystyle-\frac{Z-1}{2}\partial_{\mu}\Phi\partial^{\mu}\Phi-\frac{Zm_{0}^{2}-m^{2}}{2}\Phi^{2}-\frac{\lambda_{0}Z^{2}-\lambda}{4!}\Phi^{4}

The last line constitute “counter terms”, the field
\Phi
, the mass
m

and the coupling
\lambda
are called
renormalized
quantities. The
corresponding Feynman rules would be:
