.

To summarize:
We have seen how the introduction of counter
terms makes it possible to absorb the UV divergences into unobservable
coefficients such as
\delta_{\Phi},\delta_{m},\delta_{g}
. This process
of absorption or s̀ubtraction’ has an inherent ambiguity: exactly what
is subtracted. This is implicitly determined by imposition of a set of
renormalization conditions (eg the on-shell renormalization) or
explicitly (eg the
MS/\overline{MS}
scheme). When the pole (in
p^{2}
)
in the self-energy is not a simple pole, which happens with mass less
particle (
m_{ph}=0
), alternative subtraction schemes are needed.
Such schemes, typically imply renormalization scale dependence in the
renormalized parameters such as masses and couplings. This is governed by
the beta function(s) and the anomalous dimension(s). For the sub-class
of asymptotically free theories, this helps in improving perturbative
predictions at high energies.

A more general discussion of the renormalization group and its
application is given in subsection (
22.2
).

20
Path Integrals in Quantum Mechanics

We consider an alternative strategy to view quantum dynamics.

Recall that in a quantum framework, we have a (projective) Hilbert space
(or more generally a density operator on a Hilbert space) that encodes
the kinematics while a family of unitary operators encodes the dynamics.
Observable quantities are provided by operators whose expectation values
and uncertainties in a given state (or density operator), provide
numbers to be matched against experiments. To track time evolution of
observable quantities, the central quantity of interest is the
transition probability amplitude, for a state
|\Psi\rangle
at time
t

to make a transition at
t^{\prime}>t
to another state
|\Psi^{\prime}\rangle
. The
state
\Psi\rangle
evolves to
exp{-i(t^{\prime}-t)H}|\Psi\rangle
by
Schrodinger equation (H is taken time independent for simplicity). Its
inner product with
|\Psi^{\prime}\rangle
gives the probability amplitude.
This is denoted as:

\mbox{Transition probability amplitude}:=\langle\Psi^{\prime}|\left(e^{-i(t^{\prime}-t)H}|\Psi\rangle\right)=\langle\Psi^{\prime}|e^{-i(t^{\prime}-t)H}|\Psi\rangle

Assuming the quantum system to be describing a particle with a
configuration space
\{\vec{q}\}
, we can use the position
representation completeness relation and express the amplitude as,

\displaystyle\langle\Psi^{\prime}|e^{-i(t^{\prime}-t)H}|\Psi\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d\vec{q}^{\prime}\int d\vec{q}\ \langle\Psi^{\prime}|\vec{q}^{\prime}\rangle\langle\vec{q}^{\prime}|e^{-i(t^{\prime}-t)H}|\vec{q}\rangle\langle\vec{q}|\Psi\rangle

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\int d\vec{q}^{\prime}\int d\vec{q}\ \Psi^{*}(\vec{q}^{\prime})K(\vec{q}^{\prime},t^{\prime};\vec{q},t)\Psi(\vec{q})

The idea is to focus on the kernel
K
and get a convenient
representation for it.

Note:
We have already presumed the usual framework of
quantum theory. It is possible to develop the ideas ab initio taking the
Kernel as a central quantity with a proposed form and arrive at the
usual quantum framework. The book of Feynman and Hibbs follows this
line. We will first sketch the heuristic approach and then relate it to
the usual quantum framework.

20.1
The Ab Initio Path Integral

Consider a classical system with a configuration space
Q
which, for
convenience of notation we take to be
\mathbb{R}
. Let
q_{1},q_{2}
be
two points of it. The particle is supposed to make a transition from

q_{1}
at
t_{1}
to
q_{2}
at
t_{2}
. Such a transition takes place
classically as well and we use it in the Lagrangian framework and deduce
that the transition takes place along a curve
q(t)
which extremises
the action. In a departure from the classical dynamics, it is proposed
that there is certain
probability for the transition
(
q_{1},t_{1})\to(q_{2},t_{2})
. This is to be computed by squaring the total
probability amplitude obtained by summing over the probability
amplitudes for every path connecting the
(q_{1},t_{1})
and
(q_{2},t_{2})
.
The amplitude for each path is given as a certain phase. Thus,
heuristically,
K(q_{2},t_{2};q_{1},t_{1})\sim\sum_{paths}e^{i\varphi[q(t)]}

Questions:
What do we choose for the phase? How do we restrict the
paths? How is the ‘sum’ to be performed?

\bullet
We expect to recover classical dynamics in the limit
\hbar\to 0
. So we expect the phase must be such as the amplitude is
dominated by a single path corresponding to the classical transition.
the obvious choice is
\varphi[q(t)]\sim S[q(t)]/\hbar
!

\bullet
First guess about the paths would be smooth paths, but this
turns out to be not enough. Since the action involves derivatives of

q(t)
, we expect at least piecewise differentiability. But even this
may not suffice - we can define derivatives as differences. It seems,
continuity suffices. Without worrying about this too much, let us
proceed by
discretizing
the time interval. This will also lead us
to answer the third question.

Let
T:=t_{2}-t_{1}:=N\epsilon
where
N
is a large number eventually to
be taken to infinity. For definiteness, let the action be

S=\int_{0}^{T}dt\left[\frac{m}{2}\dot{q}^{2}-V(q)\right]\to\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left\{\frac{m}{2}\frac{(q_{k+1}-q_{k}))^{2}}{\epsilon}-\epsilon V\left(\frac{q_{k+1}+q_{k}}{2}\right)\right\}~,~q_{k}:=q(t_{k})

For uniformity of notation, denote
q_{0}=:q_{initia},q_{N}=:q_{final}
. We have used the natural discretization of the action. The
space of paths is now described by the
N-1

q_{k}
’s varying
independently over
\mathbb{R}
. The integration measure may be taken as
the product measure
\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}{\textstyle\frac{dq_{k}}{C(\epsilon)}}
, where
the constant
C(\epsilon)
is left free and will be chosen shortly.
Since
N
is arbitrary, we define a
path integral
as:

\boxed{K(q_{in},q_{fi};T):=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq_{k}}{C(\epsilon)}exp\frac{i}{\hbar}\left\{\frac{m}{2}\frac{(q_{k+1}-q_{k}))^{2}}{\epsilon}-\epsilon V\left(\frac{q_{k+1}+q_{k}}{2}\right)\right\}}

(20.1)

We can rewrite it by separating the
k=(N-1)^{th}
integral as,

\displaystyle K(q_{in},q_{f};T)=\hskip 341.43306pt

\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq^{\prime}}{C(\epsilon)}\left[exp\frac{i}{\hbar}\left\{\frac{m}{2}\frac{(q_{f}-q^{\prime})^{2}}{\epsilon}-\epsilon V\left(\frac{q_{f}+q^{\prime}}{2}\right)\right\}\cdot K(q_{in},q^{\prime};T-\epsilon)\right]

As
\epsilon\to 0
, the rapid oscillations of the
{\textstyle\frac{1}{\epsilon}}

term imply that dominant contribution to the integral comes from
q^{\prime}

very close to
q_{f}
. Therefore Taylor expanding the potential and the

K(q_{in},q^{\prime};T-\epsilon)
about
q_{f}
, we get

\displaystyle K(q_{in},q_{f};T)

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dq^{\prime}}{C(\epsilon)}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\frac{m}{2\epsilon}(q_{f}-q^{\prime})^{2}}\cdot\left\{1+\frac{-i}{\hbar}\epsilon V(q_{f})+\left(\frac{-i}{\hbar}\right)^{2}\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{2}\frac{V^{2}_{f}}{2}\dots\right\}

\displaystyle\left.\times\left\{1+(q^{\prime}-q_{f})\partial_{q^{\prime}}+\frac{(q^{\prime}-q_{f})^{2}}{2!}\partial^{2}_{q^{\prime}}+\dots\right\}K(q_{in},q^{\prime};T-\epsilon)\right|_{q^{\prime}=q_{f}}

Notice that the first braces are independent of
q^{\prime}
(
V(q)
is assumed
to be reasonably well behaved). The second braces is a power series in

(q^{\prime}-q_{f})
.

\displaystyle K(q_{in},q_{f};T)

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle e^{\frac{-i}{\hbar}\epsilon V(q_{f})}\ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{C(\epsilon)}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\frac{m}{2\epsilon}x^{2}}\cdot\left\{1+x\partial_{q_{f}}+\frac{x^{2}}{2!}\partial^{2}_{q_{f}}+\dots\right\}K(q_{in},q_{f};T-\epsilon)

In effect, we have a series of Gaussian integrals of the form:

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxx^{m}e^{{\textstyle\frac{i}{\hbar}}{\textstyle\frac{mx^{2}}{2\epsilon}}}
. The Gaussian integrals are all well known,

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxe^{-ax^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a}}~,~\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxx^{2k}e^{-ax^{2}}=\frac{1}{a^{k+1/2}}\Gamma(k+1/2)~,~\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxx^{2k+1}e^{-ax^{2}}=0\ .

For us,
a={\textstyle\frac{im}{2\hbar\epsilon}}
. For this to be defined, we have
to define the usual Gaussian integral for
a>0
and continue
analytically in the complex
a-
plane with real part of
a
being
positive. Hence, we must put
m\to m+i\varepsilon
to provide the
convergence factor. Thus,

\displaystyle K(q_{in},q_{f};T)\approx\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{-im/(2\hbar\epsilon)}}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}\times\left\{1-i\frac{\epsilon}{\hbar}V(q_{f})+\frac{i\epsilon\hbar}{2m}\partial^{2}_{q_{f}}+\dots\right\}K(q_{in},q_{f};T-\epsilon)\ .

The terms in the braces are regular as
\epsilon\to 0
and hence the
right hand side can be arranged to have a regular limit as
\epsilon\to 0

by choosing

\boxed{C(\epsilon)=\sqrt{{\textstyle\frac{2\pi\epsilon\hbar}{-im}}}.}
Additionally, we also get,

\displaystyle K(q_{in},q_{f};T)-K(q_{in},q_{f};T-\epsilon)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{i\epsilon\hbar}{2m}\partial^{2}_{q_{f}}-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}V(q_{f})\right)K(q_{in},q_{f};T)

(20.2)

\displaystyle\mbox{or}\hskip 62.59596pti\hbar\partial_{T}K(q_{in},q_{f};T)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\partial^{2}_{q_{f}}+V\right)K(q_{in},q_{f};T)

(20.3)

Thus, the
K
defined above,
satisfies the time dependent
Schrodinger equation!

What about the initial condition? To see the limit
T\to 0
, take
N=1(T=\epsilon)
. Then there is no
\int dq
. Only the
k=0
term in the
exponent survives and we get,

K(q_{in},q_{f};\epsilon\to 0)=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\frac{m}{2}(q_{f}-q_{in})^{2}-\epsilon V((q_{f}+q_{in})/2)}~~,~~C(\epsilon)=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\epsilon\hbar}{-im}}.

The right hand side is just the representation of
\delta(q_{f}-q_{in})
.
The usual quantum framework definition of the transition amplitude
satisfies the time dependent Schrodinger equation with the same initial
condition! So we have a strong hint that the
K(q_{in},q_{f};T)
defined
may indeed be identified with
\langle q_{f}|e^{-iTH}|q_{in}\rangle
We
can see this directly as well.

20.2
Derivation From Transition Amplitude

Divide the interval
[0,T]
in to
N
intervals of size
\epsilon
each,

N\epsilon=T
. Since the Hamiltonian is assumed to be time
independent, we can write,

e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}TH}=e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}H(t_{k+1}-t_{k})}=\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})H}\approx\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(1-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H+\dots\right)_{k}\ .

Insert the completeness relation
\mathbb{1}=\int d\vec{q}_{k}|\vec{q}_{k}\rangle\langle\vec{q}_{k}|
between each factor so that

\displaystyle\langle\vec{q}_{f}|e^{-\frac{iT}{\hbar}H}|\vec{q}_{in}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d\vec{q}_{1}\dots d\vec{q}_{N-1}\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\langle\vec{q}_{k+1}|e^{-\frac{i\epsilon H}{\hbar}}|\vec{q}_{k}\rangle~~~~\vec{q}_{0}=:\vec{q}_{in}\ ,\ \vec{q}_{N}=:\vec{q}_{f}

\displaystyle e^{-\frac{i\epsilon H}{\hbar}}

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle 1-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H+\dots\hskip 85.35826pt\mbox{for small
$\epsilon$.}

To simplify further, we consider types of Hamiltonian operators (we
suppress the vector arrows).

(i)

H(\hat{q},\hat{p})=f(\hat{p})+g(\hat{q})
. Then

\displaystyle\langle q_{k+1}|f(\hat{p})|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int dp_{k}\langle q_{k+1}|f(\hat{p})|p_{k}\rangle\langle p_{k}|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int dp_{k}\ f(p_{k})\langle q_{k+1}|p_{k}\rangle\langle p_{k}|q_{k}\rangle\hskip 28.45274pt\mbox{Use: }\langle p_{k}|q_{k}\rangle=\frac{e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{q}_{k}\cdot\vec{p}_{k}}}{\sqrt{2\pi\hbar}}

\displaystyle\therefore\langle q_{k+1}|f(\hat{p})|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int dp_{k}f(\hat{p})\frac{e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}}{2\pi\hbar}\hskip 56.9055pt\mbox{Likewise,}

\displaystyle\langle q_{k+1}|g(\hat{q})|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle q(\vec{q}_{k})\vec{\delta}(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})=g(\vec{q}_{k})\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\int dp_{k}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}

\displaystyle\therefore\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{H}(\hat{q},\hat{p})|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{k}}{2\pi\hbar}H_{cl}\left(\frac{\vec{q}_{k+1}+\vec{q}_{k}}{2},\vec{p}_{k}\right)^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}

We have used
g(q_{k})\to g(q_{k+1}+q_{k})/2)
when multiplied by the

\delta(q_{k+1}-q_{k})
.

(ii)

\hat{H}
contains the
\hat{q},\hat{p}
in various
ordering such as,
\hat{q}\hat{p},\hat{p}\hat{q},\hat{q}^{2}\hat{p},\hat{q}\hat{p}\hat{q},\hat{p}\hat{q}^{2},\dots
etc. As an example,
consider a term
\hat{q}^{a}\hat{p}_{b}
in the quantum Hamiltonian. Then,

\displaystyle\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{q}^{a}\hat{p}_{b}|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d\vec{p}_{k}\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{q}^{a}|p_{k}\rangle\langle p_{k}|\hat{p}_{b}|q_{k}\rangle=q^{a}_{k+1}(p_{k})_{b}\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{k}}{2\pi\hbar}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}

\displaystyle\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{p}_{b}\hat{q}^{a}|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d\vec{p}_{k}\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{p}_{b}|p_{k}\rangle\langle p_{k}|\hat{q}^{a}|q_{k}\rangle=q^{a}_{k}(p_{k})_{b}\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{k}}{2\pi\hbar}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}

\displaystyle\therefore\langle q_{k+1}|\frac{\hat{q}^{a}\hat{p}_{b}+\hat{p}_{b}\hat{q}^{a}}{2}|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{q^{a}_{k+1}+q^{a}_{k}}{2}\right)(p_{k})_{b}\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{k}}{2\pi\hbar}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}

Thus for the natural ordering, the classical Hamiltonian has its

\vec{q}
dependence in the averaged form. Here is another example
involving
\hat{q}^{2},\hat{p}^{2}
, taken in a particular order, called

Weyl order
:
Weyl(\hat{q}^{2},\hat{p}^{2}):={\textstyle\frac{1}{4}}(\hat{q}^{2}\hat{p}^{2}+2\hat{q}\hat{p}^{2}\hat{q}+\hat{p}^{2}\hat{q}^{2})
.
It is easily seen that,

\displaystyle\langle q_{k+1}|Weyl(\hat{q}^{2},\hat{p}^{2})|q_{k}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\left\{q^{2}_{k+1}\langle q_{k+1}|p^{2}|q_{k}\rangle+2q_{k+1}q_{k}\langle q_{k+1}|p^{2}|q_{k}\rangle+q_{k}^{2}\langle q_{k+1}|p^{2}|q_{k}\rangle\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{\vec{q}_{k+1}+\vec{q}_{k}}{2}\right)^{2}\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{p}^{2}|q_{k}\rangle

More generally, for monomials in
\hat{q},\hat{p}
, the Weyl order

Weyl(\hat{p}^{m},\hat{q}^{n})
equals the fully symmetrized and averaged
product. It is a result that

\langle q_{k+1}|Weyl(\hat{q}^{n},\hat{p}^{m})|q_{k}\rangle=\left(\frac{\vec{q}_{k+1}+\vec{q}_{k}}{2}\right)^{n}\langle q_{k+1}|\hat{p}^{m}|q_{k}\rangle

Hence, modulo Weyl ordering, we do get,

\boxed{\langle q_{k+1}|e^{-\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}H}|q_{k}\rangle=\int\frac{dp_{k}}{2\pi\hbar}e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}\epsilon H\left(p_{k},\frac{q_{k+1}+q_{k}}{2}\right)}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\vec{p}_{k}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}}

\displaystyle\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{iTH}{\hbar}}|q_{in}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int d\vec{q}_{1}\dots d\vec{q}_{N-1}\ \int\frac{d\vec{p}_{1}}{2\pi\hbar}\dots\frac{d\vec{p}_{N}}{2\pi\hbar}\ exp\frac{i}{\hbar}\Bigg\{

(20.4)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\left.\epsilon\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\vec{p}_{k+1}\cdot\frac{(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}{\epsilon}-\epsilon H(p_{k},\frac{q_{k+1}+q_{k}}{2})\right\}

Notice that we have
N,p_{i}
integrations, one for each interval and

N-1,q_{i}
integrations, two less than the number of points since
q_{0},q_{N}
are fixed. The exponent is clearly a discretized form of
\int_{0}^{T}dt\ \vec{p}(t)\cdot\dot{\vec{q}}(t)-H(\vec{p}(t),\vec{q}(t))=\int_{0}^{T}dt\ L(\vec{q}(t),\dot{\vec{q}}(t))
. The
d\vec{q}\frac{d\vec{p}}{(2\pi\hbar)}
measure suggests that we have paths in
the “phase space”. What type of paths?

The mis-match in the number of integration variables makes it harder to
view the multiple integrals as a measure on the space of paths in phase
space. Introduce an arbitrary momentum
\vec{p}_{0}
so that
(\vec{q}_{0},\vec{p}_{0})
denotes a point in the phase space just as
(\vec{q}_{k},\vec{p}_{k}),k=1,\dots,N
do. The
\int d\vec{p}_{N}
shows that the
momentum at the final point is integrated over. Thus, the phase space
path may be specified by an initial point
(\vec{q}_{0},\vec{p}_{0})
. The
arbitrary momentum does not enter anywhere and just serves to anchor the
initial point. The final point however is the set of all points

(\vec{q}_{N},\vec{p}_{N})
with
\vec{P}_{N}
integrated over. Thus, the
space of paths is (
\Gamma
is a phase space of dimension
2n
):

\boxed{\mbox{Space of paths}~=:~\mathpzc{P}_{\Gamma}~:=~\Big\{\ \gamma(t)\in\Gamma\ /\ \gamma(0)=(\vec{q}_{in},\vec{p}_{0})\ ,\ \gamma(T)=(\vec{q}_{f},\vec{p}),\ \vec{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.\ \Big\}}

There are arbitrary constants here, the
\vec{p}_{0}
is an arbitrary
constant vector. Since the
\vec{p}_{k},\vec{q}_{k}
are all independent,
the paths are continuous but non-differentiable everywhere. Thus we
denote:

\displaystyle\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{iT\hat{H}}{\hbar}}|q_{in}\rangle

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\int d\vec{q}_{1}\dots d\vec{q}_{N-1}\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{1}}{2\pi\hbar}\dots\frac{d\vec{p}_{N}}{2\pi\hbar}

(20.5)

\displaystyle exp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\ \epsilon\ \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left\{\vec{p}_{k+1}\cdot\frac{(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}{\epsilon}-H\left(\vec{p}_{k},\frac{\vec{q}_{k+1}+\vec{q}_{k}}{2}\right)\right\}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{\mathpzc{P}_{\Gamma}}\mathpzc{D}q(t)\mathpzc{D}p(t)\ exp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{T}dt\left(\vec{p}(t)\cdot\dot{\vec{q}}(t)-H(\vec{p}(t),\vec{q}(t))\right)\right],

(20.6)

\displaystyle\int_{\mathpzc{P}_{\Gamma}}\mathpzc{D}q(t)\mathpzc{D}p(t)

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\prod_{i=1}^{N-1}\int d\vec{q}_{k}\ \prod_{j=1}^{N}\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{j}}{2\pi\hbar}

(20.7)

For the special case of
H(\vec{p},\vec{q})={\textstyle\frac{\vec{p}^{2}}{2m}}+V(\vec{q})
, the momentum dependence is quadratic and the momentum
integrals can be done trivially. For instance,

\displaystyle\int\frac{d\vec{p}_{k+1}}{(2\pi\hbar)^{d}}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\left\{\vec{p}_{k+1}\cdot(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})-\epsilon\left(\frac{\vec{p}^{2}}{2m}+V(\frac{\vec{q}_{k+1}+\vec{q}_{k}}{2})\right)\right\}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi\hbar)^{d}}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\frac{m}{2\epsilon}(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})^{2}}\times

\displaystyle\int d^{d}p_{k}e^{-\frac{i\epsilon}{2m\hbar}\left(\vec{p}-\frac{m(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})}{\epsilon}\right)^{2}}\ e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}\epsilon V}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big(\frac{m}{2\pi\hbar(i\epsilon)}\Big)^{d/2}e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\epsilon\left\{\frac{m}{2}\frac{(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})^{2}}{Wp^{2}}-V(\frac{\vec{q}_{k+1}+\vec{q}_{k}}{2})\right\}}

The square root prefactor is just
C(\epsilon)^{-1}
. Doing all the
momentum integrals gives,

\displaystyle\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}T\hat{H}}|q_{in}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\int\frac{d\vec{q}_{1}}{(2\pi\hbar(i\epsilon/m))^{d/2}}\dots\int\frac{d\vec{q}_{N-1}}{(2\pi\hbar(i\epsilon/m))^{d/2}}\frac{e^{\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}\left\{\frac{m}{2}\frac{(\vec{q}_{k+1}-\vec{q}_{k})^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}-V\right\}}}{(2\pi\hbar(i\epsilon/m))^{d/2}}

(20.8)

Each
d\vec{q}
integral gets a factor of
C(\epsilon)^{-d}
and extra
such factor is left over from the extra momentum integration. This was
the factor introduced and determined by a regular behavior as

\epsilon\to 0
.

Thus, the upshot is that we can either take the heuristically motivated
definition of
K
and show that it matched with quantum mechanical
definition of transition amplitude
or
directly deduce it from the
quantum mechanical definition. The
K
of the transition amplitude is
the central quantity in the path integral approach.

A note:
We defined
K(q_{in},q_{f};T)
and identified it with

\langle q_{f}|exp{-(i/\hbar)TH}|q_{in}\rangle
and called it the
probability amplitude for a particle at
q_{in}
at
t_{0}
to transit to

q_{f}
at time
t_{0}+T
. This is sometimes also denoted as
\langle q_{f},T|q_{in},0\rangle
or
\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle
with
t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime}=T
. This notation can be confusing since
|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle
does
not

denote a solution of the Schrodinger equation. Rather, it denotes the

instantaneous eigenvector of the Heisenberg picture operator

\hat{Q}(t):=e^{itH/\hbar}Q_{Sch}(0)e^{-itH/\hbar}
. Thus,

Q(t)|q,t\rangle=q|q,t\rangle\leftrightarrow Q_{Sch}\left(e^{-itH/\hbar}|q,t\rangle\right)=q\left(e^{-itH/\hbar}|q,t\rangle\right)\Rightarrow e^{-itH/\hbar}|q,t\rangle=|q\rangle

Or,
|q,t\rangle=e^{itH/\hbar}|q\rangle
. If
|q,t\rangle
were the
time evolution of
|q\rangle
, we should have
e^{itH/\hbar}|q\rangle
.
Thus we have the consistent notation:

\boxed{\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{iTH}{\hbar}}|q_{in}\rangle=\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{i(t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime})H}{\hbar}}|q_{in}\rangle=\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{it^{\prime\prime}H}{\hbar}}\cdot e^{\frac{it^{\prime}H}{\hbar}}|q_{in}\rangle=\langle q_{f},t^{\prime\prime}|q_{in},t^{\prime}\rangle\ .}

Consider now
\langle q_{f},T|Q_{H}(t)|q_{in},-T\rangle
, for
t\in[-T,T]
.

\displaystyle\langle q_{f},T|Q_{H}(t)|q_{in},-T\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle q_{f}|e^{-iTH/\hbar}e^{itH/\hbar}Q_{S}e^{-itH/\hbar}e^{-iTH/\hbar}|q_{in}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int dq^{\prime}dq^{\prime\prime}\langle q_{f}|e^{i(t-T)H/\hbar}|q^{\prime}\rangle\langle q^{\prime}|Q_{S}|q^{\prime\prime}\rangle\langle q^{\prime\prime}|e^{-i(t+T)H/\hbar}|q_{in}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int dq^{\prime}dq^{\prime\prime}\langle q_{f},T|q^{\prime},t\rangle\langle q^{\prime}|Q_{S}|q^{\prime\prime}\rangle\langle q^{\prime\prime},t|q_{in},-T\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int dq^{\prime}\langle q_{f},T|q^{\prime},t\rangle q^{\prime}(t)\langle q^{\prime},t|q_{in},-T\rangle

In the last equation, we have used
\langle q^{\prime}|Q_{S}|q^{\prime\prime}\rangle=q^{\prime}\delta(q^{\prime}-q^{\prime\prime})
- the property of the Schrodinger picture operator,
carried out the
dq^{\prime\prime}
integration and as a
reminder
inserted the
argument
t
in
q^{\prime}(t)
. Using the path integral notation, we write the
last equation as,

\boxed{\langle q_{f},T|Q_{H}(t)|q_{in},-T\rangle=\int\mathpzc{D}q\ q(t)e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[-T,T]}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}dq\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[t,T]}q(t)\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[-T,t]}}

(20.9)

Next, consider the quantity,

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}q\ q(t_{1})q(t_{2})e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[-T,T]}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\int dq_{1}\int dq_{2}\left[\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[t_{1},T]}\right]q_{1}(t_{1})\times

\displaystyle\left[\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[t_{2},t_{1}]}\right]q_{2}(t_{2})\left[\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[-T,t_{2}]}\right]~~-T\leq t_{2}\leq t_{1}\leq T;

For
t_{2}\geq t_{1}
the factors will switch accordingly. We summarize the
formulae as,

\displaystyle\langle q_{f},t^{\prime\prime}|q_{in},t^{\prime}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime}]}~=:~\langle q_{f}|e^{-\frac{i}{\hbar}(t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime})\hat{H}}|q_{in}\rangle

(20.10)

\displaystyle\langle q_{f},T|Q_{H}(t)|q_{in},-T\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}q\ q(t)e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[-T,T]}

(20.11)

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\int dq_{t}\langle q_{f},T|q,t\rangle q_{t}\langle q,t|q_{in},-T\rangle

\displaystyle\langle q_{f},T|T\{Q_{H}(t_{1})Q_{H}(t_{2})\}|q_{in},-T\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}qq(t_{1})q(t_{2})e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S[-T,T]}~:=~\int dq_{1}\int dq_{2}

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\langle q_{f},T|q_{1},t_{1}\rangle q_{1}(t_{1})\langle q_{1},t_{1}|q_{2},t_{2}\rangle q_{2}(t_{2})\langle q_{2},t_{2}|q_{in},-T\rangle\ ,\\
t_{1}\leq t_{2}\\
\langle q_{f},T|q_{2},t_{2}\rangle q_{2}(t_{2})\langle q_{2},t_{2}|q_{1},t_{1}\rangle q_{1}(t_{1})\langle q_{1},t_{1}|q_{in},-T\rangle\ ,\\
t_{2}\leq t_{1}\end{array}\right.

20.3
Functional Derivative

It will be convenient to have the notation of
functional
derivative
. Recall from the variational principle of mechanics, the
action functional,
S[q(t)]:=\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}dt\ L(q(t),\dot{q}(t))
.
For any given function
q:[t_{1},t_{2}]\to q(t)\in\mathbb{R}
, the right
hand side computes a number and that number is the action. It is a
function on the space of paths/curves/functions on

[t_{1},t_{2}]
, and in
short is regarded as a
functional of any given

q(t)
. This is

not
a functional in the sense of being in the dual of vector space
- it is not linear in
q(t)
’s. Under a variation of a curve,
q(t)\to q(t)+\delta q(t)
, we compute
\delta S:=S[q+\delta q]-S[q]=\int dt\ \delta q\left\{{\textstyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}}-{\textstyle\frac{d}{dt}}{\textstyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{q}}}\right\}+
end-point contributions.
Comparing this with
df(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\Sigma_{i=1}^{n}dx^{i}\partial_{i}f
, we can identify and denote,
the functional
derivative
of the action with respect to the curve as:
\boxed{{\textstyle\frac{\delta S}{\delta q(t)}}:={\textstyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}}-{\textstyle\frac{d}{dt}}{\textstyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot{q}}}}
. Note that
S
has
no explicit
t
dependence while its functional derivative does.
Thus the idea of a functional derivative is to consider the first order
variation of a functional and read off the coefficient of the
\delta
.

We can also notice that any function
f(t)
we can write,
\delta f(t)=\int dt^{\prime}\ \delta(t-t^{\prime})\delta f(t^{\prime})\leftrightarrow{\textstyle\frac{\delta f(t)}{\delta f(t^{\prime})}}=\delta(t-t^{\prime})
. Thus we define the derivative with
respect to a function as:

\begin{array}[]{clclr}(i)&\frac{\delta}{\delta f(t)}\left(\alpha F[f]+\beta G[f]\right)&=&\alpha\frac{\delta F}{\delta f(t)}+\beta\frac{\delta G}{\delta f(t)}&\mbox{(linearity)}\\
(ii)&\frac{\delta}{\delta f(t)}F[f].G[f]&=&\frac{\delta F}{\delta f(t)}.G[f]+F[f].\frac{\delta G}{\delta f(t)}&\mbox{(Leibnitz rule)}\\
(iii)&\frac{\delta}{\delta f(t)}F(G[f])&=&\frac{\partial F}{\partial G}\frac{\delta G}{\delta f(t)}&\mbox{ (Chain rule)}\\
(iv)&\frac{\delta f(t^{\prime})}{\delta f(t)}&:=&\delta(t^{\prime}-t)&\end{array}

For an arbitrary “source function”,
J(t)
define the functional,

\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle[J]:=\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dt\left\{L(q,\dot{q})+J(t)q(t)\right\}}\ .

(20.16)

Then it follows that,

\displaystyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J(t)}\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle[J]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}qe^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dt\left\{L(q,\dot{q})+J(t)q(t)\right\}}\cdot\frac{i}{\hbar}q(t)

\displaystyle\mbox{Or,}~~\left(-i\hbar\frac{\delta}{\delta J(t)}\right)\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle[J]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}q\ q(t)e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dt\left\{L(q,\dot{q})+J(t)q(t)\right\}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|Q(t)|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}\ .

\displaystyle\left(-i\hbar\frac{\delta}{\delta J(t_{1})}\right)\left(-i\hbar\frac{\delta}{\delta J(t_{2})}\right)\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle[J]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathpzc{D}q\ q(t_{1})q(t_{2})e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dt\left\{L(q,\dot{q})+J(t)q(t)\right\}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|T\left\{Q(t_{1})Q(t_{2})\right\}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}\ .

The generalization is obvious. Evaluating the functional derivatives at

J(t)=0
gives us,

\boxed{\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|T\left\{Q(t_{1})\dots Q(t_{n})\right\}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle=(-i\hbar)^{n}\frac{\delta^{n}}{\delta J(t_{1})\dots\delta J(t_{n})}\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle\Big|_{J=0}}

(20.17)

Thus, the “correlation functions” (left hand side) are given by the
functional derivatives of the transition amplitude in presence of a
source function, evaluated at vanishing source function.

To relate it to ground state/vacuum expectation values of time ordered
products of Heisenberg picture operators, we take a closer look at the
transition amplitude with non-zero source function.

Choose the source function to have a compact support,
J(t)=0
for
t<t^{\prime},t>t^{\prime\prime}
. Choose
T^{\prime}<t^{\prime}
and
T^{\prime\prime}>t^{\prime\prime}
. Then,

\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle_{J}=\int dq^{\prime\prime}\ dq^{\prime}\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}\rangle_{J=0}\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}\langle q^{\prime},t^{\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle_{J=0}\ .

The
J=0
amplitudes can be written in the energy representation (energy
eigenvalues assumed to be discrete for convenience),

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime},t^{\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime}|e^{-i(t^{\prime}-T^{\prime})H/\hbar}|Q^{\prime}\rangle=\sum_{n}\langle q^{\prime}|\varphi_{n}\rangle\langle\varphi_{n}|Q^{\prime}\rangle e^{-i(t^{\prime}-T^{\prime})E_{n}/\hbar}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{n}\varphi_{n}(q^{\prime})\varphi^{*}_{n}(Q^{\prime})e^{-i(t^{\prime}-T^{\prime})E_{n}/\hbar}

\displaystyle\therefore e^{-iT^{\prime}E_{0}/\hbar}\langle q^{\prime},t^{\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{n}\varphi_{n}(q^{\prime})\varphi^{*}_{n}(Q^{\prime})e^{-it^{\prime}E_{n}/\hbar}e^{iT^{\prime}(E_{n}-E_{0})/\hbar}

\displaystyle\therefore\lim_{T^{\prime}\to i\infty}e^{-iT^{\prime}E_{0}/\hbar}\langle q^{\prime},t^{\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\varphi_{0}(q^{\prime})\varphi^{*}_{0}(Q^{\prime})e^{-it^{\prime}E_{0}/\hbar}~~\because E_{n}\neq E_{0}~~\mbox{terms drop out, likewise}

\displaystyle\therefore\lim_{T^{\prime\prime}\to-i\infty}e^{iT^{\prime\prime}E_{0}/\hbar}\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\varphi^{*}_{0}(q^{\prime\prime})\varphi_{0}(Q^{\prime\prime})e^{it^{\prime\prime}E_{0}/\hbar}

We have assumed that the lowest energy eigenvalue is non-degenerate,
otherwise the
\sum_{n}
will reduce to the sum over the degenerate
states. Thus we get,

\boxed{\lim_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T^{\prime}\to i\infty}}{{T^{\prime\prime}\to-i\infty}}}\frac{\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle_{J}}{e^{-iE_{0}(T^{\prime\prime}-T^{\prime})}\varphi_{0}(Q^{\prime\prime})\varphi_{0}^{*}(Q^{\prime})}=\int dq^{\prime}\ dq^{\prime\prime}\varphi_{0}^{*}(q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime})\varphi_{0}(q^{\prime},t^{\prime})\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}}

(20.18)

20.4
Ground State-to-ground state Amplitude:
Z[J]

The right hand side of eq. (
20.18
) is the ground
state-to-ground state transition amplitude, the one that we were looking
for. The left hand side tells us how to compute it from
\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle
which is similar to
\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}
. The factor in the denominator is independent of

J
and will not matter. We introduce the definition,

\displaystyle Z[J]

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\int dq^{\prime}\ dq^{\prime\prime}\ \varphi_{0}^{*}(q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime})\langle q^{\prime\prime}.t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}\varphi_{0}(q^{\prime},t^{\prime})

(20.19)

\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{n}Z[J]}{\delta J(t_{1})\dots\delta J(t_{n})}\Big|_{J=0}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}\right)^{n}\int dq^{\prime}\ dq^{\prime\prime}\varphi_{0}^{*}(q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime})\times

(20.20)

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|T\left\{Q(t_{1})\dots Q(t_{n})\right\}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle\ \varphi_{0}(q^{\prime},t^{\prime})\ .

The previous result tells us that
Z[J]
may be computed as,

Z[J]\sim\lim_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T^{\prime}\to i\infty}}{{T^{\prime\prime}\to-i\infty}}}\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle_{J}=\lim_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T^{\prime}\to i\infty}}{{T^{\prime\prime}\to-i\infty}}}\int\mathpzc{D}qexp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{T^{\prime}}^{T^{\prime\prime}}dt\left\{L(q,\dot{q})+J(t)q(t)\right\}\right]

We have dropped the unimportant denominator on the left hand side.

We have continued
T^{\prime}\to i\infty,T^{\prime\prime}\to-i\infty
, but not the
intermediate times,
t_{i}
appearing as arguments of the Heisenberg
operators. We will do so now and get to the
Euclidean formulation
.

We begin with,

\displaystyle\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|T\left\{Q(t_{1})\dots Q(t_{n})\right\}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle_{J=0}

\displaystyle\sim

\displaystyle\lim_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle T^{\prime}\to i\infty}}{{T^{\prime\prime}\to-i\infty}}}\int dq_{1}\dots dq_{n}\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|q_{1},t_{1}\rangle q_{1}\langle q_{1},t_{1}|q_{2},t_{2}\rangle

\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\dots q_{n}\langle q_{n},t_{n}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle~,~\mbox{where,}

\displaystyle\langle q_{i},t_{i}|q_{i+1},t_{i+1}\rangle

\displaystyle\sim

\displaystyle\int\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{dq_{j}}{\sqrt{2\pi i\epsilon}}exp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\epsilon\sum_{j}L\left(\frac{q_{i}+q_{i+1}}{2},\frac{q_{i+1}-q_{i}}{\epsilon}\right)\right]~,~N\epsilon=t_{i+1}-t_{i}

\displaystyle\langle q_{i},-i\tau_{i}|q_{i+1},-i\tau_{i+1}\rangle

\displaystyle\rightsquigarrow

\displaystyle\int\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{dq_{j}}{\sqrt{2\pi\epsilon^{\prime}}}exp\left[\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{\hbar}\sum_{j}L\left(\frac{q_{i}+q_{i+1}}{2},\frac{q_{i+1}-q_{i}}{-i\epsilon^{\prime}}\right)\right]~,~N\epsilon^{\prime}:=\tau_{i+1}-\tau_{i}

The analytic continuation of the
\langle T\{\dots\}\rangle
is defined
through the
\langle..|..\rangle
. Thus,

\displaystyle\langle Q^{\prime\prime},T^{\prime\prime}|T\left\{Q(t_{1})\dots Q(t_{n})\right\}|Q^{\prime},T^{\prime}\rangle_{J=0}\Big|_{t_{i}=-i\tau_{i}}

\displaystyle\sim

\displaystyle\lim_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tau_{in}\to-\infty}}{{\tau_{f}\to\infty}}}\int\mathpzc{D}q\ q(\tau_{1})\dots q(\tau_{N})\times

\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055ptexp\left[\int_{\tau_{in}}^{\tau_{f}}d\tau L(q,-\frac{dq}{d\tau})\right]

This suggests going over to a
Euclidean formulation
,

Z_{E}[J]:=\int\mathpzc{D}q\ exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\tau\left\{L\left(q,i\frac{dq}{d\tau}\right)+J(\tau)q(\tau)\right\}\right]

(20.21)

and the paths are between some
Q^{\prime}=\lim_{\tau\to-\infty}q(\tau)
and

Q^{\prime\prime}=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}q(\tau)
. The Euclidean
Z_{E}
and the
Minkowskian
Z
are related through,

\boxed{\frac{1}{Z[J]}\frac{\delta^{n}Z[J]}{\delta J(t_{1})\dots\delta J(t_{n})}\Big|_{J=0}=i^{n}\frac{1}{Z_{E}[J]}\frac{\delta^{n}Z_{E}[J]}{\delta J(\tau_{1})\dots\delta J(\tau_{n})}\Big|_{J=0}}

This will be used in the field theory Green’s functions.

20.5
Explicit evaluation of a path integral

We would like to see the various expressions above explicitly for a
1-dimensional harmonic oscillator with a source function. We have
L={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}(\dot{q}^{2}-\omega^{2}q^{2})+J(t)q(t)
and we want to compute

\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}
. Discretizing the corresponding action,
the definition gives,

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{dq_{k}}{C(\epsilon)}exp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\left\{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{1}{2}\frac{(q_{k+1}-q_{k})^{2}}{\epsilon}-\frac{\epsilon\omega^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{q_{k}+q_{k+1}}{2}\right)^{2}\right.\right.

\displaystyle\hskip 71.13188pt\left.\left.+\epsilon J_{k}\left(\frac{q_{k}+q_{k+1}}{2}\right)\right\}\right]~,~q_{0}:=q(t^{\prime}),q_{N}:=q(t^{\prime\prime}),J_{k};=J(t_{k})

All are Gaussian integrals with coupled variables. It is more convenient
to discretize a
different
action.

The equations of motion are:
\ddot{q}+\omega^{2}q^{2}=J(t)\ ,\ q(t^{\prime})=q^{\prime},q(t^{\prime\prime})=q^{\prime\prime}
. Let
q_{cl}(t)
be a classical solution of this
equation satisfying the end point conditions. Let us assume that there
is just
one
such solution. Introduce
\eta(t)
via the definition:

q(t):=q_{cl}(t)+\eta(t)
. Then
\eta(t^{\prime})=0=\eta(t^{\prime\prime})
. The
action becomes,

\displaystyle S(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dt\left\{\frac{1}{2}(\dot{q}_{cl}+\dot{\eta})^{2}-\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}(q_{cl}+\eta)^{2}+J(t)(q_{cl}+\eta)\right\}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dt\left[\left\{\frac{1}{2}(\dot{q}_{cl}^{2}-\omega^{2}q_{cl}^{2})+J(t)q_{cl}\right\}+\left\{\frac{1}{2}(\dot{\eta}^{2}-\omega^{2}\eta^{2})\right\}+\left\{\dot{\eta}\dot{q}_{cl}-\omega^{2}\eta q_{cl}+J\eta\right\}\right]

Up to a total derivative, the last term is
-\eta(\ddot{q}_{cl}+\omega^{2}q_{cl}-J)=0
. The total derivative term gives

\eta\dot{q}_{cl}|_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}=0
thanks to the end point condition
satisfied by
\eta(t)
. Thus,
\boxed{S(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})=S_{cl}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})+\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}{\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}(\dot{\eta}^{2}-\omega^{2}\eta^{2}),}
where

S_{cl}
is the action evaluated at the presumed solution
q_{cl}
. The
terms linear in
\eta
have vanished thanks to
q_{cl}
being a
solution. We now “quantize” the
\eta
variable, i.e. we
define

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\left[e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S^{J}_{cl}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})}\right]\left[\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{d\eta_{k}}{C(\epsilon)}exp\left\{\frac{i}{\hbar}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{1}{2}\frac{(\eta_{k+1}-\eta_{k})^{2}}{\epsilon}\right.\right.\right.

(20.22)

\displaystyle\left.\left.\left.\hskip 162.18062pt-\frac{\epsilon\ \omega^{2}}{2}((\eta_{k}+\eta_{k+1})/2)^{2}\right)\right\}\right]

The paths
\eta(t)
begin and end at
\eta=0
. The second factor is
independent of both
J
and
t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime}
. It depends on
T=t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime}
. Our
task is to evaluate the first factor and carry out the coupled Gaussian
integral.

The exponent in the second factor is of the form,

\displaystyle\frac{i}{2\hbar}\Big(\dots\Big)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{1}{\epsilon}(\eta_{k+1}-\eta_{k})^{2}-\epsilon\ \omega^{2}(\eta_{k+1}+\eta_{k})/2)^{2}~:=~\sum_{k,l=0}^{N-1}\eta_{k}A_{kl}\eta_{l}~~,~~\mbox{where,}

\displaystyle A_{lk}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\underbrace{2(1/\epsilon-\epsilon\ \omega/4)}_{a}\delta_{lk}-\underbrace{(1/\epsilon+\epsilon\ \omega^{2}/4)^{2}}_{b}\left\{\delta_{l,k+1}+\delta_{l,k-1}\right\}~,~l,k=1,\dots N-1.

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}a&-b&0&\dots&0\\
-b&a&-b&\dots&0\\
0&-b&a&-b&\dots 0\\
.&.&.&.&.\\
.&.&.&.&.\\
0&0&\dots&-b&a\end{array}\right)\hskip 28.45274pt\mbox{A tri-diagonal, symmetric matrix.}

\displaystyle\therefore\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\left[e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S^{J}_{cl}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})}\right]\left[\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d^{N-1}\eta}{C(\epsilon)^{N-1}}exp\left\{\frac{i}{2\hbar}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N-1}\eta_{i}A_{ij}\eta_{j}\right\}\right]

For a single variable we have
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxe^{-ax^{2}}=\sqrt{\pi/a}\Rightarrow\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxe^{iax^{2}}=\sqrt{\pi/(-ia)}
. Its multi-dimensional generalization is

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d^{n}xe^{i\sum_{ij}x_{i}A_{ij}x_{j}}=\frac{(i\pi)^{n/2}}{\sqrt{det\ A}}

Using this, our transition amplitude takes the form,

\displaystyle\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left[e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S^{J}_{cl}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})}\right]\left[\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{C(\epsilon)}\frac{1}{(\epsilon)^{N-1}}\frac{(i\pi\hbar)^{(N-1)/2}}{\sqrt{det\ A}}\right]

Using
C(\epsilon)=\sqrt{2i\pi\epsilon\hbar}
since we have taken unit
mass,
m=1
, we have,

\boxed{\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}=\left[e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S^{J}_{cl}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})}\right]\left[\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi i\hbar}(\epsilon)^{N/2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{det\ A(\epsilon)}}\right]}

(20.24)

Now we need to compute the determinant of the tridiagonal, symmetric
matrix. This is usually solved by using a recursion relation. Denote

D_{n}:=det\ A_{n\times n}
where
A
has the form given above. Clearly,

D_{1}=a
and
D_{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}
. By checking for
4\times 4,5\times 5

matrices, it is easy to see that
D_{n}
satisfies the recursion relation,

\boxed{D_{n}=aD_{n-1}-b^{2}D_{n-2}~,~D_{0}:=1,D_{1}=a~~;~~a=2\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\frac{\epsilon\ \omega^{2}}{4}\right)~,~b=\frac{1}{\epsilon}+\frac{\epsilon\ \omega^{2}}{4}\ .}

We can pull out a factor of
\epsilon^{-1}
from
A
and since our
A

is of order
(N-1)
, we pull out a factor of
(\epsilon)^{-(N-1)/2}
.
This replaces the second
[\dots]
by
\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}(2\pi\hbar\sqrt{\epsilon detA^{\prime}})^{-1}
. The
A^{\prime}
matrix has elements
a^{\prime}:=2-\epsilon^{2}\omega^{2}/2\ ,\ b^{\prime}:=1+\epsilon^{2}\omega^{2}/4
.

Note:
For a given
N,\epsilon=T/N
, hence (suppressing
the primes)
a,b
have an
N
dependence. The matrix itself is also

(N-1)\times(N-1)
and our notation
D_{n}
as the determinant of

A_{n\times n}
is valid for
n\leq N-1
. For a given
N
, the
D_{n\geq N}
is
not
defined. Hence, the recursion relation is a
difference equation with constant coefficients

Elaydi
. It is
important to keep the distinction between fixed
N
and a variable
n
.
The
a,b
are functions of
N
but independent of
n
.

Such difference equations are solved by the ansatz,
D_{n}=\lambda^{n}
.
Shifting
n\to n+2
, we write the difference equation as,

\forall\ 0\leq n\leq N-3\ :~D_{n+2}-aD_{n+1}+b^{2}D_{n}=0~~,~~D_{0}=1,D_{1}=a.

Substitution gives the characteristic equation
\lambda^{2}-a\lambda+b^{2}=0
. Its solutions, for
\epsilon\ll 1
, are

\displaystyle\lambda_{\pm}

\displaystyle\approx

\displaystyle(1-\frac{\epsilon^{2}\omega^{2}}{4})\pm\sqrt{(1-\frac{\epsilon^{2}\omega^{2}}{2})-(1+\frac{\epsilon^{2}\omega^{2}}{2})}~~\approx~1-\frac{\epsilon^{2}\omega^{2}}{4}\pm i\epsilon\ \omega

\displaystyle\therefore\lambda_{\pm}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle~1\pm i\epsilon\omega\ .~\Rightarrow~D_{n}=\alpha\lambda_{+}^{n}+\beta\lambda_{-}^{n}~~~~\forall~n\ \in\ [0,N-1].

\displaystyle\mbox{Initial conditions give,}~~\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{i}{\epsilon\omega}\right)~,~\beta=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{i}{\epsilon\omega}\right)\ .

The desired determinant is then given by,

\displaystyle D_{N-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{i}{\epsilon\omega}\right)(1+i\epsilon\omega)^{N-1}+\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{i}{\epsilon\omega}\right)(1-i\epsilon\omega)^{N-1}~,~\epsilon=T/N\

\displaystyle\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}i\left(1-\frac{iN}{\omega T}\right)(1+i\omega T/N)^{N}+\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{iN}{\omega T}\right)(1-i\omega T/N)^{N}

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle\left(-\frac{iN}{2\omega T}\right)\left(e^{i\omega T}-e^{-i\omega T}\right)~=~\frac{N}{\omega T}sin(\omega T)

\displaystyle\therefore\epsilon D_{N}

\displaystyle\to

\displaystyle\frac{sin(\omega T}{\omega}\ .

We finally get,

\boxed{\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle_{J}=\left[e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}S^{J}_{cl}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})}\right]\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi i\hbar}}\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{sin(\omega T)}}\right].}

(20.25)

Note:
All the
J
dependence is in the first factor only
while the “quantum correction” are in the second factor and
independent of
J
.

Note:
This method of evaluating the amplitude near a
classical solution can also be adopted for more general (non-linear)
equations of motion. The
S_{cl}
always comes out, the term linear in

\eta
always vanishes while the
o(\eta^{2})
terms always gives the
(determinant)
-1/2
. In the general context, it is termed as a
semi-classical approximation which is exact for the oscillator.

The calculation of the first factor requires solving the equation of
motion with the source function and then evaluating the action for

q_{cl}(t)
. This is little involved as the equation is inhomogeneous
and requires use of Green’s function. The Green’s function can be
obtained by directly solving the differential equation with
\delta
-
function source and matching the discontinuity due to the delta
function. We just note the final result [Problem 3.11 of Feynman-Hibbs,
Abers-Lee].

\displaystyle S_{cl}^{J}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{\omega}{2sin(\omega T)}\left[((q^{\prime})^{2}+(q^{\prime\prime})^{2})cos(\omega T)-2q^{\prime}q^{\prime\prime}\right]

(20.26)

\displaystyle+\frac{q^{\prime\prime}}{sin(\omega T)}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dtJ(t)sin(\omega(t-t^{\prime}))+\frac{q^{\prime}}{sin(\omega T)}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dtJ(t)sin(\omega(t^{\prime\prime}-t))

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{\omega sin(\omega T)}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}d\sigma\int_{t^{\prime}}^{\sigma}d\tau J(\sigma)J(\tau)sin(\omega(t^{\prime\prime}-\sigma).sin(\omega(\tau-t^{\prime}))

This exercise was done to illustrate the schematics of evaluating the
path integral directly using the definition.

Note:
If we have a system of two degrees of freedom, the
q(t)

and the
J(t)
which are coupled by a linear coupling,
\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime\prime}}dtJ(t)q(t)
, then the
S_{cl}^{J}(t^{\prime},t^{\prime\prime})
can be viewed as an effective
action contribution after integrating out the
q(t)
degree of freedom.
This has the form
\sim\int dtJ(t)\alpha(t)-\int dtJ(t)\int^{t}d\sigma\beta(t,\sigma)J(\sigma)
. This last term is a
non-local
term
.

20.6
Alternative Expression for
Z[J]

We now consider another method which is closer to what is done is field
theory. We begin by modifying the Hamiltonian operator as:

\boxed{\hat{H}\to(1-i\epsilon)\hat{H}}~
Srednicky
. Then,

\displaystyle|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}t^{\prime}\hat{H}}|q^{\prime}\rangle=\sum_{n}\varphi_{n}^{*}(q^{\prime})e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}t^{\prime}E_{n}}|n\rangle\to\sum_{n}\varphi_{n}^{*}(q^{\prime})e^{\frac{i}{\hbar}t^{\prime}(1-i\epsilon)E_{n}}|n\rangle

Assuming
E_{0}=0
for convenience and taking the limits, we get

\boxed{|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle~\xrightarrow[t^{\prime}\to-\infty]{}~\varphi^{*}_{0}(q^{\prime})|0\rangle\hskip 28.45274pt\mbox{and}\hskip 28.45274pt\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|~\xrightarrow[t^{\prime\prime}\to\infty]{}~\langle 0|\varphi_{0}(q^{\prime\prime})\ .}

(20.27)

Thus,
|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle,\langle q^{\prime\prime},t^{\prime\prime}|
both go to the (presumed
non-degenerate) ground state as
t^{\prime}\to-\infty
and
t^{\prime\prime}\to\infty
,

provided
we make the substitution:
\hat{H}\to(1-i\epsilon)\hat{H}
. We will work with the limits.

Consider, for our 1-dimensional oscillator,
H=p^{2}/2+\omega^{2}q^{2}/2
,

\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}=\int\mathpzc{D}p\mathpzc{D}qexp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\left\{p\dot{q}-(1-i\epsilon)H+J(t)q\right\}\right]

We do momentum integration by using
(1-i\epsilon)p^{2}/2\approx{\textstyle\frac{p^{2}}{2(1+i\epsilon)}}
. This gives the term

{\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}(1+i\epsilon)\dot{q}^{2}
and we get,

\boxed{\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}=\int\mathpzc{D}qexp\left[\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\left\{\frac{1}{2}(1+i\epsilon)\dot{q}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\omega^{2}(1-i\epsilon)q^{2}+J(t)q\right\}\right].}

(20.28)

Define the Fourier transform,

\tilde{q}(\nu):=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dte^{i\nu t}q(t)\leftrightarrow q(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\nu e^{-i\nu t}\tilde{q}(\nu)

and similarly for
J(t)
. Substitution give,

\displaystyle L

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu^{\prime}}{2\pi}e^{-i(\nu+\nu^{\prime})t}\Big[\big\{-(1+i\epsilon)\nu\nu^{\prime}-(1-i\epsilon)\omega^{2}\big\}\tilde{q}(\nu)\tilde{q}(\nu^{\prime})

\displaystyle\hskip 156.49014pt+\frac{\tilde{J}(\nu)\tilde{q}(\nu^{\prime})+\tilde{J}(\nu^{\prime})\tilde{q}(\nu)}{2}\Big]

The expression in the braces simplifies to
\{\dots\}=\nu^{2}-\omega^{2}+i\epsilon(\nu)~,~\epsilon(\nu):=\epsilon(\nu^{2}+\omega^{2})
. Define

\tilde{x}(\nu):=\tilde{q}(\nu)+{\textstyle\frac{\tilde{J}(\nu)}{\nu^{2}-\omega^{2}+i\epsilon(\nu)}}
. The the action becomes,

S=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\left[\tilde{x}(\nu)\big(\nu^{2}-\omega^{2}+i\epsilon(\nu)\big)\tilde{x}(-\nu)-\frac{\tilde{J}(\nu)\tilde{J}(-\nu)}{\nu^{2}-\omega^{2}+i\epsilon(\nu)}\right]

The shift,
\tilde{q}(\nu)\to\tilde{x}(\nu)
is a
constant
shift
, the shift is independent of
\tilde{q}
. Hence the Jacobian of
the transformation will be 1 and
\mathpzc{D}\tilde{q}(\nu)=\mathpzc{D}\tilde{x}(\nu)
. Taking Fourier transform, the shift takes the
form
q(t)\to x(t)+f(t)
with
f(t)
independent of
q(t)
. This is
also a constant shift and in the time domain too, and we expect

\mathpzc{D}q(t)=\mathpzc{D}x(t)
.

\displaystyle\therefore\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle exp\left[\frac{i}{2\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\left(\frac{\tilde{J}(\nu)\tilde{J}(-\nu)}{-\nu^{2}+\omega^{2}-i\epsilon(\nu)}\right)\right]\times

(20.30)

\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\left[\int\mathpzc{D}\tilde{x}(\nu)exp\frac{i}{2\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\tilde{x}(\nu)\big(\nu^{2}-\omega^{2}+i\epsilon(\nu)\big)\tilde{x}(-\nu)\right]

The second factor is a path integral independent of
J
and hence equals

\langle 0|0\rangle_{J=0}
. However, without any source interaction, the
ground state remains a ground state and hence
\boxed{\langle 0|0\rangle_{J=0}=1!}
. This gives finally,

\boxed{\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}=exp\frac{i}{2\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\left(\frac{\tilde{J}(\nu)\tilde{J}(-\nu)}{-\nu^{2}+\omega^{2}-i\epsilon(\nu)}\right)}

(20.31)

We never needed to evaluate the path integral!

The above expression can also be expressed in the time domain as,

\displaystyle\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle exp\frac{i}{2\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt^{\prime}dt^{\prime\prime}J(t^{\prime\prime})G(t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime})J(t^{\prime})\hskip 42.67912pt\mbox{with,}

(20.32)

\displaystyle G(t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\frac{e^{-i\nu(t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime})}}{-\nu^{2}+\omega^{2}-i\epsilon(\nu)}~=~\frac{i}{2\omega}e^{-i\omega|t^{\prime\prime}-t^{\prime}|}\hskip 0.0pt\mbox{(by
contour integration)}~~~~~

(20.33)

Note:
The
\nu
dependence in the
\epsilon(\nu)
does not
affect the contour integration.

We have discussed two different methods of computing the transition
amplitude in the limit of infinite time separation. Notice that the

\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}
above is the same as the
Z[J]
defined earlier
in eq. (
20.19
) since
\int dq^{\prime}|q^{\prime},t^{\prime}\rangle\varphi_{0}(q^{\prime},t^{\prime})=|0,t^{\prime}\rangle
and likewise for
\langle 0,t^{\prime\prime}|
.

The above frequency domain form is very convenient to obtain the correlation
functions as seen below.

Our general formula (
20.17
) tells us that
\langle 0|T\{Q(t_{1})\dots Q(t_{n})\}|0\rangle
is given by the functional
derivatives of
Z[J]
evaluated at
J=0
. Choosing the above form of

Z[J]
we see that,

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\{Q(t_{1})Q(t_{2})\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-i\hbar)^{2}\frac{\delta^{2}\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}}{\delta J(t_{1})\delta J(t_{2})}\bigg|_{J=0}

(20.34)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-i\hbar)^{2}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(t_{1})}\left\{\frac{i}{2\hbar}2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt^{\prime}G(t_{2}-t_{1})J(t^{\prime})\times\right.

\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt\left.exp\Big(\frac{i}{2\hbar}\int\int JGJ\Big)\right\}\bigg|_{J=0}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-i\hbar)^{2}(i/\hbar)G(t_{2}-t_{1})=-i\hbar G(t_{2}-t_{1}).

(20.35)

The derivative of the
e^{\int JGJ}
does not contribute in the limit of

J=0
. Taking one more derivative to get the three point function, we
have

\displaystyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J_{1}}\frac{\delta}{\delta J_{2}}\left\{\frac{i}{\hbar}\int dtG(t_{3}-t)J(t)\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}\right\}~~=\hskip 199.16928pt

\displaystyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J_{1}}\left\{\frac{i}{\hbar}G(t_{3}-t_{2})\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}+\frac{i}{\hbar}\int dt\ G(t_{3}-t)J(t)\cdot\frac{i}{\hbar}\int dt^{\prime}\ G(t_{2}-t^{\prime})J(t^{\prime})\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}\right\}

\displaystyle~=~0+0~=0~\hskip 28.45274pt\because~\mbox{there is always a
factor of $J$ which kills the term at $J=0$.}

For 4 derivatives, we will have,

\displaystyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J_{0}}\bigg\{\frac{i}{\hbar}G(t_{3}-t_{2})\cdot\frac{i}{\hbar}\int dtG(t_{1}-t)J(t)\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}+\hskip 170.71652pt

\displaystyle\frac{i}{\hbar}G(t_{3}-t_{1})\cdot\frac{i}{\hbar}\int dtG(t_{2}-t)J(t)\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}+\hskip 170.71652pt

\displaystyle\frac{i}{\hbar}\int dtG(t_{3}-t)J(t)\cdot\frac{i}{\hbar}G(t_{2}-t_{1})\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}+\hskip 170.71652pt

\displaystyle\Big(\frac{i}{\hbar}\Big)^{3}\int dtG(t_{3}-t)J(t)\cdot\int dt^{\prime}G(t_{2}-t^{\prime})J(t^{\prime})\cdot\int dt^{\prime\prime}G(t_{1}-t^{\prime\prime})J(t^{\prime\prime})\cdot\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}\bigg\}

Carrying out the
J_{0}
differentiation and putting
J=0
, only the first
3 terms contribute since they have a single factor of
J(t)
. For a
4-point function, this is multiplied by
(-i\hbar)^{4}
and we get,

\boxed{\langle 0|T\{Q(t_{0})Q(t_{1})Q(t_{2})Q(t_{3})\}|0\rangle=(-i\hbar)^{2}\Big\{G_{01}G_{23}+G_{02}G_{31}+G_{03}G_{12}\Big\}~,~G_{ij}\leftrightarrow G(t_{i}-t_{i})\ .}

(20.36)

We recognize this as the same pattern seen in the vacuum expectation
value calculation using the Wick’s theorem. Indeed, the quantum field
theory Wick’s theorem shows up here just as a result of the functional
differentiation.

We now have all the definitions, notations and pattern of computation
needed in the field theory generalization.

21
Path Integrals in Quantum Field Theory

We consider the path integral formulation of a field theory,
specifically a scalar field theory. While discussing the field as a
dynamical system, we had already noted that the notation

\phi(t,\vec{x})
refers to infinitely many degrees of freedom labeled
by
\vec{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}
(for us). Thus we could view

\phi(t,\vec{x})
as
\phi_{\vec{x}}(t)
and draw analogy with
q_{i}(t)
.
Each of these degrees of freedom can be quantized a la path integral
exactly as the single degree of freedom discussed before. In place of

\int\mathpzc{Dq}(t)\xrightarrow[T=\epsilon N]{}\int\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}{\textstyle\frac{dq_{k}}{C(\epsilon)}}
, we now have

\int\mathpzc{D}\phi(x)\xrightarrow[T=\epsilon N]{}\int\prod_{\vec{x}\in\Sigma}\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}d\phi_{\vec{x},k}
. We have dropped the

C(\epsilon)
which will be subsumed in the overall normalization
constant. The action for the field theory is as the usual one. Thus, the
vacuum-to-vacuum transition amplitude in presence of a source is denoted
as,

\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}:=\int\mathpzc{D}\phi exp\frac{i}{\hbar}\int d^{4}x\Big\{\mathcal{L}(\phi,\partial_{\mu}\phi)+J(x)\phi(x)\Big\}~=:~Z[J]

(21.1)

The ‘paths’ implicit in the measure
\mathpzc{D}\phi
are of course paths in
the configuration space of the field i.e. the space of all

\phi(\vec{x})
at any fixed
t
. A path itself connects

\phi_{1}(\vec{x},t_{1})
to
\phi_{2}(\vec{x},t_{2}),\ \forall\ \vec{x}
. The
paths are
not
paths in the space-time.

For the Lagrangian density
\mathcal{L}
, we write
\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{0}+\mathcal{L}_{1}
, with
\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{0}:=-{\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\partial^{\mu}\phi\partial_{\mu}\phi-{\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}m^{2}\phi^{2}.}
The
m^{2}
has
-i\epsilon
implicit, in
anticipation. The
\mathcal{L}_{1}
will typically involve interaction
terms, polynomials in
\phi
such as
g_{3}\phi^{2}(x)+g_{4}\phi^{4}(x)\dots
etc. Consider

Z_{0}[J]:=\int\mathpzc{D\phi}\ exp\Big\{\frac{i}{\hbar}\int d^{4}x(\mathcal{L}_{0}+J(x)\phi(x))\Big\}\ .

We go to the momentum space as in the case of the single particle.

Let
\tilde{\phi}(k):=\int d^{4}xe^{-ik\cdot x}\phi(x)\leftrightarrow\phi(x)=\int{\textstyle\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}}e^{ik\cdot x}\tilde{\phi}(k)
, with

k\cdot x:=-k^{0}x^{0}+\vec{k}\cdot\vec{x}
and
k^{0}
is the integration
variable in
d^{4}k
and not
k_{0}
. Substituting in the action and doing
the
d^{4}x
integration gives,

S_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\left[-\tilde{\phi}(k)(k^{2}+m^{2})\tilde{\phi}(-k)+\tilde{J}(k)\tilde{\phi}(-k)+\tilde{J}(-k)\tilde{\phi}(k)\right]

Note that
S_{0}
is
not

\int\mathpzc{L}_{0}
, but includes the source.

Define
\tilde{\phi}(k):=\tilde{\chi}(k)+{\textstyle\frac{\tilde{J}(k)}{k^{2}+m^{2}}}
. Then
\mathpzc{D\phi}=\mathpzc{D\chi}
since we
have a “constant shift transformation”. This also holds in the

\phi(x)
space. Then, as in the case of the single oscillator, we get

S_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\left[\frac{\tilde{J}(k)\tilde{J}(-k)}{k^{2}+m^{2}}-\tilde{\chi}(k)(k^{2}+m^{2})\tilde{\chi}(-k)\right]\ .

The path integral
\int\mathpzc{D\chi}
, just gives a factor independent of

\tilde{J}
, namely
\langle 0|0\rangle_{J=0}=1
and we write,

\boxed{\hbar=1\ \mbox{from now on}}
,

\displaystyle\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle Z_{0}[J]=exp\left[i\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\frac{\tilde{J}(k)\tilde{J}(-k)}{k^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}\right\}\right]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle exp\left\{i\int d^{4}x\int d^{4}x^{\prime}\ \frac{1}{2}J(x)\Delta(x-x^{\prime})J(x^{\prime})\right\}~~\mbox{where,}

\displaystyle\Delta(x-x^{\prime})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\ \frac{e^{ik\cdot(x-x^{\prime})}}{k^{2}+m^{2}-i\epsilon}~~,~~\mbox{(Feynman
propagator)}

Note that the Feynman propagator arose because of the
-i\epsilon

included in the mass term in the
\mathpzc{L}
.

As discussed for the oscillator, we get

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\left\{\phi(x_{1})\phi(x_{2})\right\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-i)\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{1})}\cdot(-i)\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{2})}\cdot Z_{0}[J]\Big|_{J=0}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(-i)\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{1})}\left\{Z_{0}[J]\cdot\int\Delta(x^{\prime}-x_{2})J(x^{\prime})d^{4}x^{\prime}\right\}(-i)(i)\Big|_{J=0}~\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\left\{\phi(x_{1})\phi(x_{2})\right\}|0\rangle

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-i\Delta(x_{1}-x_{2})\ .

Exactly as for the Oscillator, we get

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\left\{\phi(x_{1})\phi(x_{2})\phi(x_{3})\phi(x_{4})0\right\}|0\rangle=\hskip 256.0748pt

\displaystyle(-i)^{2}\Big[\Delta(x_{1}-x_{2})\delta(x_{3}-x_{4})+\Delta(x_{1}-x_{3})\delta(x_{2}-x_{4})+\Delta(x_{1}-x_{4})\delta(x_{2}-x_{3})\Big]

which easily generalizes to,

\displaystyle\langle 0|T\left\{\phi(x_{1})\dots\phi(x_{2n})\right\}|0\rangle=\hskip 256.0748pt

\displaystyle(-i)^{n}\Big[\sum_{pairings}\Delta(x_{1}-x_{2})\delta(x_{3}-x_{4})\dots\Delta(x_{2n-1}-x_{2n})+\mbox{permutations}\Big]

This is what we had obtained as the
Wick’s theorem
.

Note:
Wick’s theorem expressed the time ordered product of
quantum fields in terms of the normal ordered product plus contractions.
The normal ordering was for all Poincare generators to ensure invariance
of the vacuum. The theorem was also proved for free fields for which we
do have Fourier decomposition.

Here too the “Wick’s theorem” is again seen for free fields. Here it
is no more than the chain rule of differentiation.

Consider now interacting fields, by which we mean
\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{0}+\mathcal{L}_{1}
. Recall that
\langle 0|Q(t)|0\rangle=\int\mathpzc{Dq}\ q(t)e^{iS}
and we can get the
q(t)
in the integrand by

{\textstyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J(t)}}S_{J}|_{J=0}
(remember
S=S_{J}|_{J=0}
).
Thus, insertion of
q(t)
’s or
\phi(x)
’s in field theory, can be
effected by
{\textstyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}}S_{J}|_{J=0}
. If we expand

e^{i\int\mathcal{L}_{1}(\phi)}=\Sigma_{n=0}^{\infty}[i\int\mathcal{L}_{1}]^{n}/n!
, then we have integrals of polynomials of the
fields which can be expressed as
{\textstyle\frac{\delta}{\delta J}}S_{J}
. The

\delta_{J}
can be taken outside of the path integration. Thus we write,

\displaystyle Z[J]

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\langle 0|0\rangle_{J}^{int}:=\int\mathpzc{D\phi}\ exp\ i\int d^{4}x\Big(\mathcal{L}_{0}(\phi)+\mathcal{L}_{1}(\phi)+J(x)\phi(x)\Big)

\displaystyle\propto

\displaystyle e^{i\mathcal{L}(-i\delta_{J(x)})}\cdot\int\mathpzc{D\phi}e^{i\int d^{4}x\{\mathcal{L}_{0}+J(x)\phi(x)\}}\hskip 56.9055pt\mbox{or,}

\displaystyle Z[J]

\displaystyle\propto

\displaystyle\left[exp\ i\int d^{4}x\mathcal{L}_{1}\left(-i\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}\right)\right]\cdot Z_{0}[J]~,~\mbox{with}

(21.2)

\displaystyle Z_{0}[J]

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle exp\Big(\frac{i}{2}\int d^{4}x\int d^{4}yJ(x)\Delta(x-y)J(y)\Big)

(21.3)

In the oscillator case, for
Z_{0}[J]
we had the
exp{\textstyle\frac{i}{2}}\int\int J\Delta J
term and a Gaussian path integral which turned out to be
equal to
Z_{0}[J=0]
. By taking the asymptotic time limits, we could
assert this to be equal to 1 since it was vacuum-to-vacuum amplitude
without any source. In presence of interactions, even with
J=0
, the
vacuum may not remain unaffected and we cannot justify
\langle 0|0\rangle^{int}_{J=0}=1
. Instead, the proportionality constant is
determined by
demanding

Z[J=0]=1
.

The prescription to compute
Z[J]
via the

e^{i\mathcal{L}_{1}(-i\delta_{J})}Z_{0}[J]
, is in effect the perturbative
prescription. Let us see how this works in an example

\mathcal{L}_{1}(\phi)=g\phi^{3}(x)/3!
. Then
Z[J]\propto e^{{\textstyle\frac{g}{6}}\delta^{3}_{J}}\cdot Z_{0}[J]
. Expand the exponential,

\displaystyle Z[J]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\sum_{v=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{v!}\left[\frac{ig}{3!}\int d^{4}x\left(-i\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}\right)^{3}\right]^{v}\times

\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\sum_{p=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{p!}\left[\frac{i}{2}\int d^{4}y\int d^{4}zJ(y)\Delta(y-z)J(z)\right]^{p}\ .

This too is a power series in
J
as is
Z_{0}[J]
, but with different
coefficients. Consider a particular term in this double sum with a fixed

v
and
p
.

\bullet
Then we have
3v
derivatives acting on
2p\ J
’s, leaving

E=(2p-3v)J
’s. Clearly,
E\geq 0
must hold and there are several
such term;

\bullet
The overall
numerical factor
associated with such a group of
terms is:

\left(\frac{ig}{3!}\right)^{v}\frac{(-i)^{3v}}{v!}\frac{(i/2)^{p}}{p!}=\frac{i^{v-3v+p}}{(3!)^{v}v!p!}g^{v}=\left(\frac{g}{3!}\right)^{v}\frac{1}{v!p!}(i)^{E+v-p}

\bullet
The
combinatorial factor
resulting from the number of ways he
derivative acts is:
3v
derivatives on
2pJ
’s give

{\textstyle\frac{(2p)!}{(2p-3v)!}}
(This is because the first derivative can act
on
2p
J’s, second on
(2p-1)
, …
(3v)^{th}
on
(2p-3v+1)
J’s.)

We can generate and keep track of the various derivatives by denoting

\begin{array}[]{lcccl}\frac{ig}{3!}\frac{\delta^{3}}{\delta J^{3}(x)}&\hskip 21.33955pt\leftrightarrow&\hskip 21.33955pt\frac{ig}{3!}&\hskip 21.33955pt\vbox{\hbox{

}}&\hskip 21.33955pt\mbox{Has $\int d^{4}y\int d^{4}z$}\ ,\end{array}

and the operation of evaluating the derivative by joining the free ends
from the ‘vertices’ to the free ends of the ‘propagator lines’ - exactly
as we represented the Wick contractions.

The number of terms with a give
v,p
is the number of ways of joining
the free ends and generating
a diagram
. Some of the diagrams may
have the identical factors associated with them For example, the
3\delta_{J}
’s at a given vertex can be permuted in joining up with the
propagator lines. This clearly gives a factor of
3!
. Likewise ends of
propagator lines gives a factor of
2!
. The diagram will look the same
if the
v
vertices are themselves permuted (the
\int d^{4}x
are dummy
variables) and this gives
v!
. Similarly the propagator lines give

p!
. Thus, all the numerical factors, except
i,g
cancel out.

Compared to the previous counting based on Wick’s theorem, we have a
double expansion and lines (pairs of
J
’s) to be contracted with the
edges of the vertices. Secondly, in the Wick’s theorem, thanks to the
normal ordering of the interaction terms, we don’t have self
contractions at the vertices (
\Delta(x,x)
propagators). In the present
approach, there is no “normal ordering” and we do get such term. Eg.

\begin{array}[c]{cl}\vbox{\hbox{
\hbox to130.63pt{\vbox to87.15pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.42638pt\lower-43.5742pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

Thus we have more diagrams and different ways of working out the total
combinatorial factor. The above bulleted points have gotten rid of all
explicit factors, but could involve an over counting. This is
compensated by
dividing
by a factor called the
symmetry
factor
. This is a geometrical problem of identifying the groups of
diagrams. Here are a couple of examples
Srednicky
.

:

We can exchange the two loops in 2 ways.
We can exchange the ends of each loop in
2\times 2
ways. Therefore the total symmetry factor is

2\cdot 2\cdot 2=8
.

:

The 3 propagators can be permuted in
3\cdot 2

ways. The 2 vertices can be exchanged in 2 ways. So the
symmetry factor is:
3!2!=12
.

A general statement and a derivation may be seen in the appendix of
Sterman’s book
Sterman
.

In the double expansion, we have terms with no
J
’s, a single
J
,

2J
’s …etc. When
J=0
is put, only the terms with no
J
survive.
These are termed as the “vacuum bubbles” and are the contributions to
the
Z[J=0]
.

A general contribution to a
given number
of left over
J
’s would
consist of product of topologically connected diagrams. Let

C_{\gamma}
denote the contribution of a particular topologically
connected diagram,
\gamma
. In a given diagram,
\Gamma
, let
\gamma

occur
n_{\gamma}
times. The symmetry factor resulting from
permutations within each
\gamma
, are included in the contribution

C_{\gamma}
. But now we can also have permutations across different,
topologically connected diagrams. Such permutations can leave the
product diagram invariant if the different copies of a given
\Gamma

are permuted as a whole. Hence, we have an additional symmetry factor of

n_{\gamma}!
by which we have to divide. A product diagram with
different
\gamma
’s thus has a symmetry factor of
\prod_{\gamma}n_{\gamma}!
.

Returning to the full
Z[J]
which we can now represent as a
contribution from a sum of diagrams
\Gamma
, each of which can have
several topologically connected
\gamma
’s with
n_{\gamma}
copies.
Hence,

\displaystyle Z[J]

\displaystyle\propto

\displaystyle\sum_{\{n_{\gamma}\}}C_{\Gamma}~\sim~\sum_{\{n_{\gamma}\}}\prod_{\gamma}\frac{(C_{\gamma})^{n_{\gamma}}}{n_{\gamma}!}~:=~\mathcal{N}\prod_{\gamma}\sum_{n_{\gamma}=0}^{\infty}\frac{(C_{\gamma})^{n_{\gamma}}}{n_{\gamma}!}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\prod_{I}exp[C_{\gamma}]=\mathcal{N}exp\Big[\sum_{\gamma}C_{\gamma}\Big]\ .

Thus,
Z[J]
is proportional to the exponential of the sum of
contributions of topologically connected diagrams. In this sum, are also
the contributions topologically connected vacuum diagrams i.e.
Z[J=0]
.
Imposing the normalization condition,
Z[J=0]=1
, gives

\boxed{\mathcal{N}\times exp(\mbox{topologically connected vacuum
bubbles})=1.}
. Hence, the normalization is trivially incorporated by
simply dropping the contributions of the vacuum diagrams and we are left
with,

\boxed{Z[J]=exp\Big[iW[J]\Big]~,~iW[J]=\sum\Big(\mbox{topologically connected diagrams.}\Big)}

(21.4)

The Green’s functions that we get from
Z[J]
, now get expressed as,

\langle 0|\phi(x)|0\rangle=-i\frac{\delta Z[J]}{\delta J(x)}\bigg|_{J=0}=\frac{\delta W[J]}{\delta J(x)}\bigg|_{J=0}~~,~~\because~\frac{1}{W[J=0]}=1.

This gives the contribution of diagrams with a single
J(x)
and gets
removed when
J=0
is put.

Similarly other Green’s functions can be expressed in terms of the
derivatives of the
W[J]
.

As an illustration of the organization of the topologically connected
diagrams in
W[J]
, consider the two point function.

\displaystyle G(x_{1},x_{2})

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle(-i)^{2}\frac{\delta^{2}}{\delta J_{1}\delta J_{2}}Z[J]\Big|_{J=0}=-i\delta_{J_{1}}\left(e^{iW}\delta_{J_{2}}W\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{iW}\left(\delta_{J_{1}}W.\delta_{J_{2}}W-i\delta^{2}_{J_{1}J_{2}}W\right)_{J=0}

\displaystyle\therefore G(x_{1},x_{2})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle G_{c}(x_{1})G_{c}(x_{2})-G_{c}(x_{1},x_{2})~~,~~\mbox{where,}

\displaystyle G_{c}(x):=\delta_{J(x)}W[J]|_{J=0}~,~G_{c}(x,y):=i\delta^{2}_{J(x)J(y)}W[J]|_{J=0}

x_{1}
G
x_{2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\underbrace{\vbox{\hbox{

The
G_{c}
denote, contributions from connected (to external points) and
topologically connected diagrams. This continues to the other
n-
point
functions, as proved by the argument leading to eqn. (
21.4
). To
conclude,

G(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})

:

\Sigma
of all connected diagrams

:

(-i)^{n}\frac{\delta^{n}}{\delta J(x_{1})\dots\delta J(x_{n})}Z[J]\bigg|_{J=0}

G_{c}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})

:

\Sigma
of topologically connected
diagrams

:

(-i)^{n-1}\frac{\delta^{n}}{\delta J(x_{1})\dots\delta J(x_{n})}W[J]\bigg|_{J=0}

n=0

:

\Sigma
of
all
vacuum diagrams

:

Z[J=0]=1

n=0

:

\Sigma
of all topologically connected

:

W[J=0]=0

vacuum diagrams

The computation of the diagrams uses the same Feynman rules that we
discussed earlier. The
Z
and
W
provide a convenient way of dealing
all the diagrams together and serve as
generating functions
for
the Greens functions.

21.1
The 1-point function: Renormalization
\leftrightarrow

normal ordering

The 1-point function of a scalar field has a distinction. Since this
represents the
\langle 0|\Phi(x)|0\rangle
, the Poincare invariance
allows this to be
a non-zero constant, say
v
. No other Lorentz
covariant field can have its vacuum expectation value to be non-zero
since there are no Lorentz invariant spinors or vectors
15
15

15

A
second rank, symmetric tensor field
can have

\langle 0|\hat{h}_{\mu\nu}(x)|0\rangle=\Lambda\eta_{\mu\nu}
. But
this typically arises only when gravity is included.
. However, if we
want the quanta exchanged during interactions to have the appropriate
quantum numbers, the vacuum should
not have any quantum numbers
.
As noted in the discussion of uniqueness of vacuum, a non-unique vacuum
would have to carry non-trivial representation labels of the symmetry
group which will add to the labels of the exchanged quanta.
Consequently, we must have a unique vacuum and then, by the mode
expansion of the quantum field, its expectation value must vanish.
Does our path integral definition of
n-
point function satisfy this
property?

Consider computation of the 1-point function in the
(\phi)^{3}_{n}
theory.
Notice that topologically disconnected diagrams contributing to the

1-
point function can only be the vacuum bubbles giving a
multiplicative contribution of
1
. So we can limit to only
topologically connected diagrams. Furthermore, if we have
1PR

diagrams, their contribution is again of a product form:

(1PI)\times\Delta(x-y)\times(1PI)\times\Delta(z-w)\times(1PI)\cdots
.
Hence it suffices to consider only the
1PI
diagrams. Thus we have,
